session.title: Monday plenary programme

title: Address from the TDWG Chair: highlights of the year and TDWG at a crossroads

programme.title: Address from TDWG Chair
programme.session: Monday plenary programme (monday-plenary)

actual.identification_notes: Speaker introduces himself as 'Dave Bloom ... the chair of TADWIG' (ASR renders TDWG as 'TADWIG'/'TIDWEG'). Preceded by a short announcement about game night and thanking volunteer 'Stan' (placed in unassigned). Talk ended at roughly 10:13 local time against a 9:45 scheduled end because the welcome and housekeeping ran first. The grant name in the transcript sounds like 'Bicycle AI' in ASR and remains unresolved.

summary: TDWG chair David Bloom reviewed the past year's highlights: ratification of the Darwin Core Data Package, progress of the Biodiversity Data Quality and MIDS standards toward public review, a completed Darwin Core public review affecting the Humboldt and new mineralogy extensions, a new Image Quality and AI Readiness task group, Community Support Fund awards, Living Data 2025 in Bogotá, and a new editor-in-chief for the BISS journal. He then traced TDWG's history from a taxonomy-focused group in the 1980s, through the occurrence-data and portal era, to a new focus on linked open data. He set out current challenges (documentation and archives, participation, volunteer succession, sustainable standards maintenance, finances, and AI) and appealed to attendees to get involved.
one_line_takeaway: TDWG has had a productive year, but a growing, more diverse community and the rise of AI put it at a crossroads that needs more volunteers, better documentation and more sustainable maintenance and funding.
why_it_matters: It is the organisation's own view of where its standards work stands and what it needs next. It flags upcoming public reviews, new groups and elections that community members can join, and names the structural risks: volunteer burnout, maintenance load and documentation debt.
key_points: The Darwin Core Data Package (DwC-DP) has been ratified after a multi-year effort led largely by the Darwin Core Maintenance Group.
The Biodiversity Data Quality Interest Group's standard is heading toward public review, and the Minimum Information about a Digital Specimen (MIDS) standard is about to enter public review.
The second Darwin Core public review of the year passed all proposals, leading to significant changes to the Humboldt extension and a new mineralogy extension (pending Executive Committee approval).

A new Image Quality and AI Readiness task group has formed. The TDWG Community Support Fund made four awards totalling just over US$15,000 (mineralogy, sensitive species, invasive species in environmental samples, eDNA).
Living Data 2025 in Bogotá had more than 900 participants, over 700 of them in person.
BISS (Biodiversity Information Science and Standards, hosted by Pensoft) has a new editor-in-chief and will expand to peer-reviewed papers. Discounted fees for TDWG members are being considered.
TDWG's focus has moved from taxonomy/names (1980s) to primary occurrence data and portals such as GBIF and VertNet (2000s, both marking 25 years), and now to linked open data and data packages.

Challenges named: archival and online documentation (a new task group will review documentation tools and processes), participation (Executive Committee elections, subcommittees, working groups), succession in an all-volunteer organisation, a maintenance load that now needs four or five people per standard, finances (a new donate button), and AI.
Bloom argued that the use of AI makes TDWG's work even more important.

standards: Minimum Information about a Digital Specimen (MIDS)
questions: How should TDWG handle archival documents and the online documentation of standards so they reach a wider audience?
How can standards be maintained more equitably and sustainably together with partners such as GBIF and OBIS?
What does AI mean for TDWG's community and how quickly will it change how the community works?

Talk to Executive Committee members, subcommittee chairs and group conveners during the week to find a role.
Consider BISS for peer-reviewed papers. Volunteer as co-editor for this year's collection of extended abstracts.
Use the week to think about how AI affects your own work and your institutions.
future_work: A new task group will soon launch to review TDWG's documentation tools and processes.
MIDS and the Biodiversity Data Quality standard are to enter public review.
DiSSCo has a GBIF capacity enhancement grant to plan mapping its data to DwC-DP. TDWG awaits an EU decision on a recent grant submission.

TDWG will explore broader financial support through partnerships and giving.

session.title: Monday plenary programme

title: AI for Nature at Large Scale and High Resolution

programme.title: AI for Nature at Large Scale and High Resolution
programme.session: Monday plenary programme (monday-plenary)
programme.abstract:
Computation has fundamentally changed the way we study nature. New data collection technologies, such as GPS, high-definition cameras, autonomous vehicles under water, on the ground, and in the air, genotyping, acoustic sensors, and crowdsourcing, are generating data about life on the planet that are orders of magnitude richer than any previously collected. Yet, our ability to extract insight from these data lags substantially behind our ability to collect it.

The talk will discuss both recent advances and potential opportunities in AI that can turn these data into high resolution information source about living organisms, enabling scientific inquiry, conservation, and policy decisions. We will also address the challenges in scaling biodiversity research and action with AI, particularly in AI-ready cyber-and data infrastructures, as well as complex multimodal, multi-sensor, multi-scale data analysis, modeling, and visualizations.

speakers.name: Tanya Berger-Wolf
speakers.affiliation: The Ohio State University (Translational Data Analytics Institute; Imageomics Institute; AI and Biodiversity Change (ABC) Global Center)

actual.identification_notes: Introduced by David Bloom as Dr. Tanya Berger-Wolf; the content matches the keynote abstract. ASR errors include 'Image Genomics' for Imageomics, 'Hilmar Labbé' for Hilmar Lapp, 'Yasin Bakkies' for Yasin Bakiş and 'ADWIC' for TDWG. The keynote ran about 44 minutes plus about 7 minutes of Q&A, ending around 01:35 in the recording; the break was moved to 11:05.

summary: Berger-Wolf argued that computation does not change the scientific method but lets scientists 'look at more things, more carefully', at larger scale and higher resolution. Biodiversity data, however, are heavily biased toward where wealthy people are, and AI methods tuned to benchmarks tend to learn more about what we already know. She presented Imageomics work that builds biological knowledge into machine learning. The examples were BioCLIP (a foundation model trained on 214 million images of about a million species captioned with full taxonomy), biologically meaningful interpretability with attention and sparse autoencoders, automated trait measurement of NEON ground beetles, and drone-based behaviour data. She then showed that AI agents fail mainly at finding and preparing data rather than at analysis. She ended on data readiness: the FAIR for AI checklist and agent, sovereign data supply chains, and infrastructure that returns value to primary data collectors.
one_line_takeaway: AI can help fill biodiversity knowledge shortfalls only if biological knowledge is built into the models and the data infrastructure is FAIR for AI and returns value to primary data collectors, because 'there is no AI without data'.
why_it_matters: The keynote connects state-of-the-art machine learning to TDWG's core business. Its evidence that AI agents fail mostly at data discovery, API construction and data preparation, rather than at analysis, argues that standards, metadata and provenance are the bottleneck for AI in biodiversity science. It also calls for provenance and attribution to flow back from ML-derived products to the original data providers.
key_points: Following Poincaré's Science and Method, computation lets scientists look at more things more carefully, but data remain strongly skewed geographically, taxonomically and by wealth. Observations track where rich people are, not where biodiversity is.

Estimated species numbers have risen to roughly 30-50 million while only about two million (perhaps 1.5 million unique) are named, so the Linnean shortfall is growing. A recent prospective paper maps each biodiversity shortfall to AI research that could help fill it.
'AI' here means mostly (about 99%) machine learning, not LLMs. Benchmark-driven ML improves performance on the data-rich bulk of skewed distributions rather than the long tail where discovery lies.

BioCLIP was trained on about 214 million images of about a million species (sources include EOL, GBIF, iNaturalist, FathomNet and BIOSCAN), simply captioned with full taxonomic strings. It learns taxonomy implicitly and can classify at any rank.

BioCLIP's embedding space holds biology it was never given: clusters for life stage, sex and disease, a Darwin's finch axis aligned with beak size, and a freshwater versus marine split in fish. Similarity search surfaces diseased plants and pollinator interactions.

Biologically meaningful interpretability: attention-based part highlighting, and sparse autoencoders that manipulate features to show what about a trait (for example the shape of a house sparrow's beak) distinguishes a species. This supports trait discovery, dichotomous keys and separating mimic species.

An imaging pipeline for NEON ground-beetle bycatch segments specimens and measures landmark distances more accurately than calipers. The traits are being tested as predictors of drought and soil moisture.
Drone-based systems collect population-level behaviour and movement data. This work motivates FAIR-for-AI drone data standards.

In a benchmark of about 300 data-driven ecological questions split into four stages (find data, extract/API, organise, analyse), AI agents failed badly at building the right API and preparing data. With data and method given they reached about 60% accuracy at a cost of thousands of dollars in tokens.

'AI-ready' is question-specific. FAIR for AI is the general layer between FAIR and task-specific readiness. A community-built FAIR for AI checklist (90+ criteria) is assessed by an agent that gives constructive feedback.

Data flow one way toward aggregators. ML-derived improvements (bounding boxes, deduplication, updated taxonomy, provenance) should flow back to primary data providers through lightweight AI-ready infrastructure layered on existing repositories.
themes_raw: AI-ready and FAIR for AI data
AI agents for scientific data analysis
data provenance and value return to primary data collectors

entities.name: AI and Biodiversity Change (ABC) Global Center
ICICLE (NSF AI Institute for Intelligent Cyberinfrastructure with Computational Learning in the Environment)
Max Planck Institute of Animal Behavior

datasets: BioCLIP training data (about 214 million images, about 1 million species)
Benchmark of about 300 data-driven ecological questions
methods: taxonomic-string captioning for contrastive foundation-model training
image segmentation and landmark-based trait measurement
AI agent evaluation across a staged scientific workflow
questions: How do we build data infrastructure and standards that link multi-scale, multi-modal data and send ML-derived value back to primary data sources?
Should the implicit knowledge that AI agents currently cannot access be made machine-accessible?
How can ML benchmarks be redesigned so the ML community works on biologically meaningful problems and the long tail?

notable_claims.claim: Biodiversity observations correlate with average income per unit area: we have data where rich humans are, not where nature is.
Estimated species numbers have jumped to about 30-50 million while only about two million are named, so the Linnean shortfall is growing.
BioCLIP 2 was trained on about 214 million images of about a million species, roughly half of all named species.
Within BioCLIP's representation space, Darwin's finches align along a dimension corresponding to beak size, although no beak-size information was given to the model.
Image-based landmark measurement of ground beetles is more accurate than measuring with calipers.
AI agents failed badly at constructing the right API to get data. This reflects data readiness rather than agent ability.
Given the data and analysis method, AI agents answered to about 60% accuracy at a cost of thousands of dollars in tokens.
The FAIR for AI checklist now has more than 90 categories/criteria, so an agent was built to perform the assessment.

recommendations: Publish ground-truthed datasets with well-defined, biologically relevant benchmark tasks to engage the ML community.
Make aggregators such as GBIF, NEON and iNaturalist FAIR for AI, with annotations attached to the original datasets.
Return ML-derived products (bounding boxes, deduplication flags, updated names, provenance) to primary data providers.
Read the Latin American and Caribbean white paper on sovereign data supply chains.
results_findings: BioCLIP learns taxonomy implicitly and supports classification at any taxonomic level without being trained for classification.
BioCLIP embeddings separate life stages, sexes and disease states, and encode traits such as finch beak size and fish habitat type.
Sparse-autoencoder feature manipulation showed that a house sparrow's distinctiveness lies in a thicker, larger, wider beak.
Image-based beetle trait measurements beat calipers for accuracy.
AI agents' pass rate rises with token spend, but they fail mainly at API construction and data preparation.
limitations: AI agent benchmarking used state-of-the-art agents from about four months earlier; the state of the art has since changed.
Much implicit knowledge and metadata needed to prepare data is not accessible to AI agents.
ML-ready datasets published in ML venues often lose their connection to, and attribution of, the primary data.
Definitions of FAIR for AI and related standards are still being debated.
future_work: Re-running beetle-community drought prediction with precise trait measurements to test soil-moisture hypotheses.
Expanding FAIR for AI drone data standards.
Integrating provenance and name-reconciliation links built on GBIF data into GBIF and sending them back to data providers.
Adapting BioCLIP-like approaches to paleontological collections, which need multimodal (3D, DNA, chemical) models.
examples_case_studies: Flagging new moth species with BioCLIP (David Rolnick, McGill, with the Montreal Insectarium)
INQUIRE: finding trophic interactions in iNaturalist data (Sara Beery)
NEON ground-beetle bycatch trait pipeline
Drone behaviour studies in Kenya (Jenna Kline)
Multi-sensor instrumentation experiment at The Wilds, Ohio
Diseased milkweed and moth-pollinator similarity searches

q_and_a.question: Could the BioCLIP approach be extended to paleontological collections?
q_and_a.answer_summary: Probably yes; GBIF already holds some bone and skeletal material, but data are needed. Paleo is strongly multimodal (often 3D images, DNA, chemistry, single teeth), so its models differ somewhat, though a connection is possible.

q_and_a.question: Where should curated, AI-ready biodiversity datasets be deployed (for example Kaggle or OpenML, with Croissant and provenance metadata) so they do not degrade among low-quality data?
q_and_a.answer_summary: She distinguished FAIR for AI (a property of the source dataset, with annotations kept on the original) from FAIR4ML/model-ready copies, which lose provenance and attribution. The goal is not new repositories but a lightweight AI-ready layer over existing infrastructure such as GBIF that keeps provenance chains and returns derived products (bounding boxes, deduplication, updated names) to primary providers.

representative_excerpt.text: So the goal is not to create new repositories of any kind, but to create a data infrastructure that amends existing one and create kind of a relatively lightweight AI-enabled and AI-ready infrastructure on top of it that brings value all the way up and down the data chain.

notable_moments.description: Poincaré's Science and Method: computation lets scientists look at more things, more carefully.
Geographic and income bias in GBIF, iNaturalist and eBird data.
How BioCLIP was built by captioning images with full taxonomy.
Emergent biological structure in BioCLIP's embedding space (life stages, sex, disease, finch beak size).
Sparse autoencoders showing what about a house sparrow's beak makes it distinctive.
AI agent benchmark: agents fail at data discovery and preparation, not at analysis.
'There is no AI without data': FAIR for AI and returning value to primary data collectors.
Q&A on where AI-ready datasets should live and how to keep provenance.

programme_match.notes: Scheduled 9:45-10:30 AM. It actually started about 10:15 and ran to about 11:05 including Q&A, so the coffee break was pushed back and the next session announced for 11:05.

session.title: Monday plenary programme

title: Sámi perspectives on biodiversity data governance: when biodiversity data travel, does their governance travel with them?

programme.title: Sámi perspectives on biodiversity Data Governance and more inclusive Data Standards
programme.session: Monday plenary programme (monday-plenary)
programme.abstract:
As more biodiversity data become available through global platforms such as GBIF, there is a growing need to consider how Indigenous rights, traditional knowledge, and community interests are reflected in these systems. For Sámi communities, biodiversity data are often closely connected to Sámi knowledge, traditional land use, livelihoods, and relationships with nature. This presentation introduces ideas behind a proposed Sámi-hosted biodiversity data portal and discusses how Local Contexts tags and labels might be used to make Sámi interests and connections to data more visible. Could these tools help provide information about provenance, cultural significance, appropriate use, and community expectations when or whether data are shared and reused?

The presentation will explore whether the CARE Data Maturity Model can provide a useful framework for assessing and guiding Sámi biodiversity data governance. Do their indicators related to collective benefit, control, ownership, and ethics reflect Sámi realities, or is there a need for additional approaches? We apply the most updated and transdisciplinary Sámi ethical guidelines as guiding principles for the project.

Finally, the presentation will discuss data rematriation and the importance of building Sámi-controlled archives, repositories, and data infrastructures. Returning data to communities is not only about access, but also about creating the capacity and governance needed to manage and use data in ways that benefit Saami communities.

The aim is to start a conversation about how these tools can support Sámi data governance in practice.

speakers.name: Máret J. Heatta
speakers.affiliation: Tromsø (Assistant Professor; introduced as part of the CARE task group)

actual.identification_notes: Introduced by Dag (ASR: 'Dag Andersen', likely Dag Endresen, GBIF Norway) as 'Marit Hetta' from Tromsø; the chair later calls her 'Mara'. Topic (Sámi biodiversity data governance, CARE, GBIF Indigenous data governance task group) matches event-006. The talk centred on a lichen monitoring case study, UNDRIP, CARE/FAIR, GIDA Sápmi, SODA and the CARE Data Maturity Model; the Sámi-hosted portal from the abstract was not described and Local Contexts labels and data rematriation were only touched on briefly. No Q&A due to time.

summary: Máret Heatta, a Sámi biologist, uses lichen monitoring data she helped collect on NINA permanent plots on the Finnmark Plateau in 2005 as a thought experiment for Indigenous data governance. She shows how an apparently simple lichen occurrence record is also information about Sámi reindeer winter grazing lands, and how a report finding of increased lichen cover became a newspaper headline of 'better grazing' without reindeer herders' knowledge of snow, ice and access. She grounds Indigenous data sovereignty in UNDRIP and self-determination, contrasts FAIR with CARE, and surveys Sámi and international initiatives (GIDA Sápmi, the 2023 Tromsø conference, SODA, Finnish Sámi research ethics guidelines, IEEE 2890-2025, the GBIF Indigenous data governance task group, Māori data infrastructure), closing with questions for biodiversity infrastructures about existing, reused and newly collected data.
one_line_takeaway: Biodiversity data about lands, ecosystems and species can be Indigenous data, so infrastructures must ask whether context, authority and responsibilities travel with the data as FAIR makes them easier to reuse.
why_it_matters: For GBIF and TDWG, the talk challenges the assumption that species occurrence data are neutral and 'not about people', and sets out concrete questions (recognising the significance of existing data, keeping context attached on reuse, building CARE in at collection) that the GBIF Indigenous data governance task group and standards such as Local Contexts labels and IEEE 2890 are starting to address.
key_points: The same lichen occurrence record is an occurrence for an infrastructure, ecological evidence for a researcher, land-use evidence for a planning authority, and pasture information for a reindeer herder.

Indigenous data include data about individuals, about collectives, and about non-human relations (land, water, ecosystems, plants, animals); biodiversity data need not mention a Sámi person to be relevant to Indigenous data governance.
Indigenous data sovereignty begins with rights and self-determination (UNDRIP, especially Articles 11-13), not with data; Indigenous data governance is putting that authority into practice.
Two dimensions: data for governance (access to data for own decision-making) and governance of data (authority over how data are governed).

FAIR assessment can largely be a technical exercise, whereas CARE requires engagement with people across the whole data lifecycle; technically reusable is not the same as appropriate or ethical reuse.

The NINA report's measured increase in lichen cover and thickness was communicated publicly as 'better grazing', although grazing conditions for herders also depend on snow, ice, access and reindeer land use; more lichen does not by itself mean better grazing.
Sámi historical experience of being researched, including racial biology and the extraction of remains and objects, explains caution towards data sharing; trust must be earned, not requested.

Sámi and international developments are moving from principles to practice: GIDA Sápmi (2021), the 2023 Tromsø conference on Sámi research data governance, the 2024 Finnish Sámi research ethics guidelines, the Sámi Council's SODA principles, IEEE 2890-2025 on provenance of Indigenous peoples' data, the GBIF Indigenous data governance task group (2025), guidelines for Indigenous data in scholarly publishing, and Māori-controlled data storage.
The CARE Data Maturity Model is presented as an iterative way to operationalise CARE rather than something done at the end of a project.

For infrastructures such as GBIF there are three situations: existing data that may have Sámi significance, reuse of those data after aggregation, and new data collection where CARE can be designed in from the start.

Expert Ethical Committee for Sámi Health Research
United Nations Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples (UNDRIP)

standards: CARE Principles for Indigenous Data Governance
Sámi Ownership and Data Access (SODA) principles
Ethical guidelines for research involving the Sámi people in Finland (2024)
datasets: NINA permanent monitoring plots in reindeer winter grazing areas, Finnmark Plateau (1998, 2005)
questions: Where does biodiversity data end and Indigenous data begin?
How do we recognise when apparently ordinary biodiversity data already in GBIF have particular significance for Sámi communities?
Can relevant context, provenance and governance information remain connected to data as they are aggregated, downloaded and reused?
Whose knowledge is included in interpreting data, and who gets to define what findings mean?
When biodiversity data travel, does their governance travel with them?

notable_claims.claim: Across the monitoring plots, average lichen cover increased from about 18% in 1998 to 28% in 2005 and average lichen thickness from 22 to 28 mm, with considerable differences between areas.
Biodiversity data do not have to contain information about a Sámi person to be relevant for Indigenous data governance; this is the most important point for biodiversity infrastructures.
Public communication turned measured lichen increases into 'better grazing', but lichen amount alone cannot determine grazing conditions, which depend on snow, ice, access and herders' knowledge.
Assessing FAIR can largely be a technical exercise, but CARE cannot be addressed by looking only at the dataset; it requires engagement with people throughout the data lifecycle.
In 2025 GBIF established an Indigenous data governance task group examining how CARE can be supported in the GBIF network, including Local Contexts labels and notices; the work is ongoing.

recommendations: Consider CARE throughout the data lifecycle, from the research question and data collection to sharing and future reuse, rather than only at publication.
Build trust through meaningful participation, transparency, relationships, accountability and a say in what happens to data after collection.
For new data collection, decide on participation, governance arrangements, data management plans and access/reuse protocols at the design stage.
For existing data, recognise and reconnect Indigenous context, potentially using mechanisms such as Local Contexts labels.
future_work: The GBIF Indigenous data governance task group's work on Local Contexts labels/notices and keeping Indigenous context connected to biodiversity data is ongoing.
examples_case_studies: Lichen monitoring on NINA permanent plots in Sámi reindeer winter grazing areas on the Finnmark Plateau (1998 and 2005)
Newspaper headline 'Better grazing on Finnmarksvidda' derived from the NINA report
First international conference on Sámi research data governance, Tromsø, January 2023
Māori-owned data storage network in Aotearoa New Zealand

representative_excerpt.text: So making data technically reusable is not the same thing as making their reuse appropriate or ethical.

notable_moments.description: One lichen record viewed from four perspectives: infrastructure, researcher, planning authority, reindeer herder.
What counts as Indigenous data: individuals, collectives and non-human relations.
How 'more lichen' became the headline 'better grazing' and the knowledge gap this reveals.
Three situations for GBIF-type infrastructures: existing data, reused data, new data collection.
Closing question: when biodiversity data travel, does their governance travel with them?

session.title: Monday plenary programme

title: From biodiversity data to knowledge in the age of AI: where do ontologies and standards fit?

programme.title: From biodiversity data to knowledge in the age of AI: Where do ontologies and standards fit?
programme.session: Monday plenary programme (monday-plenary)
programme.abstract:
Data - specimens and collections, human-and sensor-mediated observations, images, sequences, traits, and environmental measurements - provide the raw material for biodiversity informatics and broader life sciences, yet they come with questions: What do our data mean? Which concepts are equivalent, related, or distinct? How do we represent context, provenance, uncertainty, and evidence? As new computational systems are applied to biodiversity data, a new question becomes increasingly visible and urgent: How do we support discovery and reuse without allowing fluent answers or plausible connections to obscure ambiguity, erase complexity, or reinforce errors? For four decades, TDWG has helped build the standards, ontologies, identifiers, metadata practices, and community agreements that make biodiversity data valuable. These are the same tools we need to create AI-ready biodiversity data.

Working across plant science, ontology development, and biomedical data management has reinforced one enduring lesson: the hardest data problems are rarely technical. They are problems of meaning, context, trust, and governance. AI does not eliminate these challenges-it magnifies them. Ontologies, standards, and community governance provide the shared semantic foundation that enables both people and machines to interpret data responsibly, transparently, and at scale. In an era when machines can generate answers faster than we can evaluate them, our greatest opportunity is not simply to build smarter AI, but to build richer, more trustworthy knowledge. The future of biodiversity informatics will depend not only on the intelligence of our algorithms, but on the quality of the shared knowledge infrastructure we create.

speakers.name: Ramona Walls
speakers.affiliation: Data Collaboration Center, Critical Path Institute (C-Path), Tucson, Arizona

actual.identification_notes: Introduced by name by the chair (Javier); title and content match event-007. ASR renders TDWG as 'TADWIG'/'TABB' and C-Path as 'CPATH'/'Seapath'; 'RDS resource description format' is RDF; 'SSLM' is an unclear standard name the speaker could not recall. Started a few minutes late after a slide-video playback problem; no Q&A due to time.

summary: Ramona Walls, now leading the Data Collaboration Center at C-Path in the biomedical regulatory world, argues that the path from observation to data to evidence to knowledge depends on meaning, trust (provenance, context) and relevance ('context of use'). Using the Information Artifact Ontology's definition of data, examples such as a feather versus a paw print as evidence, and DNA analysis of 'Yeti' specimens, she asks whether AI generates data and knowledge, concluding that it generates data and candidate knowledge that only becomes knowledge when supported by trusted evidence. She stresses the roles of standards bodies, governance ('good governance makes altruism possible') and ontologies (Plant Phenology Ontology, BCO), and offers biomedical models (OMOP CDM and vocabulary, FHIR, European Health Data Space, a C-Path knowledge graph) as potential lessons for biodiversity, concluding that TDWG builds the infrastructure that turns data into evidence.
one_line_takeaway: AI can generate data and candidate knowledge, but only standards, ontologies, provenance and governance let data become trusted evidence and therefore knowledge, which is why TDWG matters more than ever.
why_it_matters: It reframes TDWG's standards and ontology work as infrastructure for evidence generation in an AI era, and brings an outside perspective from biomedical regulation, where independent, long-lived standards bodies and portable governance determine what regulators will trust.
key_points: Data are the result of an observation or measurement, almost always a sample, and are intended to represent the truth; this aligns with the Information Artifact Ontology definition of a data entity as a subclass of information content entity.
The knowledge pyramid places information above data, the opposite of IAO's hierarchy, illustrating that how terms are defined determines how entities are understood within a worldview.
Transforming data into knowledge requires meaning, trust (provenance, context) and relevance (context of use), which together produce evidence.
Different kinds of data carry different strengths of evidence (a feather versus a paw print).

AI generates data (text, images, synthetic data, predictions, classifications, inferred values) but not new empirical observations; it reproduces knowledge and creates candidate knowledge, which becomes knowledge only when supported by trusted evidence.
Secondary reuse of data is the only way to scale inquiry, so collectors' minimal notes are insufficient without standards and context.
Regulators such as the FDA trust international, independent, long-lived standards organisations rather than individual academic ontology projects; TDWG (since 1985) plays that role for biodiversity.

Governance controls access and use; C-Path's strong, flexible governance lets partners share data they would share with nobody else, and portable governance travelling with data may be feasible in three to five years.
Standards and controlled vocabularies improve interoperability but have loose semantics; ontologies are human- and machine-readable artifacts that encode domain semantics.

Biomedical models (OMOP Common Data Model and vocabulary, FHIR, European Health Data Space) and C-Path's ontology-annotated knowledge graph enabling cross-dataset queries are offered as possible models for biodiversity data.
questions: Does AI generate data, and does it create knowledge?
If a model predicts the trait distribution within a species, is that evidence?
Can governance be made portable so that it travels with the data?

notable_claims.claim: Data are intended to represent the truth, which distinguishes data from arbitrary information.
Sequencing of purported Yeti specimens showed they belonged to bears and one dog, while yielding new knowledge of the evolutionary history of Himalayan bears.
AI generates data but not new empirical observations of the world, at least not yet.
AI discoveries only become knowledge if there is reason to believe they are true, which requires provenance and context of use.
Regulators do not trust a single academic-funded ontology project; they want an international, independent standards organisation that will exist in 10-20 years.
Good governance makes altruism possible: when data owners can control who sees data, the common excuse for not sharing disappears.
The Plant Phenology Ontology has been valuable for integrating phenology data from iNaturalist, the National Phenology Network, NEON and others into a global analysis.

title: Building a New Foundation for the Biodiversity Heritage Library

programme.title: Building a New Foundation for the Biodiversity Heritage Library
programme.session: Monday plenary programme (Taste of TDWG)
programme.abstract:
In 2025, the Biodiversity Heritage Library (BHL), one of the world’s most critical resources of biodiversity knowledge, was placed at risk when its long-term host, the Smithsonian Institution, announced it would cease to host BHL's administrative and technical operations. This triggered a rapid, international response and a transition to a distributed, autonomous, community-supported global consortium.

In 2026, BHL is celebrating both its 20th anniversary and its first year operating independently. This presentation provides an overview of that transition, highlighting new governance and funding approaches, diversified technical and institutional support, and the role of transparent, community-driven communication in maintaining trust and engagement during a period of significant uncertainty.

With this new foundation in place, BHL is now well positioned to advance its role within the biodiversity informatics ecosystem as core infrastructure linking literature with taxa, specimens, institutions, and datasets across centuries. This creates new opportunities to enhance the accessibility, discoverability, and interoperability of biodiversity knowledge, supporting large-scale text and image mining, knowledge graph development, persistent identifier integration, and emerging AI-driven applications.

While BHL’s long-term sustainability is not yet fully secured, it is rapidly filling with opportunities. As the opening presentation for this symposium, this talk sets the stage for the presentations that follow, framing BHL’s evolution and the possibilities ahead, and inviting participants to engage with how biodiversity literature can be transformed into data, connections, and new forms of knowledge.

Public fundraising now matters for the first time. She said BHL is only secure through 2027, described the platform modernisation now under way, and asked the community for partnerships and funding.

session.title: Monday plenary programme

title: Reducing the lag from observation to action

programme.title: Reducing the lag from observation to action
programme.session: Monday plenary programme (Taste of TDWG)
programme.abstract:
Early detection and rapid response are among the most effective strategies for reducing the impacts of invasive alien species (IAS). Yet there is often a substantial lag between observing a species in the field and that information becoming actionable.

These delays arise throughout the biodiversity data lifecycle. Observations may remain in notebooks, local databases or disconnected systems. Identification can take time, particularly for difficult taxa. Data often require manual cleaning, standardisation and validation before publication. Even after publication, fragmented infrastructures and limited interoperability can slow the translation of biodiversity data into decision-ready information.

This presentation explores the concept of “lag” in biodiversity information systems and its implications for IAS management. Using examples from IAS monitoring and alert workflows, we discuss how delays propagate from field observation to policy uptake, and how these delays weaken early-warning capacity and reduce opportunities for rapid intervention.

Addressing these problems requires action on many fronts. Shared data standards, FAIR data mobilisation, interoperable infrastructures and automated publication workflows can shorten the path from detection to visibility. At the same time, progress also depends on strengthening taxonomic capacity, improving feedback, supporting near-real-time data publication, and creating incentives that reward timely sharing rather than delayed release.

Reducing lag is not only a technical challenge, but also an institutional and cultural one. Accelerating the movement of biodiversity observations into shared and reusable systems may be one of the most practical ways biodiversity informatics can support more responsive environmental governance.

actual.identification_notes: Introduced by name by the convener; topic matches event-011.

summary: Quentin Groom looked at the delay between a biodiversity observation and the moment someone can act on it, with a focus on early detection of invasive species. He showed that recent GBIF monthly observation counts drop because data has not yet been mobilised, and used iNaturalist data to show that identifications can take months to become stable. He separated unavoidable lags from operational choices such as embargoes, unconnected systems and waiting for a dataset to be 'finished'. He then proposed a new 'Wangari Maathai shortfall' for timeliness, to add to the known biodiversity knowledge shortfalls. Q&A covered publishing data directly instead of through papers, and data valuation mechanisms.
one_line_takeaway: Timeliness is a missing biodiversity knowledge shortfall: publish soon, publish often, and improve continuously.
why_it_matters: For invasive species, pests and conservation action, data that arrives years late loses much of its value. As automated sensors take over from human observers, alert systems are needed so that unexpected species are noticed at all.
key_points: GBIF monthly observation counts fall off over the last two years because observations have not been mobilised yet, not because people stopped observing. The lag goes back further and covers tens of millions of records.
For invasive species, delays let a species establish and spread, raising the cost of eradication until it is no longer feasible.
Informal networks (emailing someone you know) work locally but do not scale.

Within about five years, data from eDNA, camera traps, acoustic sensors and automated imaging may outnumber human observations. Without a human in the loop, invasive species that are not specifically looked for will go unseen.
Lag builds up across observation, identification, digitisation, standardisation, validation, publication, aggregation, analysis, alerting and action.
In iNaturalist, bird identifications are right on day one about 50% of the time, but plants only about 10%. Identifications can take months to years to stabilise.
Some lags are real difficulties (remote fieldwork, taxonomic uncertainty). Others are operational choices (embargoes, unconnected systems, waiting for a dataset to be finished).
Groom argued for a publish, improve, update cycle instead of collect, clean, validate, analyse, then publish.

The OneSTOP project is building an open-source GBIF alert system (by Nico, of Binary Forest) for customised invasive species alerts by species and area. A Norwegian implementation exists but is not yet public.
He proposed a 'Wangari Maathai shortfall': the delay between an observation being made and the information becoming accessible for action. It would sit alongside the seven shortfalls of Hortal et al.
methods: extrapolating the growth curve to estimate publication lag

notable_claims.claim: Recent GBIF observation counts drop off because people have not yet mobilised their data, and this lag accounts for tens of millions of observations.
Within perhaps five years, observations from eDNA, camera traps, acoustic sensors and automated imaging will outnumber human-made observations.
In iNaturalist, only about 10% of plant observations get the correct identification on day one, compared with about 50% for birds.
The widely cited biodiversity shortfalls framework does not define a distinct shortfall for timeliness.

recommendations: Publish soon, publish often, and improve continuously.
Name and work on a timeliness shortfall so that it can be measured and reduced.
Treat data collection as a discipline of its own, somewhat separate from individual research questions.
results_findings: Time to stable identification in iNaturalist varies by taxon: birds are quickest, then mammals, then insects, with plants slowest.
limitations: There are few ways yet to tell users whether published data is raw, improving or checked.
examples_case_studies: Reporting a grey squirrel in Brussels through informal networks
A Norwegian GBIF alert system built by Walter Kock

q_and_a.answer_summary: Groom said it is a big question: PhD students need careers and are wary of releasing data. He suggested separating data collection from specific research questions, with data collection as a discipline of its own.

q_and_a.question: Could data-valuation mechanisms (attribution, impact, financial contributions to data sources) speed up access to data?
q_and_a.answer_summary: Groom pointed to short grant cycles and the lack of long-term funding for data-collecting infrastructures (for example NEON, and European efforts). He argued for better-focused indicators, while humans remain vital for the 'unknown unknowns' that AI tends to ignore.

representative_excerpt.text: So I would define that as a delay between the biodiversity observation being made and that information becoming accessible to be able to act on it.

title: Keeping Colliders in Physics: Rebuilding the ALA taxonomic backbone

programme.title: Keeping Colliders in Physics: Rethinking the Construction of Taxonomic Backbones and Names- matching in Large Data Aggregators
programme.session: Monday plenary programme (Taste of TDWG)
programme.abstract: A taxonomic backbone is essential to any biodiversity database displaying data in a systematic way for users. Perversely, one of the biggest challenges facing biodiversity databases is constructing, matching and displaying data using a taxonomic backbone. The Atlas of Living Australia (ALA) is a collaborative, digital, open infrastructure that pulls together biodiversity data from multiple sources. As with many countries, the taxonomy widely used in Australia is not always consistent with global views. This requires a national view of species names that government, researchers and industry can recognise. For many years, the ALA has constructed its taxonomic backbone using a process colloquially known as the "Large Taxon Collider" (LTC) that automatically combines taxonomic checklists from different sources. For the past 2 years, the ALA has done an overhaul of its taxonomic backbone, seeking to remove erroneous combinations, repetitions and align with nationally recognised taxonomic checklists centred upon the Australian Biological Resources' National Species List. This reduced the number of "accepted names" (not including synonyms) from over 500,000 to 233,000 and introduced governance. We found the LTC was valuable in combining different sources yet automation caused structural issues partly caused by the contributing taxonomic checklists themselves. This enabled us to disentangle these from issues arising from matching data to the taxonomic backbone using names-matching. The Catalogue of Life's ChecklistBank is now an essential part of our process, as are matching metrics. We have re-considered our approach to taxonomy, names, matching homonyms and how we measure success. We will discuss these issues, responses the ALA has developed so far, as well as next steps.

actual.identification_notes: Introduced as 'Pam Cameron Sluiter' and addressed as 'Cam' (ASR errors for Cameron Slatyer). Topic (large taxon collider, ALA taxonomic backbone) matches event-012. Mentions co-author Simon.

summary: Cameron Slatyer explained how the Atlas of Living Australia (ALA) rebuilt its taxonomic backbone. It had been assembled by an automated 'large taxon collider' that merged the ABRS National Species List with the Catalogue of Life, the New Zealand Organism Register and ad hoc sources. He argued that a backbone for matching data is different from a taxonomic checklist, and that a fully automated, human-free backbone is a fiction. ALA stopped the colliding: it now adds sources one at a time around the NSL, with metric checks and feedback loops through ChecklistBank and data matching. This sharply cut duplicates and unmatched records.
one_line_takeaway: Taxonomic checklists are not backbones: data aggregators need a curated single hierarchy with quality-control feedback loops, not automated merging of checklists.
why_it_matters: Names matching decides whether millions of occurrence records can be found and used, including for threatened species assessments, sensitive data handling and AI. ALA's metrics-driven approach is a practical model for other aggregators.
key_points: ALA holds more than 184 million records. Its backbone is built on the ABRS National Species List because of endemism, Australia-specific taxonomy, undescribed phrase-name species, names fixed in legislation, invasive species risk and traditional ecological knowledge.
The large taxon collider merged checklists automatically. It relied on consistent hierarchies and complete name combinations; any variance produced errors and duplicates.

Example: records of the endangered common bent-wing bat, long misidentified as Miniopterus schreibersii, did not connect to the endemic species because the misidentification was not a synonym in the NSL.
Listing a misapplied name both under the taxon it was misapplied to and in its correct place, which is common in checklists, is a disaster for data matching.
The old backbone had jumbled concepts and duplicates. More than 10 million records (10% of holdings) matched nothing, and one name had 78 variants.

A backbone needs a single hierarchy, not necessarily a fully scientifically valid one. It needs names inserted (prioritising legislated species), concepts removed or moved to avoid mis-routing records, and sometimes a commonly accepted name used over the best current name.
ChecklistBank metrics (duplicates, orphan taxa) plus data matching (higher matches and no matches) guide curation. The team extracted all 2.06 million names-match parameter combinations.
The collider code is still used, but sources are now added one at a time around the NSL core, bottom up, with feedback loops at every step.
methods: analysis of higher matches and no matches

notable_claims.claim: Automatically building an error-free, human-free taxonomic backbone is a fiction.
In the earlier backbone, more than 10 million records (10% of ALA data holdings) did not match anything, and one scientific name had 78 variations.
Accepted taxonomic units fell from 380,000 to 233,000 over three years, close to the number of named species in Australia.
More than 99% of species on Australian government lists now match current scientific names correctly.

recommendations: Treat backbones as separate from taxonomic checklists and curate them for data matching.
Use metric checks and feedback loops against real data to guide backbone improvements.
Feed data-quality issues back to checklist providers such as ABRS.
results_findings: Fewer than 1.5% of records are now affected by names matching issues.
More than 10,000 species that previously had no data now have enough data to be publicly available.
For the first time, reliable metrics on taxonomic and spatial data gaps now feed ALA's data mobilisation and digitisation priorities.
limitations: At least a third of the remaining 1.5% of unmatched data should match, and the cause is not yet known.
There is no good solution yet for pro parte synonyms; records end up under only one synonym.
Homonyms are still a persistent problem.
Handling of genetic data and of populations (groups below taxonomic resolution) on government lists needs work.
future_work: Solve pro parte synonyms, homonyms, genetic data and population-level names.
examples_case_studies: Common bent-wing bat (Miniopterus schreibersii misidentification vs endemic Miniopterus orianae)

q_and_a.question: Quentin Groom: if you could change one thing in the nomenclatural codes, what would it be?
q_and_a.answer_summary: Slatyer asked for time to think; the convener said he would answer later in the conference.

representative_excerpt.text: At a high level, our core realization is, as I've already kind of indicated, and which seems really obvious in hindsight, that taxonomic checklists are not the same as taxonomic backbones. A backbone is there to display data against the best available name, not to correctly reflect all the taxonomic decisions and pathways that have led to that best available name.

State of the old backbone: 10 million unmatched records, 78 variants of one name

title: DwC-DP Integration at GBIF

programme.title: DwC-DP Integration at GBIF
programme.session: Monday plenary programme (Taste of TDWG)
programme.abstract:
Following the public review of the Darwin Core Data Package (DwC-DP) standard, the GBIF Secretariat has committed to integrating DwC-DP into its existing data publishing infrastructure and ingestion pipeline. This talk presents recent engineering progress across four key areas:

IPT Extensions: The Integrated Publishing Toolkit (IPT) is being extended to handle data packages, enabling publishers to map and publish DwC-DP datasets through a familiar interface.

Data Validation: GBIF's validation services are being expanded to support DwC-DP, offering publishers meaningful quality metrics, including column population statistics, primary key uniqueness checks, referential integrity validation across schemas, and data type conformance reporting.

Registry and Metadata Synchronization: The GBIF Registry will automatically synchronize dataset metadata from Data Package descriptors, ensuring records remain accurate and up to date without manual intervention.

Ingestion Pipeline: The core ingestion pipelines are being updated to index occurrence and sampling-event records, together with their related extensions, published via DwC-DP. This work lays the foundation for broader community adoption of DwC-DP.

Together, these developments mark a significant step toward full DwC-DP support across the GBIF data publishing lifecycle, from authoring and validation to registration and indexing.

The programme lists Mikhail Podolskiy as the second co-presenter, so that name is used for indexing. Vimeo ASR rendered the introduction as 'Nicola'/'Nicola Raibek' and later 'Nikolaj'; the recording alone does not verify the co-presenter’s identity.

summary: Federico Mendez and a GBIF colleague (introduced as Nikolaj) described how GBIF is integrating the Darwin Core Data Package (DwC-DP) into its publishing and ingestion infrastructure. Mendez stressed that Darwin Core Archives are not going away. He explained that DwC-DP adds a Frictionless-style datapackage.json with typed fields, constraints and referential integrity, and that the IPT will support mapping and publishing DwC-DP. Nikolaj covered the stricter validation, metadata synchronisation to the registry, and a new ingestion that maps DwC-DP into GBIF's internal model, with examples from the Nice Botanic Garden herbarium. Everything is currently only in GBIF's test environment.
one_line_takeaway: GBIF is close to supporting Darwin Core Data Packages end to end, with typed and stricter validation, while keeping Darwin Core Archives fully supported.
why_it_matters: DwC-DP is the biggest change to the Darwin Core publishing model in years. How GBIF validates, ingests and displays it will decide how data publishers can express richer, relational biodiversity data.
key_points: Darwin Core Archives (core plus extensions, meta.xml and EML) will stay supported. Publishers who are happy with them can keep using them.
GBIF's 20-year review found that publishing around central entities (occurrences, events, taxa) was not enough for existing data or for engaging new communities.
The DwC-DP conceptual model was ratified in May 2026. The final review's no-dissent period ended on 15 September, and ratification and release by the TDWG Executive is expected soon.

The IPT will support mapping, metadata editing, validation and publishing of DwC-DP, but only in the test environment for now.

Validation checks the datapackage.json against its schema and against the standardised TDWG definitions, then checks unique and primary-key constraints and referential integrity, and reports statistics such as unique and populated values per column.
Metadata synchronisation mainly uses EML, falling back to datapackage.json where needed.

The new ingestion maps DwC-DP into GBIF's internal structure so it can be shown on gbif.org next to DwC-A data without loss. Richer views will follow. Examples used the Nice Botanic Garden herbarium, including material, media and usage-policy links that were not possible before.
Authenticated publishers will be able to see validation results, and simplified navigable table views of the raw published data are planned.

title: Using automation to consolidate biodiversity occurrence data in South African National Parks

programme.title: Using automation to consolidate biodiversity occurrence data from multiple sources to assist conservation decision making in South African National Parks.
programme.session: Monday plenary programme (Taste of TDWG)
programme.abstract: South African National Parks manages 21 National Parks within South Africa that includes more than 4 million hectares spanning both the Marine and Terrestrial environments. To support evidence-based decision making at park level data from multiple sources need to be consolidated allowing users and park managers to easily access this consolidated data through dashboards. Automation and AI allows consolidation of open access data from sources outside of the organisation, as well as open access data from parks like collection data and sensitive park specific data to be viewed and used together by decision makers. APIs allow automated harvests of data from platforms like GBIF as well as information around conservation statuses of species from IUCN sites which is required for managing species at park level. Additional features allow integration of the data using selection features like selecting a certain park/area, taxonomic group, time frame or conservation status without any prior knowledge of GIS or data integration needed. Further features allow a user to download climate data for a particular area, create species lists and obtain additional information and graphs on the conservation status of taxonomic groups in these areas and how these have changed over time. This presentation will showcase this system and highlight how it uses AI and automation to generate easily accessible evidence.

summary: Judith Botha presented the SANParks Biodiversity Information Management System (BIMS), built with the Freshwater Research Centre and technical partner Kartoza. It brings together GBIF occurrence data, SANParks monitoring data and data captured from literature for South Africa's 21 national parks. The system produces annotated species checklists (needed for five-yearly park management plans), summary dashboards, Red List status and Red List Index trends, and climate station dashboards. Harvesting, taxonomic checks against the GBIF backbone, value assignment and dashboard generation are all automated.
one_line_takeaway: Automating the harvest, integration and summary of biodiversity data lets park staff get evidence-based species lists and dashboards without laborious manual compilation.
why_it_matters: This shows aggregated biodiversity data and standards reaching conservation managers and rangers as practical decision-support tools, and replacing the manual work behind statutory species lists.

South Africa has about 67,000 animal species, many poorly known and highly endemic.
Park management plans every five years need updated species lists, which used to be compiled by hand from literature.

BIMS harvests species and occurrence data from GBIF (occurrences for each reserve plus a buffer and catchment) and adds unpublished literature, databases, books, reports and theses captured by dedicated staff.

title: Extending Darwin Core to Represent Sociobiodiversity and Traditional Knowledge

programme.title: Extending Darwin Core to Represent Sociobiodiversity and Traditional Knowledge
programme.session: Monday plenary programme (Taste of TDWG)
programme.abstract:
Biodiversity data standards increasingly support automation, artificial intelligence, and large-scale interoperability. However, current standards still provide limited mechanisms to represent sociobiodiversity data, particularly traditional ecological knowledge, species uses, and the communities that generate and maintain this knowledge. As a result, much community-based biodiversity knowledge remains difficult to integrate into interoperable and machine-actionable infrastructures.

This contribution presents the ongoing development of a Darwin Core (DwC) extension for sociobiodiversity data, coordinated by the Brazilian Biodiversity Information System (SiBBr) and collaborators. The proposed extension aims to improve the semantic representation of biocultural information associated with species uses and traditional knowledge systems. Proposed terms include species use categories, plant parts used, preparation methods, medicinal and cultural applications, associated communities, territorial context, and provenance information.

The initiative recognizes that sociobiodiversity data are often generated through participatory and ethnobiological practices that require ethical and inclusive governance approaches. The work aligns not only with FAIR principles, but also with concerns regarding data sovereignty, attribution, and responsible reuse of traditional knowledge.

The proposal is being developed collaboratively through open discussions, use-case analyses, and iterative vocabulary design. Initial case studies involve ethnobotanical and historical datasets related to medicinal plants and traditional ecological knowledge from Brazilian coastal restingas and other socioecological contexts in the Global South.

actual.identification_notes: Introduced as 'Clara Barango Fonseca'. She says she is from the 'Brazilian Information System', probably SiBBr. Content matches event-015.

summary: Clara Baringo Fonseca described Brazil's work on a Darwin Core extension for sociobiodiversity data: the relationships between biodiversity and sociocultural diversity, including traditional uses, practices and knowledge of Indigenous peoples, local communities and family farmers. A 2024 project with Colombia and Argentina produced draft terms (such as use-to, use-form, used-by holder) that were tested in three case studies. The case studies exposed missing fields, ambiguous terms and questions about who should be the data publisher. She also covered the new Entre Ciências intercultural project and templates for registering associated traditional knowledge under Brazil's biodiversity law.
one_line_takeaway: Representing traditional knowledge in biodiversity standards needs new terms, knowledge-centred (not species-centred) models, and careful governance of who holds and publishes the data.
why_it_matters: It extends Darwin Core towards Indigenous and local knowledge in a way that respects community data ownership and consent, and links to benefit-sharing law, data sovereignty and Darwin Core Data Package work.
key_points: Sociobiodiversity data is defined (Brazilian National Sociobiodiversity Plan) as data on the interrelationship between biodiversity and sociocultural diversity: resources, traditional practices, uses and knowledge.
Communities and territories are the main source and are knowledge holders and data owners. Data should be shared only with their consent and under their governance.

Other sources include scientific articles, collections (often in occurrence remarks), 17th–19th century naturalists' works, market inventories and films. These are produced in different contexts and make it hard to identify the knowledge holder.

A 2024 project with Brazil, Colombia and Argentina produced draft extension terms, with controlled vocabularies (use-to, used-by type, source type) and free text (used-by holder, use-form, use-to description), kept on GitHub.
Three case studies: translating a 17th-century book, working directly with a community on the Rio de Janeiro coast, and a living collection of medicinal plants at the Rio de Janeiro Botanical Garden.

Findings: missing used-by holder and used-where data, ambiguous interpretation of use-to, and debate over whether the researcher or the community is the publisher, which matters for GBIF citation tracking.

The GEF-funded Entre Ciências project (started two months ago, three years) works with eight territories, six in the Amazon and two in the Cerrado, on data sovereignty, governance and locally chosen monitoring.

Under Brazil's biodiversity law, research on genetic heritage and associated traditional knowledge must be registered for benefit sharing. The team built templates, based on Colombia's, that put the knowledge rather than the species at the centre.

session.title: Monday plenary programme

title: What if biodiversity data systems were designed to behave like ecosystems?

programme.title: What if biodiversity data systems were designed to behave like ecosystems?

speakers.name: Kit Lewers
speakers.affiliation: University of Colorado Boulder; NASA Goddard Space Flight Center

programme.session: Monday plenary programme (Taste of TDWG)
programme.abstract:
Despite advances in global infrastructures such as the GlobalBiodiversity Information Facility (GBIF), a major gap remains between remote sensing data and biodiversity records. Most satellite and airborne observations begin as raw digital numbers and move through rigid, fragmented pipelines that rarely translate cleanly into interoperable, GBIF-ready data.

This talk reframes that problem through a systems lens inspired by ecological cascades. In ecosystems, small changes propagate through interconnected components, reshaping behavior, and structure over time. I argue that biodiversity data should function similarly and not as static products, but as events that trigger downstream processing and integration.

Building on this idea, I will introduce an event-driven, microservices-based approach to biodiversity data pipelines. Modular services handle key transformations (from radiance to reflectance, to derived products, to biodiversity integration) while responding dynamically to new data. This enables a continuous, traceable pathway from sensor-level measurements (L0/L1) to analysis-ready outputs (L2/L3) and ultimately to GBIF-ready records.

By shifting from static workflows to adaptive systems, this approach better supports reproducibility, interoperability, and cross-institutional collaboration. Rather than reducing complexity, it embraces it by designing biodiversity infrastructures that can evolve, respond, and scale alongside the ecosystems they represent.

speakers.name: Kit Lewers
speakers.affiliation: University of Colorado Boulder; NASA Goddard Space Flight Center

actual.identification_notes: Introduced by name; self-identifies as a PhD candidate at CU Boulder and a NASA fellow/researcher at Goddard. Content matches event-016.

summary: Kit Lewers used the 1995 reintroduction of wolves to Yellowstone and the trophic cascades that followed as an analogy for biodiversity information infrastructure. The argument was that system-level behaviour emerges from interactions between loosely coupled components, not from any single blueprint. Lewers proposed event-driven, modular, microservices-style architectures in which new data arriving triggers workflows and updates that cascade through the system. They framed Darwin Core as an existing 'data contract' that already lets diverse institutions interoperate, and suggested making that implicit modularity explicit. NASA remote sensing processing levels were given as an example of adding data without changing the whole paradigm.
one_line_takeaway: Biodiversity information systems should be designed like ecosystems: loosely coupled, event-driven components linked by shared standards, able to reorganise as conditions change.
why_it_matters: It offers a conceptual design pattern for bringing new data types (such as remote sensing) into biodiversity infrastructure without monolithic redesign, and treats standards like Darwin Core as connective infrastructure.
key_points: Molly Beattie (US Fish and Wildlife Service director from 1993) oversaw the 1995 reintroduction of 14 wolves to Yellowstone, with 17 more the next year, despite opposition and uncertainty.
Trophic cascades are nonlinear, spatially uneven and still debated. Change came from networks of interactions, not simple chains.

An ecosystem can be seen as information unfolding in real time. Biodiversity information systems are likewise interdependent, loosely coupled, heterogeneous and only partly coordinated information ecosystems.
Data gains value through interaction: a new dataset arriving is an event that triggers workflows, updates products and recalibrates models, and the outputs become new events.
Lewers proposed event-driven modular systems based on microservices, where ingestion, processing, analysis, transformation and dissemination run independently through well-defined interfaces.
Loosely coupled does not mean structureless. Shared standards and governance let components understand each other.

Darwin Core already works as a data contract that lets museums, the NEON Biorepository, iNaturalist and NASA contribute without the same internal systems. Making this explicit prompts questions about translation, embedded assumptions, provenance and who maintains interfaces.

NASA data passes through L0 (raw), L1 (calibrated radiance) and L2 (reflectance) before derived products. Darwin Core would represent biodiversity observations derived from imagery, not the imagery itself.
The goal is not to eliminate complexity or 'solve' the information ecosystem, but to create conditions in which it can keep evolving.
questions: What would it mean to build information systems that can cascade and reorganise like ecosystems do after a restored interaction?

notable_claims.claim: In January 1995, 14 wolves from Canada were released into Yellowstone, with 17 following the next year.
Darwin Core already provides something like a data contract, letting institutions map locally managed information into a shared vocabulary without changing their internal systems.
Remote sensing would enter GBIF not as satellite imagery via Darwin Core but as biodiversity observations derived from that imagery.

recommendations: Design biodiversity information systems as loosely coupled, event-driven components linked by shared standards and governance.
Treat standards like Darwin Core explicitly as connective infrastructure, and ask where translation happens, what assumptions and provenance are kept, and who maintains interfaces.
examples_case_studies: 1995 Yellowstone wolf reintroduction
NASA remote sensing data processing levels

representative_excerpt.text: Similarly, data does not become valuable simply because it exists in a repository or an aggregator. Its greater value emerges through interaction.

notable_moments.description: Central question: design information systems like ecosystems respond to disruption
Data arrival as an event that cascades through the system
Darwin Core as an existing data contract enabling modularity
Restoring infrastructural relationships can change what a system can do

title: Mainstreaming high-throughput biodiversity monitoring using AI

programme.title: Mainstreaming high-throughput biodiversity monitoring using AI
programme.session: Monday plenary programme (Taste of TDWG)
programme.abstract:
The rapid development of AI image and sound recognition technology in combination with reduced costs of camera traps and passive acoustic monitoring (PAM) devices opens opportunities to mainstream data driven species monitoring. Several user portals have been developed over the past years that bring these AI technologies to new user communities like ecologists and managers of natural resources. ARISE is the acronym for “Authoritative and Rapid Identification System for Essential biodiversity information” and is one such initiative that was launched in November 2025. ARISE provides end-users with a data management system for camera-trap, insect camera and PAM monitoring data and a library with different AI algorithms that can be used to analyse the data. At present 10 AI algorithms are available ranging from MegaDetector to remove images with humans or vehicles to SpeciesNet, DeepFaune and Trapper AI for camera-trap images and AvesEcho-v1 for PAM sound recordings. The number of available AIs is rapidly increasing.

The ‘Biodiversity Meets Data’ or BMD project aims to make these technologies available to monitor the state of conservation of species and habitats that are protected under the EU Nature Directives that are implemented in the Natura 2000 and Emerald Networks, together covering more than 30,000 protected sites across Europe. The managers of natural resources are BMD’s main stakeholder community that are provided with these new technologies. Directing our focus to the feasibility of wider adoption, we discuss the performance metrics of these automated pipelines alongside an assessment of their financial and computational costs-including model training and cloud operation -providing an example for scalable, economically viable AI-driven nature conservation.

actual.identification_notes: Introduced as 'Niels Reyes' (ASR); coordinator of the Biodiversity Meets Data project, describing Naturalis's ARISE platform. Matches event-017.

summary: Niels Raes, coordinator of the Horizon Europe project Biodiversity Meets Data (BMD), described how the project is scaling AI-based high-throughput monitoring (camera traps, audio and eDNA) to site managers across Natura 2000 and Emerald Network sites. He showed Naturalis's ARISE platform: 4G sensor upload, data management, a library of image and audio AI models, overnight processing on supercomputers, and export as Camtrap DP for publication to GBIF matched to the Catalogue of Life. He also gave compute and cost figures for inference and for training Naturalis's multi-source model. Q&A covered invertebrate monitoring, the cost of deployment on devices, and human-in-the-loop verification.
one_line_takeaway: AI identification platforms like ARISE can take sensor data automatically to GBIF-published, standardised data for protected-area managers, but training costs are high and human verification still matters.
why_it_matters: It shows a working, continental-scale pipeline from automated sensors to standardised GBIF data and management tools, with rarely shared figures on the compute cost of the AI involved.
key_points: BMD is a Horizon Europe innovation action that mainstreams existing technology to new stakeholders. The primary audience is natural resource site managers, then policymakers, with academia last.

Scope: better implementation of the EU nature directives across about 27,000 Natura 2000 sites, extended to the Emerald Network (UK, Norway, Switzerland, Ukraine), about 30,000 potential sites, as a pilot. The project is in month 19.

'Virtual research environments' were renamed 'biodiversity analysis tools' because the term did not resonate with stakeholders. The tools are co-designed with stakeholders, for example a biodiversity status tool showing which directive-listed species were observed.
The target workflow is 4G-connected sensors with solar or battery power, automated upload, remote status control, archiving, AI identification and publication to GBIF.

ARISE (Authoritative and Rapid Identification System for Essential biodiversity information, Naturalis) offers audio models developed under MAMBO (birds, bats, frogs, insects, cicadas/crickets) and image models (MegaDetector, SpeciesNet, and Naturalis's multi-source model).
MegaDetector runs first to remove humans and licence plates for GDPR. Processing is batched overnight on supercomputers because on-the-fly processing is costly.

Results are exported as Camtrap DP, mapped to Darwin Core, published to GBIF and matched to the Catalogue of Life, then feed analysis tools such as species distribution models of climate change effects.

Image recognition takes about 0.03 s per image on GPU (0.06 s on CPU); training takes about 8 s per image. The multi-source model covers about 44,000 taxa, was trained on 42 million labelled images, combines 39 models, serves 100 million requests a year, and takes five months to train plus one month of validation each year, costing roughly €93,000–130,000 on Snellius.
