title: AI-vision for integrated management of pest insects and their natural enemies

programme.title: AI-vision for integrated management of pest insects and their natural enemies
programme.session: SYM30A AI for Biodiversity Data
programme.abstract: Precision farming is being adopted by many farmers, but the number of reliable tools for controlling weed, pest invertebrates and disease in arable cropping system is still quite limited. Most decision support models for plant protection against invertebrate pests consider the pest invertebrate, the plant and abiotic factors affecting them. Natural enemies of invertebrate pests are seldom considered as a factor in the decision support models. Recent advancements in precision technologies used in weed management rely on machine vision models and algorithms where weeds are identified from the cultivated plant and the chemical herbicides are applied only where weeds are identified, without broadcast uniform spraying an entire field, resulting in a 40-97% reduction in the use of chemical herbicides. Our focus in this project is therefore to reveal whether similar techniques could be adapted for precise control of pest insects while protecting and conserving their natural enemies. Our aim is to develop an Artificial Intelligence (AI) workflow that utilizes identification of pest insects and their natural enemies identification for automatic crop management systems. This work begins with the creation of a labelled and annotated image dataset for selected crops with the key pests and natural enemies. Thereafter, the dataset will be used to identify the best modelling toolbox for AI-based machine vision model for automatic species identification of pests and their natural enemies. The result will serve as basis toward designing a framework for pest monitoring and conservation biological control in the selected crops at field level.

title: Soundscape China: Listening to the Sounds of Nature with AI

programme.title: Soundscape China - Listening to the Sounds of Nature with AI
programme.session: SYM30A AI for Biodiversity Data
programme.abstract:
With the rapid advancement of artificial intelligence and acoustic sensing technologies, the use of sound for biodiversity monitoring has evolved from localized experiments to widespread application. The construction of a national intelligent monitoring network based on natural sounds has become a key research direction in the field of ecological monitoring. The "Soundscape China" project is precisely centered on the goal of intelligent natural soundscape monitoring. It addresses multiple critical components-ranging from sensor development and intelligent species identification modeling to the construction of big data platforms-and is dedicated to creating an integrated technological chain that encompasses "acquisition, recognition, and management." The project strives to provide a standardized, replicable, and scalable model for the industry.

To date, Phase I of the "Soundscape China" project has deployed over 120 acoustic monitoring devices nationwide, which have automatically collected and aggregated more than 2 million valid recordings. The monitoring coverage spans diverse ecosystem types, including forests, wetlands, farmlands, grasslands, and deserts, thereby providing robust data support for national biodiversity monitoring. The project has been officially selected for inclusion in the United Nations' "Decade of Science" program. In the future, it aims to further expand the intelligent natural soundscape monitoring network, while also deepening cross-disciplinary practices such as citizen science education and sound art. This will promote multi-disciplinary synergy and foster an innovative framework of positive interaction among technology, ecology, and society.

title: Cross-Modal Coordination for Biodiversity Monitoring at Scale: Lessons from SmartWilds

programme.title: Cross-Modal Coordination for Biodiversity Monitoring at Scale: Lessons from SmartWilds
programme.session: SYM30A AI for Biodiversity Data
programme.abstract:
No single sensing modality is sufficient to monitor biodiversity at scale. Camera traps miss vocalizing birds, acoustic recorders miss silent species, drones struggle with species ID from altitude, and citizen science is opportunistic. Each modality has its own mature AI ecosystem (BirdNET, BioCLIP, MegaDetector, foundation models for drone imagery, iNaturalist), but automating biodiversity data collection, preparation, and interpretation at scale requires moving beyond single-modality pipelines toward cross-modal coordination, with smart sensors making decisions at the edge.

Coordinating across modalities is fundamentally a multi-scalar problem across both time and space. Standardizing these streams into datasets that support multimodal AI requires AI itself: foundation models for cross-modal alignment, LLM-assisted metadata extraction, and shared schemas like Darwin Core that make the result machine-actionable. We present SmartWilds, a co-located multimodal deployment at The Wilds Conservation Center, Ohio, combining camera traps, autonomous recording units, drones, citizen science, and field text across 220 hectares, with 380K Darwin Core occurrences and complete sensor configuration metadata.

We evaluate where each modality-specific AI pipeline is mature and where it is not, with drone species ID from altitude showing the largest gap, bird vocalization classification being robust but limited to vocal taxa, and camera-trap individual re-identification at scale remaining unsolved. We report annotation effort, computational cost, and known failure modes alongside performance, supporting honest assessment of which components are ready for edge deployment and which require centralized compute or human review.

title: Trapper 2.0: scalable, open-source platform for managing camera trapping projects with integrated AI pipelines

programme.title: Trapper 2.0: scalable, open-source platform for managing camera trapping projects with integrated AI pipelines
programme.session: SYM30A AI for Biodiversity Data
programme.abstract:
Camera trapping has become a powerful tool for wildlife monitoring, but the resulting multimedia datasets, often comprising millions of images and videos, present significant analytical challenges. Manual annotation is time-consuming, expensive, and difficult to scale, making AI integration essential for modern biodiversity monitoring workflows.

Trapper is an open-source, web-based platform designed to manage camera trap data at any scale, from individual research projects to large citizen science initiatives. It allows users to build automated AI analysis pipelines consisting of a variety of open-source AI models used for object detection, tracking objects in videos, species classification and distance and movement speed detection. Trapper’s architecture allows for easy integration of new models as they are being developed.

The results of AI analysis can be reviewed and corrected by human experts. This human-in-the-loop approach maximises annotation efficiency without sacrificing data quality. The recently released version, Trapper 2.0, features support for processing videos as well as images. Trapper is compatible with the Camtrap DP data standard, ensuring interoperability with GBIF and broader biodiversity data infrastructures.

An important feature of Trapper’s design is deployment flexibility. The entire Trapper stack, including the AI processing components, can be run on a personal computer, a local server or a cloud server, as well as on microservers like Raspberry Pi. AI processing can be done using CPU alone, with GPU acceleration or using Hailo-based processing, enabling computation on edge devices. This helps to significantly decrease computation costs, making AI-assisted biodiversity monitoring more accessible even with limited resources.

title: Are plant image datasets ready for AI-enabled community assessment? A systematic review of bias, representativeness and annotation quality

programme.title: Assessing the Readiness of Plant Image Datasets for AI-enabled Spatially Explicit Ecological Monitoring: A Systematic Review of Bias, Representativeness, and Annotation Quality
programme.session: SYM30B AI for Biodiversity Data
programme.abstract:
Despite rapid advances in AI models, the applicability of ecological monitoring remains constrained by limitations in dataset quantity and quality. While most plant image datasets focus on classification for species identification, object detection and segmentation datasets remain underdeveloped. These tasks are critical for spatially explicit ecological inference, including individual localisation, abundance estimation, and vegetation structure analysis.

This review systematically identified and analysed plant image datasets developed for ecological monitoring. An assessment framework inspired by clinical image datasets evaluation was adapted to ecological monitoring requirements and applied to 42 datasets. The framework evaluated dataset scale, ecological representativeness, annotation protocols, and data management practices.

The results revealed that most datasets lacked clearly documented annotation protocols and cross-annotator consistency controls, undermining the reliability of annotations as ground truth for AI-based ecological inference. Inconsistencies in taxonomic and geographic distribution further limit both model generalisability and the applicability of image-based monitoring at global scales. Agricultural weed detection dominated current applications, while broader biodiversity monitoring remained limited.

These findings highlight that while datasets are increasingly available, their design is often not aligned with the ecological levels required for biodiversity monitoring. Both annotation quality and ecological representativeness of available datasets fall short of the requirements for robust and generalisable image-based monitoring. Future work should prioritise ecologically representative and well-documented datasets for biodiversity monitoring.

summary: Yuchen Zhao (Newcastle University) argued that ecological AI is constrained less by model architecture than by the quantity and quality of training data. She presented a four-dimension framework, inspired by clinical reporting frameworks and FAIR, for assessing plant image dataset readiness: training-relevant characteristics, image acquisition characteristics, annotation protocol, and accessibility. A systematic review of in-situ, non-crop plant object detection and segmentation datasets screened 360 unique studies and found only 40 eligible datasets, with strong geographic bias toward Europe and Asia, a dominance of agricultural applications (19 of 40 focused on wheat), neglect of background plants, and generally unsatisfactory annotation protocols.

title: The WildLIVE Portal: Towards Scalable Wildlife Monitoring through the Integration of Citizen Science and Human-in-the-Loop AI Workflows

programme.title: The WildLIVE Portal: Towards Scalable Wildlife Monitoring through the Integration of Citizen Science and Human-in-the-Loop AI Workflows
programme.session: SYM30B AI for Biodiversity Data
programme.abstract: Global biodiversity monitoring delivers an ever-increasing volume of recorded data, with even medium-sized projects gathering data in the order of hundreds of thousands of images annually. These vast amounts of data frequently overwhelm the manual review capacity of domain experts and small research teams. As a result, the scale of these observations creates significant bottlenecks that hinder timely data annotation and analysis for conservation efforts. AI-generated baseline annotations can reduce this workload, but they still require expert review before they can be treated as reliable scientific evidence. The primary challenge lies in establishing trust and quantifiable confidence in these annotations, regardless of their source. To address this challenge, Senckenberg’s WildLIVE portal combines AI workflows with Human-in-the-Loop (HITL) refinement. The platform supports multi-model object detection, including open-vocabulary approaches in which detections can be guided by textual category descriptions rather than being limited to a fixed label set. Through an active-learning infrastructure, the platform prioritises observations most in need of review, directing citizen scientists and domain experts toward images where labelling effort can have the greatest impact on model confidence. These evaluations are preserved as layered annotations linking back to AI4WildLIVE’s FAIR Digital Object-based data model. By integration of an AI-assisted annotation pipeline, active learning, AI-readiness of data and citizen science engagement, the WildLIVE portal establishes a shared, human and machine operable collaborative framework through which biodiversity monitoring data becomes a trusted, community-wide scientific resource.

title: HerbAudit: Validating AI-Driven Herbarium Transcriptions

programme.title: HerbAudit: Validating AI-Driven Herbarium Transcriptions
programme.session: SYM30B AI for Biodiversity Data
programme.abstract: Millions of herbarium specimens are now digitized and accessible online, yet transforming specimen label images into structured, queryable data remains a major bottleneck in biodiversity informatics. While OCR and LLM technologies are increasingly applied to this challenge, the community lacks a shared framework to measure tool performance and identify data gaps. To fill this gap, we developed HerbAudit, an open source tool combining herbarium label transcription with systematic quality evaluation, to be publicly available by September 2026. We also compiled a gold standard benchmark dataset of 90 typed and handwritten specimens from 63 institutions worldwide, each manually transcribed using Label Studio. HerbAudit consists of two core components. The transcription component builds on VoucherVision logic, processing images via LLMs like Google Gemini and OpenAI to output Darwin Core formatted data. It includes a resolution adjustment submodule and reports estimated cost and carbon footprint metrics per image. The evaluation component offers two distinct pathways. First, OCR tool outputs are compared directly against the gold standard manual annotations. Second, AI tool predictions in Darwin Core format are cross checked against GBIF and POWO, incorporating a built-in synonym check. Fields are scored using domain specific methods, such as geographic coordinates via the Haversine formula and author names via Character Error Rate. Users can apply transcription and AI evaluation to their own datasets, with the latter requiring records on GBIF to pinpoint errors and visualize where tools fall short. All results are compiled into an interactive HTML report, giving developers and researchers a shared foundation to benchmark, compare, and improve digitization pipelines.

title: AI-assisted digitisation of printed identification keys: from book to structured data in minutes

programme.title: AI-assisted digitisation of printed identification keys: from book to structured data in minutes
programme.session: SYM30B AI for Biodiversity Data
programme.abstract:
Printed identification keys are a major reservoir of curated biodiversity knowledge, but mobilising them into machine-readable form is hampered by the cost of expert transcription, taking days of work per key. We present a working pipeline that produces structured-key drafts from heterogeneous sources in minutes.

The pipeline runs in two stages. An extraction agent (local OCR plus targeted vision reads of figures) builds a taxa tree and atomic characters. A fresh-context audit agent then re-reads the draft against the source, catching character states that overlap or leave source-mentioned values uncovered, numeric characters without actual measurements, and described traits missing from the output - fixing each until a deterministic verifier signs off. Two transformations bridge dichotomous prose and matrix-form output: splitting bundled traits ("brown hairs, green stem, white dots") into separate characters, and merging synonymous states ("whitish yellow" / "pale yellow") across the file. All such decisions are documented for the taxonomist to consider; target output is an editable draft, not a finished publication.

We have run the pipeline on various inputs: dichotomous keys in scanned books, combined prose descriptions of species from multiple field guides, and online interactive keys. We also include a domain-aware language translation step which maintains context and user-provided terminology.

Costs depend on the input format and structure, but are limited to at most a few dollars per species, and will be presented in detail. The Clavis output format and its place in combined AI-plus-key identification workflows are addressed in a companion talk in "May the Data Be Structured" (SYM32).

actual.identification_notes: Introduced as a session organiser ('Wouter'/'Walter'); content matches the abstract.

summary: Wouter Koch explained why identification keys remain essential alongside image recognition (pictures often lack diagnostic characters, models do not explain why, and training needs labelled data) and showed combining image-recognition top-5 suggestions with digital keys to ask only the discriminating questions. He then described an LLM agent pipeline, demonstrated on a new key to Norwegian rodents compiled from six books none of which alone covered all species: local OCR, one agent per source extracting modular, precise statements (using both keys, descriptions and images), a fresh audit agent with 'nothing to defend', merging and harmonising characters (with documented decisions and moving shared traits to higher taxa, optional translation), and a grounding agent verifying every statement against the sources. A single key costs about $10 in an hour, six books under about $30, producing a draft for expert review rather than a finished key; generated illustrations still fail.
one_line_takeaway: An agentic LLM pipeline can turn printed keys and descriptions into a structured draft identification key for tens of dollars, shifting experts from transcribers to reviewers.
why_it_matters: Identification knowledge underpins observational data; cheaply mobilising keys from books improves accessibility, education and data quality.

Digital (multi-access) keys remove the linear dead-end problem of printed keys.
Image recognition can filter a key to the characters separating its top candidates.
OCR should be done locally and once, for cost and environmental reasons.

A fresh audit agent works better than having the original agent correct its own work.
Merging treats indistinguishable descriptions (pale yellow vs whitish yellow) as the same and documents every such decision.

title: AI-assisted georeferencing a posteriori of herbarium specimens: a case study on Italian herbaria

programme.title: AI-assisted georeferentiation a-posteriori of herbarium specimens: a case study on Italian herbaria
programme.session: SYM30B AI for Biodiversity Data
programme.abstract:
Italy’s largest herbaria have recently undergone a large-scale digitization, making more than 4 million specimens available online through the national portal PlantData and the GBIF. Most specimens only had textual locality descriptions without geographic coordinates, limiting their use in many ecological analyses such as species distribution models. To address this limitation, we started a process of georeferentiation a-posteriori.

The data presented different challenges: locality labels were often in Latin or partially illegible, mixing locality names with habitat notes, altitude and collector annotations. Initial georeferencing approaches using national gazetteers and OpenStreetMap Nominatim achieved success rates below 10%, as geocoding services were frequently confused by excessive contextual details in locality strings. Workflows based on Google Maps APIs improved results (~50%) but remained highly sensitive to spelling errors and historical orthographic variants.

Thus, we developed pipelines that combine lightweight large language models (LLMs) with geocoding services. The models use the full label context to separate locality names from ancillary text and correct spelling inconsistencies before georeferencing. Small LLMs combined with Nominatim achieved ~71% successful georeferentiations at very low cost. Small LLMs paired with Google Maps improved this result to ~78%, while using Frontier LLMs reached up to 84% accuracy, but they remain too expensive for high volume data.

title: Towards Scalable Trait Measurements from Digitized Specimens

programme.title: Towards Scalable Trait Measurements from Digitized Specimens
programme.session: SYM30B AI for Biodiversity Data
programme.abstract:
The increasing digitization of natural history collections creates opportunities for large-scale extraction of quantitative specimen traits. Morphological traits such as specimen shape and size are important for research in ecology and biodiversity. To obtain reliable and comparable traits from images, pixel measurements are converted into metric units using a scale conversion factor (CF), typically calculated by measuring pixel distances between ruler tick marks.

We build upon our previous work on automated ruler detection and scale estimation for herbarium specimens by improving its robustness and scalability. The original approach relied solely on image keypoint matching for CF estimation, which performed well for conventional rulers but was unreliable for simpler ruler types. We extend the original method with a hierarchical framework that first identifies the ruler type and then selects the most appropriate method for CF estimation. These simple rulers, such as lines, blocks, and grids, are processed differently, using a combination of computer vision methods and LLMs.

To evaluate this new approach, our dataset has been expanded beyond herbaria to a broader range of domains, including zoological, entomological, geological, and microscopy images. Furthermore, we show how the estimated CF values can be stored as standardized metadata to support interoperability and how markers can simplify scale estimation in future digitization workflows. Finally, we show how the scale estimation method can be combined with segmentation models to automatically extract specimen traits.

actual.identification_notes: Introduced as 'Kenzo Melville'; content matches the abstract.

summary: Kenzo Milleville presented a method to convert pixel measurements on specimen images into metric units by reading the ruler on the sheet. Instead of predicting scale directly, the ruler is detected and normalised, similar rulers are retrieved from an annotated reference set with a CLIP-like similarity model, and a keypoint-matching model transforms the known tick marks onto the new image, requiring in principle only one labelled example per ruler type. The reference set grew to about 2,000 rulers (21,000 annotated points, ~350 institutions), and 96% of predictions now have under 1% error (mean ~0.3%, below the ~0.8% manual annotation error). A proof of concept with Segment Anything 3 measured leaf sizes across taxa and geography. He recommended including ArUco markers or QR codes of known size during digitisation, and noted a proposal to Audiovisual Core to standardise such metadata and the idea of sharing length annotations via DiSSCo.
one_line_takeaway: Matching rulers to an annotated reference set lets specimen images be calibrated to real-world units with under 1% error in 96% of cases.
why_it_matters: Normalised measurements are a prerequisite for comparing traits across collections and at global scale from digitised specimens.
key_points: Rulers are highly diverse but frequently reused across institutions.
Pipeline: object detection, normalisation, similarity retrieval (top 3), keypoint matching, post-processing.
Main improvement over last year's Living Data version comes from a larger dataset and renewed models, especially keypoint matching.
Robust to lower resolution and partial occlusion; high-contrast popular rulers perform best; simple block rulers worst.
Annotation error is roughly constant in pixels regardless of image resolution.
No standard yet for storing calibration metadata; proposal submitted on GitHub for Audiovisual Core.
datasets: Annotated ruler reference set (~2,000 rulers, ~21,000 points, ~350 institutions)

Average error is around 0.3%, while manual annotation error is around 0.8%, which bounds achievable accuracy.

recommendations: Include a computer vision marker (ArUco or QR code) of known size, or calibrate, when digitising new images.
results_findings: Most common, high-contrast rulers perform best.
limitations: Fails on totally new, unique rulers.
Lens distortion was not accounted for.
future_work: Standardise calibration metadata in Audiovisual Core.
Extend to other domains.
Store length annotations on a platform such as DiSSCo for reuse.
Combine with trait extraction for global analyses.

programme.title: Reconsidering the original vision for a global biodiversity information facility
programme.session: SYM08A BHL at 20: A New Chapter for Biodiversity Literature and Data - Reimagining BHL: Foundations, Partnerships and Future Infrastructure
programme.abstract: A global biodiversity information facility was recommended in 1999 by the OECD Biodiversity Informatics Subgroup of the Megascience Forum. In 2001, 25 years ago this month, GBIF, the Global Biodiversity Information Facility, embarked to meet the challenges outlined by the Forum. Soon thereafter the scope was narrowed due to limited funding to meet the challenge. The original vision was a more encompassing of data from literature, traits, and taxonomy. GBIF focused on species occurrences and community building. Critically GBIF continues to grow as an intergovernmental organization, not affiliated with the United Nations, which provides sustainability. Other important infrastructure projects such as BHL, COL, EOL (and others) filled the void but lacked GBIF’s governance framework. What if the original vision had been funded and pursued? Would it have worked? Given the considerable stress on science and infrastructures today, could the original vision work now?

actual.identification_notes: Introduced by Nicole Kearney as GBIF Executive Secretary. A long Q&A/discussion followed, which is kept with this talk.

summary: Joe Miller, GBIF Executive Secretary, offered a 'provocation' for GBIF's 25th anniversary: a personal timeline of biodiversity infrastructures (LTER, GenBank, TDWG, the 1992 Rio conventions, TreeBASE, Species 2000/Catalogue of Life, OBIS, GEO BON, BHL, EOL) leading to the 1999 OECD Megascience Forum recommendation for a Global Biodiversity Information Facility. He revisited the report's figure: GBIF was to encompass names, specimen data, a 'species bank' and biodiversity literature, but funders narrowed it to occurrence data and the nodes network, and other initiatives (Catalogue of Life, BHL, EOL) filled the gaps. Today's landscape achieves 'synergisms among existing investments' through collaboration, but he asked whether that is enough. The Q&A debated how to make the case for closer BHL-GBIF links: Miller said the community, not the Secretariat, must bring such a case to the Governing Board; Donat Agosti argued literature data are already integrated at scale; and a commenter called for a new, AI-informed, impact-focused community vision.

programme.session: SYM08A BHL at 20: A New Chapter for Biodiversity Literature and Data - Reimagining BHL: Foundations, Partnerships and Future Infrastructure
programme.abstract: In December 2025, University of South Florida Libraries’ was honored to join the Biodiversity Heritage Libraries as a member, as well as to provide redundancy support for the technical team. As part of this new step, the team at USF is curating materials from their more than 30 collections of Florida Environment and Natural History (FLENH) materials and their extensive rare books collections. Ornithological research, including published and unpublished works, form the core of these holdings. While mixed in their formatting, the materials are rich in data that remained layered behind human prose, handwritten notes, and inconsistent checklists. Making these materials computer readable and adaptable for scientists to process at scale requires a heavy human lift. From local Audubon Society sanctuary records to the vast holdings of the Searchable Ornithological Research Archive (SORA), USF is exploring existing and adapted methods for ingesting their content into BHL over the next few years. Along the way, the team is working with scientists and student interns in various fields to test the accuracy of human and AI-methods to extract data. The team is hopeful that its efforts will provide a fresh case study for loading archival materials that can build on the work of other BHL members while leveraging internal expertise in cataloging, copyright, digital preservation, GIS, and data management. This talk will showcase the possibilities and priorities for the more than 106,000 already digitized records across the FLENH collections.

title: BHL and the Planetary Knowledge Base: Structuring Biodiversity Literature for the Next Generation

programme.title: BHL and the Planetary Knowledge Base: Structuring Biodiversity Literature for the Next Generation
programme.session: SYM08A BHL at 20: A New Chapter for Biodiversity Literature and Data - Reimagining BHL: Foundations, Partnerships and Future Infrastructure
programme.abstract:
As BHL enters its second decade, the Natural History Museum (NHM) is assisting in its evolution into a machine-actionable, FAIR-aligned biodiversity information infrastructure. This work is connected to NHM's Planetary Knowledge Base (PKB), which integrates fragmented natural history literature, collections, observations, genetic and environmental data into an explainable system for research, policy and action for nature.

The BHL work focuses on developing a biodiversity knowledge-extraction and discovery layer that operates alongside the BHL, linking users back to BHL pages, publications and metadata while enabling new forms of structured search and analysis. NHM has prototyped workflows that transform BHL's page-centric volumes into structured, machine-actionable scholarly resources through modern OCR, article-level segmentation, figure and table extraction, persistent identifier assignment, and entity extraction for taxa, people, institutions, localities, specimen identifiers, habitats and stratigraphy.

These outputs will support semantic discovery, programmatic reuse, knowledge graph construction, and alignment with biodiversity infrastructures such as GBIF, Catalogue of Life, Wikidata, GRSciColl, etc. All extracted entities and relationships retain provenance links to the original BHL pages and bibliographic records, with confidence and workflow metadata. The dataset also serves as a foundational evidentiary layer for the Planetary Knowledge Base (PKB), helping ground biodiversity knowledge in the underlying BHL literature.

These activities position BHL as a distributed, resilient, interoperable evidentiary layer for biodiversity research, connected to specimens, taxa, collections, observations, and external datasets.

summary: Qianqian Hiris Gu described NHM London's work making BHL machine-readable and connecting it to the NHM's Planetary Knowledge Base. Building on Neil Brummitt's decade of trait extraction from English-language BHL literature (about 700,000 trait terms across 81 standardised traits), an AWS prototyping sprint of four weeks on under 40,000 pages of a botanical journal combined modern OCR with computer vision for article title-page detection (~98%, ~100% with a table of contents), entity extraction (taxa, people, localities, institutions, habitats; F1 ~96%) into a knowledge graph and GraphRAG search. Benchmarking with BHL-provided ground truth showed printed text reaching human-level transcription, and word-level confidence from OCR models can gate what goes back into BHL. The work is now in production: re-OCR of the whole corpus by around January 2027, an open gold-standard dataset in early 2027, and an Explorer interface in Q2 2027.

title: Possibilities to enhance the semantic navigation of BHL: further developing the 'unit of work'

programme.title: Possibilities to enhance the semantic navigation of BHL - further developing the "unit of work"
programme.session: SYM08A BHL at 20: A New Chapter for Biodiversity Literature and Data - Reimagining BHL: Foundations, Partnerships and Future Infrastructure
programme.abstract:
The BHL data resource includes page images, scanned OCR text and bibliographic metadata regarding its holdings. Data are ingested into BHL using the units of volumes, parts and pages. Later projects such as biostor have asserted more useful units of work such as articles within serial titles by allocating a series of pages to an article with a title and authorship. The BHL user interface has a long-standing feature enabling navigation via the results of taxonomic indexing, which looks for occurrences of scientific names within page texts.

This talk will discuss the possibilities for building on the article identification concept and creating more domain specific units of work from the examination of contents pages, standard body pages and index pages to determine the layout and organisation of the information held within the part. Units of work could comprise biographical entries organised alphabetically by person name, dictionary or glossary entries organised alphabetically, species entries in specimen catalogues, monographs and floristic works ordered taxonomically, or field work sites and gazetteer entries organised geographically. Identification of these would help drive wider use of BHL-mobilised data and build stronger links with user communities such as those working with biographical data about collectors and identifiers in the Bionomia project, those seeking historical geographic data for georeferencing and taxonomic projects such as the World Flora Online

actual.identification_notes: Introduced as 'Nikki Nicholson' from Kew; content matches the abstract.

summary: Nicky Nicolson, starting from Kew's IPNI (funded by Darwin's legacy) which indexes names to the exact page, argued that BHL has been built primarily as a library (volumes, pages, then articles via BioStor), whereas as a biodiversity data source its pages are richly structured, containing people directories, multilingual glossaries and gazetteers that are not best reached via articles. She contrasted bottom-up entity discovery across 64 million pages with top-down, community-driven subsetting, and proposed that BHL learn from GBIF's hosted portals: branded, pre-filtered views that let communities and funders see their slice (e.g. DiSSCo UK), which could also address contributors like Madrid who keep content out of BHL's viewer for branding reasons. Comments from Donat Agosti (GBIF hosted portals for journals) and a TaxonPages developer (need for BHL API endpoints) followed.
one_line_takeaway: Letting user communities carve BHL into branded, pre-filtered 'hosted portals' could serve diverse needs, satisfy funders and drive innovation.
why_it_matters: Rethinking BHL's units of navigation beyond volumes and articles could expose the structured entities in literature to the communities that need them.

title: Biological occurrence data from historic scientific correspondence: enabling automated approaches for structured data extraction from body text

programme.title: Biological occurrence data from historic scientific correspondence: enabling automated approaches for structured data extraction from body text
programme.session: SYM08B BHL at 20: A New Chapter for Biodiversity Literature and Data - Transforming BHL: Data Extraction, Semantic Navigation and Future Interfaces
programme.abstract:
Historical species occurrence data are essential for incorporating the past into analyses of biodiversity change. In addition to sources specifically intended to document occurrences, such as surveys, occurrence data are also implicitly contained in many other historical documents, where they are embedded in diverse linguistic structures.

Here, prerequisites for scalable information extraction of biodiversity-relevant data from written sources were investigated using content from the scientific journals published by the Museum für Naturkunde Berlin: the Deutsche Entomologische Zeitschrift and Zoosystematics and Evolution and their predecessor periodicals accessible through the Biodiversity Heritage Library.

Focussing on information concerning the observation of biological species (occurrences), together with data on habitats and related preserved specimens, a data model was developed to align natural-language text elements with facets of occurrence instances. Based on this model, a text corpus derived from the journals was manually annotated to generate ground-truth text annotations and occurrence data. The data associated with the identified observation events were serialized as RDF (Resource Description Framework) graphs and aligned with the Darwin Core standard and the data schemas of Wikidata and the Global Biodiversity Information Facility.

We outline how the annotated corpus can be used to develop and evaluate AI-based information-extraction workflows for species occurrence data from natural-language prose. In addition, the project generated insights into the acquisition and use of copyright-protected sources for text-and data-mining approaches in contrast to open access models.

actual.identification_notes: Pre-recorded presentation (speaker present in the room but answering questions via Whova). ASR renders the name 'Christian Bühling'. Content matches the abstract.

summary: Christian Bölling presented a Museum für Naturkunde Berlin project building an annotated reference corpus of historical scientific correspondence and articles from MfN journals (Deutsche Entomologische Zeitschrift, Zoosystematics and Evolution, Fossil Record and predecessors), to evaluate whether machine learning can reliably extract occurrence data at scale. A tag set (taxon, place, date, habitat, quantity, person, material, plus org/ID) aligned to Darwin Core annotates occurrences anchored at the taxon name; the first campaign found nearly 1,600 occurrence reports in 165 articles using INCEpTION. Places were matched to Wikidata (1,215 of 1,333) and taxa to GBIF IDs (1,041 of 1,154), and data serialised in RDF. He highlighted difficulties with document retrieval, erratic publisher APIs, annotation consistency and historical place names, and suggested BHL add entity recognition for persons and places and richer journal relationship metadata.
one_line_takeaway: A Darwin Core-aligned annotated corpus from MfN journals provides a reference for evaluating automated occurrence extraction from historical texts.
why_it_matters: Legacy reports contain largely untapped occurrence data; a gold-standard corpus is needed before AI extraction can be trusted.
key_points: Historical society meeting reports (e.g. Berlin Entomological Society 1915) detail dozens of observations.
A valid occurrence requires a taxon name plus place and/or date.
Places appear in almost all instances; dates, persons, quantities and materials in about a third; habitats and specimen IDs rarely.
681 distinct place entities and 741 distinct taxa were identified.
Full-text coverage for some journals was much lower than articles published; new OCR was needed for many pre-1970 articles.

Place matching to Wikidata succeeded for 1,215 of 1,333 instances; taxon matching to GBIF for 1,041 of 1,154.

BHL could add metadata linking related journals such as predecessors.
limitations: Document retrieval was complicated by inconsistent bibliographic databases and erratic publisher APIs.
Annotation is demanding and occurrence language has no clear boundary.
Historical place names need expert context to map to modern units.
future_work: Extend corpus with more sources and tags.
Use the corpus to evaluate and fine-tune AI relation extraction.

title: A closer look at steps needed to extract research-ready biodiversity data from legacy literature

programme.title: A closer look at steps needed to extract research-ready biodiversity data from legacy literature
programme.session: SYM08B BHL at 20: A New Chapter for Biodiversity Literature and Data - Transforming BHL: Data Extraction, Semantic Navigation and Future Interfaces
programme.abstract: Research-ready biodiversity data must follow established standards. However, this is not easily achieved in the case of data extracted from legacy literature. The literature is unstructured and heterogenous in format, content and style, which is why data extraction presents many challenges, some of which will be illustrated during this talk. One of the problems is synonymy, a problem which goes much further than mere taxonomic or nomenclatural synonymy. Another common phenomenon is coreference, this is, two or more expressions referring to the same object. Do we need to apply or develop computer-linguistic solutions for these problems... or can we just rely on LLMs to solve them for us? This talk will discuss approaches applied in the BIOfid text mining and annotation pipeline which is under development with a focus on a German-language corpus of biodiversity legacy literature, but we expect that this approach will also help solve problems with corpora in other languages.

actual.identification_notes: Introduced as 'Gavin Kasparek'; mentions involvement in the BioFID project (ASR 'BioFit'). Content matches the abstract.

summary: Gerwin Kasperek surveyed the obstacles to extracting research-ready data from legacy literature, using a 1969 German botanical article as an example. OCR errors propagate through NLP stages, and OCR quality evaluation itself is hard; synonyms are numerous (The Plant List had 44% synonyms and 33% accepted names) and abbreviated genus names are ambiguous across groups; taxon concepts shift over time (e.g. Linnaeus' Quercus robur) and modifiers like sensu lato/stricto matter; homonyms span taxa and places (Liparis, Paris); coreferences (C. viride, 'var. nanum') span sentences; and documents mix languages including Latin. He called for coordinated technical solutions (better OCR and its evaluation, domain-aware NLP, nomenclatural ontologies, per-sentence language detection) and taxonomic rigour (stronger backbones, Taxon Concept standards, temporal disambiguation).
one_line_takeaway: Legacy literature data can only be unlocked by combining better OCR/NLP with taxonomic rigour that accounts for synonymy, shifting concepts, coreference and mixed languages.
why_it_matters: Clarifies why AI extraction from historical texts is harder than it looks and which standards and tools are needed to get research-ready historical baselines.
key_points: Historical baselines of biodiversity need literature data.
OCR errors reduce keyword search reliability and degrade NER further.
Abbreviated names like E. rubiginosa can refer to plants, worms or fungi.
Shifting taxon concepts are more challenging than synonymy.
Coreference resolution needs general transformer NLP plus nomenclatural ontologies.
Many NLP tools assume one language per document; Latin is low-resource.

notable_claims.claim: In The Plant List, synonyms made up 44% of names with only 33% accepted names.
Shifting taxonomic concepts are far more challenging than mere synonymy problems.

recommendations: Improve OCR tools and OCR evaluation tools.
Develop comprehensive taxonomic backbones and taxon concept standards.
Integrate nomenclatural ontologies in NLP.
Detect language per sentence or paragraph.
examples_case_studies: 1969 German botanical article with OCR errors (Listera cordata), synonymy (Epipactis rubiginosa/atrorubens) and coreference (Coeloglossum viride)
Quercus robur sensu Linnaeus vs modern authors

representative_excerpt.text: After all, a name in 1850 may not mean the same today. Our systems must account for that.

notable_moments.description: OCR error propagation and difficulty of OCR evaluation.
Shifting taxon concepts.
Call for a coordinated technical and taxonomic approach.

title: Multimodality for Knowledge Extraction from Historical Entomology Literature

programme.title: Multimodality for Knowledge Extraction from Historical Entomology Literature
programme.session: SYM08B BHL at 20: A New Chapter for Biodiversity Literature and Data - Transforming BHL: Data Extraction, Semantic Navigation and Future Interfaces
programme.abstract:
Historical entomological publications combine textual descriptions and scientific illustrations that contain complementary biodiversity knowledge. While texts describe insect taxa, host plants, and ecological interactions, illustrations capture life cycles, morphological traits, and species interactions. Existing biodiversity knowledge extraction approaches mainly focus on text and rarely integrate visual information from historical illustrations.

We propose a multimodal knowledge graph for representing entities, traits, and ecological interactions extracted from historical entomological literature. As a case study, we analyze 50 articles and illustrations from Maria Sibylla Merian’s Der Raupen wunderbare Verwandelung, und sonderbare Blumennahrung (1679). Our workflow combines OCR, semantic annotation, image-region linking, and knowledge graph construction to align textual and visual information. The workflow includes: (i) extracting text with OCR, (ii) defining an annotation ontology for concepts and events in illustrations, (iii) annotating articles with these concepts, and (iv) linking illustration regions to corresponding text passages.

The workflow generates semantic triples from text and illustrations, e.g., {(tulip, instance_of, petal), (petal, has_color, purple), (caterpillar, has_shape, elongated)}. Beyond visual traits, extracted relations represent biologically relevant information such as insect-host plant associations and developmental stages. The resulting knowledge graph supports semantic enrichment and automated caption generation for historical biodiversity collections.

actual.identification_notes: Introduced as Jana Hoffmann (ASR earlier 'Regiane Hoffmann'); co-presented with Sefika Efeoglu who explains the workflow. Content matches the abstract.

summary: Jana Hoffmann and Sefika Efeoglu of Senckenberg's new Semantic Data Systems and Knowledge Engineering group presented a prototype linking text and illustrations in historical entomological literature, using Maria Sibylla Merian's 1679 'Der Raupen wunderbare Verwandlung' (50 plates, digitised and published on Zenodo, soon in BHL). The workflow uses olmOCR for text, an ontology of concepts, detection of visual entities, relations and attributes in illustrations, annotation of text entities using those visual entities, merging into a multimodal sub-knowledge graph, and verbalisation into evidence-grounded captions, since historical plates often lack captions. Next steps are scaling to all 50 articles, provenance, and expert human-in-the-loop validation.
one_line_takeaway: Aligning text and illustrations in a multimodal knowledge graph can generate evidence-grounded captions and recover knowledge lost by text-only extraction.
why_it_matters: Illustrations carry complementary morphological, life-stage and interaction evidence that text-only pipelines ignore.
key_points: Text describes organisms, host plants and feeding interactions; illustrations show morphology, developmental stages and spatial relations.
Merian volume from the Senckenberg German Entomological Institute library in Müncheberg.
Generated captions are restricted to what is supported by the graph; freer generation adds hallucinated content.

datasets: Digital edition of Merian's 1679 caterpillar book (50 plates)

notable_claims.claim: Many extraction pipelines focus on OCR and text alone, so evidence contained in illustrations is disregarded.

limitations: Prototype tested on a few selected examples only.
future_work: Run on the full set of 50 articles.
Consolidation, provenance and documentation.
Specialist validation of extracted information and captions.
Generalise the workflow to other collections.
examples_case_studies: Merian's 'Der Raupen wunderbare Verwandlung und sonderbare Blumen-Nahrung' (1679)

title: Future interfaces for BHL

programme.title: Future interfaces for BHL
programme.session: SYM08B BHL at 20: A New Chapter for Biodiversity Literature and Data - Transforming BHL: Data Extraction, Semantic Navigation and Future Interfaces
programme.abstract:
As part of TDWG 2026 there is a workshop on future interfaces for the Biodiversity Heritage Library. The workshop will be a mostly "hands on" exploration of live demos, often based on a subset of BHL content.

This talk puts the workshop in context by surveying user interfaces employed by digital libraries in other fields. It explores different approaches to search, the use of maps, and navigating by terms or entities (such as people or taxa). It considers some of the new possibilities offered by AI-based approaches, such as searching for similar images, and wrapping complicated queries in easy to use natural language interfaces.

Having found what you are looking for, how do you want that item displayed? The talk considers various approaches, such as PDFs, such as custom-built viewers, or viewers based on the IIIF standard. Increasing adoption of IIIF has resulted in a flurry of new approaches to annotating content, including overlaying published maps on a shared map of the world, or using in-browser machine-learning tools to classify images.

The success (or otherwise) of the various demos will give insights into what interfaces will enable users to get the most value from BHL.

actual.identification_notes: Introduced as 'Professor Rod Page'; talk is a taster for his Thursday BHL workshop. Content matches the abstract's scope.

summary: Rod Page previewed live demos for Thursday's BHL interfaces workshop, emphasising he could not promise BHL would adopt them. He hoped to have an MCP chatbot over a BHL RDF knowledge graph by Thursday and asked which ideas the community found useful.

title: Role-Based Access Control (RBAC) for RASD: The Flemish Biodiversity Portal Approach

programme.title: [No sound] Role-Based Access Control (RBAC) for RASD: The Flemish Biodiversity Portal Approach
programme.session: SYM23 To see or not to see - that is the question. Managing restricted access data (RASD)
programme.abstract:
Managing Restricted Access Species Data (RASD) becomes complex when regional portals must balance local sensitivity requirements with global data sharing through aggregators like GBIF. The Flemish Biodiversity Portal (VBP), built on the Atlas of Living Australia (ALA), addresses this by utilizing a "twin dataset" architecture, ensuring that high-resolution data remains secure while a more generalized version is made publicly available. This strategy prevents the exposure of precise coordinates on global platforms while the dataset structure, metadata and most of the identifiers stay the same.

In this presentation, we detail how VBP manages these twins using Role-Based Access Control (RBAC) logic embedded within the dynamicProperties field. By utilizing machine-readable flags-such as {"rbac":true, "rbac_allowed":"HIGHRES"}-the portal dynamically determines data visibility. Users with authorized roles access the high-resolution "twin," while the general public is directed to the low-resolution version.

This dual-dataset approach ensures that "not seeing" high-resolution data is a deliberate, governed choice rather than a technical limitation. We will discuss the synchronization challenges inherent in maintaining twins and how this workflow aligns with the TDWG RASD extension’s goal of standardizing the reasons and treatments for data restriction. By providing a transparent metadata trail for why a dataset is restricted or generalized, VBP demonstrates a scalable model for regional nodes to contribute to the global biodiversity data commons without compromising local conservation priorities.

title: Restricted access species data in Finland

programme.title: [No sound] Restricted access species data in Finland
programme.session: SYM23 To see or not to see - that is the question. Managing restricted access data (RASD)
programme.abstract: The Finnish Act on the Openness of Government Activities (621/1999) necessitates that species data in Finland is not made publicly available if it would endanger the protection of the species or area in question. The Finnish Biodiversity Information Facility (FinBIF) is a service for researchers, government and the public. The data harmonised in FinBIF's data warehouse includes the results of national monitoring programs, scientific collections and citizen science projects. FinBIF is the body primarily responsible for managing Finnish restricted access species data (RASD). FinBIF coordinates an expert panel, the Public Authorities Working Group, that maintains a list of taxa that require some level of data restriction. The Public Authorities Working Group determines the level of restriction and circumstances under which it should be applied. Each taxon included on the list must be subject to a concrete threat: persecution, harvesting, or disturbance. The list was first compiled in 2015, and a comprehensive update was carried out in 2025. Minor updates are made as needed. There are currently 155 listed taxa. Species data that is mobilised by FinBIF has restrictions applied on being harmonised in the data warehouse, before being made publicly available. The unrestricted data is made available in a parallel data warehouse that can only be accessed by registered users from statutory public authorities. Other data users may make a request for access to restricted data. Requests are fulfilled via a data access platform on a case by case basis with the consent of the data providers or relevant proxies. We outline the system for handling RASD in Finland and discuss how current and proposed biodiversity data standards may aid data providers and users.

actual.identification_notes: The beginning of the talk (and its introduction) is lost in the no-sound period; the recording picks up mid-talk at 00:17:29. summary: The recorded portion of Will Morris' talk explains how FinBIF applies Finland's government-maintained restricted species list (first published 2015, updated 2025, a little over 150 species) to all data it mediates. Restrictions range from full concealment to generalisation to 1-100 km grids and may be limited by region, season or specific sites; field notes are withheld and multi-record events are unlinked so co-observed species cannot reveal locations. Restricted data are published through a public portal and API, while a logged government authorities portal gives unrestricted access and a request service lets others ask providers for restricted data. He noted that GBIF-bound Darwin Core Archives only use informationWithheld and dataGeneralizations, and that much of the restriction information has no standard home yet.

why_it_matters: A national-scale implementation showing both the mechanics of restricting data (generalisation, unlinking events) and the gap that motivates the TDWG RASD extension.
key_points: A working group of government authorities (e.g. Finnish Environment Institute, Parks and Wildlife) maintains the list of restricted species and the restrictions to apply; the list was first published in 2015 and updated in 2025.
FinBIF conservatively applies these restrictions to all data it mediates, not only government data.

The list has just over 150 species and mirrors taxonomic bias: about half are birds (about a third of Finland's breeding birds), nearly all bats, some reptiles, amphibians, butterflies and a moth, and many vascular plants (largely orchids).
Restrictions include full concealment or generalisation to 1, 5, 10, 25, 50 or 100 km grids, possibly limited to parts of Finland, seasons (breeding, wintering) or specific sites.
Field notes that might reveal locations are withheld, and multi-record events are unlinked so an unrestricted co-observed species does not reveal a restricted one.

A public portal, API and bulk download service (with persistent identifiers) serve restricted data; a separate logged authorities portal gives unrestricted access to government employees; others can use a data request service mediated between users and providers.

Data published to GBIF use Darwin Core informationWithheld and dataGeneralizations, but the sensitive species checklist is only an Excel spreadsheet and information about restricting entities and access routes is not shared via any standard.

title: Restricted Access Species Data: The Swedish Model

programme.title: Restricted Access Species Data: The Swedish Model
programme.session: SYM23 To see or not to see - that is the question. Managing restricted access data (RASD)
programme.abstract:
For some 20 years, Sweden has used a central system, UserAdmin, for managing users and their roles. Certain roles decide which restricted access species data (RASD) a user is authorized to view. Out of the more than 158 million records in the Species Observation System (SOS) about 1.5 million are protected, belonging to 111 different species.

Records are automatically obscured if a species belongs to any of classes 3-5 on the national protection list. Additionally, a reporter can choose to manually hide any of their observations up until a future date of their choice. These will be handled as if they belong to class 3.

A protected observation is still visible to the reporter and the observers. They can also be available to authorized verifiers, authorities and agencies.

How can RASD be utilized?

1) A user can ask authorized staff in the local region if there is anything of concern in a certain area. They can give advice without revealing any sensitive data.

2) Upon authorization, some authorities/agencies can use Signal Search that answers yes/no if anything can be found that matches a broader taxonomic and geographic selection.

3) Restricted access can only be granted a person, who will then be screened in accordance with Swedish law and must sign a non-disclosure contract. This person is either allowed to do their own searches or to receive specific exports made by authorized staff. Receiving such exports is free of charge for official authorities but comes with a fee for commercial requests.

All observations in SOS can be accessed by logging in to either the web application Fynddata (fynddata.artdatabanken.se), maintained by SLU Swedish Species Information Centre, or Artsök (www.artkoll.se/artsok), a GIS based system managed by the County Administrative Board.

actual.identification_notes: Introduced as 'Johan Wiljegard' (ASR) from the Swedish Species Information Centre; content matches the abstract (UserAdmin, SOS, 158 million/1.5 million records).

summary: Johan Liljeblad traced Sweden's handling of restricted species data from a simple role table in the first citizen-science observatory (2000) to the UserAdmin role system launched with Artportalen 2 (2014) and a federation system harvesting other datasets (2021). About 1.5 million of 158 million records, belonging to 111 species, are protected in diffusion classes (5, 25 or 50 km squares), with users also able to hide or diffuse their own records. He explained authorised access via contracts, three access systems and 'signal search', which tells authorised users whether any sensitive records exist in an area without revealing species, and noted the trend is to restrict less over time.
one_line_takeaway: Sweden combines a long-running role system, diffusion classes and a yes/no 'signal search' to manage 1.5 million protected records while gradually restricting fewer species.
why_it_matters: Illustrates a mature national approach with practical tools (signal search, logged searches, delegated role management) and identifies the need for standardised authorised APIs and verification categories to exchange sensitive data.
key_points: Timeline: 2000 citizen observatory with one role per account; offline sensitive observation database until 2008; 2014 UserAdmin with Artportalen 2 allowing role switching; 2021 federation system harvesting other Swedish datasets via APIs; new version of UserAdmin a few years ago.
About 158 million records in total, of which about 1.5 million are protected, belonging to 111 species; the list is published as an Excel spreadsheet.
Protection classes generalise to 5, 25 or 50 km squares; users can hide their own observation until a future date (treated as class three) or privately diffuse it.
The system is revised roughly every five years, and the trend is to restrict less, because hidden observations can't be protected if nobody knows about them.

Access routes: ask authorised staff, signal search, or sign a contract giving access to certain classes, usually for a region and taxonomic group; accessed through Artsök, Navet (Swedish Forest Agency) and the Centre's own system.

County administrative boards grant roles to their own staff, so role management is not centralised; searches are logged so leaks can be traced, though leaks usually come from Facebook groups or research papers.

Signal search answers yes/no for whether sensitive data exist in an area for a list of species, with at least a one-year date window; large diffusion areas (e.g. nesting eagles) make it say yes for much of southern Sweden.
Harvesting sensitive data from iNaturalist and observation.org needs authorised APIs and standardised verification categories so verified records can be returned to source.

notable_claims.claim: About 1.5 million of about 158 million Swedish records, belonging to 111 species, are protected.
The trend in Sweden is to restrict fewer species over time because hidden observations are hard to protect.
Leaks usually come from Facebook groups or research papers rather than the system.

recommendations: Standardise authorised APIs for exchanging sensitive data and the verification categories used when returning verified records to source datasets.
limitations: Signal search says yes too often for widely diffused species such as nesting eagles.
No authorised APIs yet for harvesting sensitive data from other platforms.

notable_moments.description: Scale: 1.5 million protected records out of 158 million.
How signal search works.
Need for standards for harvesting sensitive data and returning verifications.

title: Toward RASD Implementation in Brazil: Integrating Conservation, Open Data, and Traditional Knowledge Safeguards

programme.title: Toward RASD Implementation in Brazil: Integrating Conservation, Open Data, and Traditional Knowledge Safeguards
programme.session: SYM23 To see or not to see - that is the question. Managing restricted access data (RASD)
programme.abstract: Brazil, a megadiverse country with extraordinary biological and sociocultural diversity, faces complex challenges in managing and publishing Restricted Access Species Data (RASD). Open-access platforms strengthen science, conservation, and policy, but also amplify risks of misuse of sensitive information. Sensitivity varies across taxonomic groups and use contexts. Key concerns include illegal hunting, wildlife trafficking, predatory collection of commercially valuable species, and pressure on threatened, endemic, or low-density populations. A further dimension involves species linked to associated traditional knowledge (ATK) of Indigenous peoples and local communities. Frameworks such as the CBD, Nagoya Protocol, ILO Convention 169, and Brazil's Law 13.123/2015 require free, prior, and informed consent for use of these resources-rarely met in practice. They provide important safeguards but also reveal limits: fragmented implementation, weak traceability, and uneven recognition of community protocols. Paradoxically, traditional territories remain a critical gap in national repositories, despite their recognized role in conservation. Precise occurrence data are essential for monitoring, enforcement, and policy, producing tension between FAIR and CARE principles and effective protection. We discuss challenges faced by Brazilian data providers in handling RASD and present approaches for differentiated access, including spatial generalization, multi-level sensitivity classification, and controlled access to precise coordinates. The work aligns with TDWG efforts on vocabularies and metadata extensions for RASD, advancing interoperable solutions that balance transparency, conservation, ATK protection, and visibility of traditional communities in biodiversity science.

actual.identification_notes: Introduced as Clara Baringo from the 'Brazilian Biodiversity Information System'; content matches the abstract.

summary: Clara Baringo Fonseca explained that Brazil's national biodiversity information system currently handles sensitive data only by generalisation, informationWithheld and splitting data into private and public datasets. She identified three areas needing distinct rules: endangered species, ongoing research, and socio-biodiversity data and traditional knowledge. Focusing on the last, she argued that communities must control their data, that it is often attributes such as uses, local names or preparation methods rather than the species that must be restricted, and that semi-restricted access (for example for the patent office) and traceability are needed.
one_line_takeaway: Protecting traditional knowledge requires community-controlled, attribute-level and semi-restricted access, not just hiding species locations.
why_it_matters: Brings Indigenous and traditional knowledge into the RASD discussion and shows that restriction needs go beyond location obfuscation of threatened species.
key_points: Brazil's system is growing fast and is trying to repatriate Brazilian data held in repositories outside the country.
Currently only dataGeneralizations, informationWithheld and separate private/public datasets are used.

Three topic areas with different risks and access rules: endangered species (hunting, trafficking), ongoing research, and socio-biodiversity data/traditional knowledge (misappropriation via biopiracy).
International law is not enough; systems must carry community-defined conditions at data level and within a legal framework.
Traditional territories are underrepresented in repositories, but without restriction mechanisms there is little point collecting more data; FAIR and CARE principles should both apply.

Needs include appropriate public metadata, community authorisation of what is shared, semi-restricted access (e.g. patent office can check whether a species has associated traditional knowledge) and traceability.
Use cases: religious or sacred use (kept only for preservation), species use (attributes restricted), and hunting inside protected areas that managers want to monitor.
Restrictable attributes include scientific or local names, type of use, preparation method, time and location; control must always rest with the community.

notable_claims.claim: For traditional knowledge it is usually not the species but its attributes (use, local name, preparation) that must be restricted.
Without mechanisms to restrict data there is little point adding more data from traditional territories.

recommendations: Give communities control over what is sensitive and who can access it.
Provide semi-restricted access, e.g. for patent offices, and traceability of data use.
examples_case_studies: Sacred/religious use knowledge kept only for community preservation.
Monitoring sustainable hunting by communities within protected areas.

notable_moments.description: Three categories needing different access rules.
Three traditional-knowledge use cases.
It is the attributes, not the species, that need restricting.

title: The Edge: Insights into problems that arise from implementing data solutions for restricted access (sensitive) species data

programme.title: The Edge: Insights into problems that arise from implementing data solutions for restricted access (sensitive) species data
programme.session: SYM23 To see or not to see - that is the question. Managing restricted access data (RASD)
programme.abstract: With the rising of Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning, organisations and individuals are increasingly concerned about data on species that they wish to restrict for a wide variety of reasons including everything from the terms and conditions of data licence agreements through to concern about the poaching of attractive species. These so-called sensitive species or restricted access species data (RASD), present problems for the public display, dissemination and use of biodiversity data. Common treatment approaches to RASD involve generalising data through truncation of latitude and longitude, using grids to display data, or withholding points altogether. Many implementations use a list of identified sensitive species as the basis of generalisation. The Atlas of Living Australia (ALA) is a collaborative, digital, open infrastructure displaying biodiversity data from multiple sources, making it accessible and reusable. Data is presented in a consistent, current form, taking into account RASD, for scientists, policy makers, environmental planners, land managers, and industry. To do this, the ALA complies with 8 different approaches to RASD across governments jurisdictions as well as the requirements of diverse entities, from iNaturalist to Indigenous communities. Australia developed an agreed national framework for the management and sharing of RASD in 2023 (www.rasd.ord.au). In developing governance mechanisms to implement the framework, we have identified a range of surprising issues surrounding RASD arising from the complexities of taxonomy, geography and data coming from different sources with different approaches. We will discuss these issues and what responses the ALA has developed to each of them in order to represent data as systematically as possible.

actual.identification_notes: Presented by the session convener himself ('I'm the next speaker'); title referenced as 'The Edge' from U2.

summary: Convener Cameron Slatyer presented the Atlas of Living Australia's experience of edge cases that arise when implementing RASD treatments across more than 184 million records using government-supplied lists. Taxonomy was the biggest problem: undescribed species, disagreements between states, and mismatch between subspecies-level sensitivity and species-level data force precautionary generalisation at higher ranks or whole species. Data errors (wrong coordinates outside a treatment polygon, names or locality in the wrong field, as common with eDNA data) can expose restricted data, and AI mining makes such leaks easier, including an experimental ALA AI tool that exposed a locality recorded in the wrong field.
one_line_takeaway: Plan RASD treatments carefully, because taxonomy, data errors and associated records can silently defeat simple rules like 'generalise to 10 km'.
why_it_matters: Practical lessons from one of the largest RASD implementations, directly relevant to anyone automating sensitive-data treatments.
key_points: Reasons for RASD range from conservation to discouraging entry to bombing ranges and protecting biosecurity eradication sites for trade reasons.

The ALA applies treatments (withholding records and images, generalising, modifying fields) to over 184 million records, driven by lists from state, territory and Commonwealth governments, plus data-provider requests.
Main message: plan the approach - what is being restricted, flow-on effects, and risks.
Taxonomic problems: undescribed RASD species, disagreement among states over current names, and sensitivity at subspecies level while providers supply species-level data (or vice versa).

Rule of thumb: when taxonomic resolution can't be resolved, go up a level; species absent from the backbone attach at genus, so genus-level records get generalised; populations can't be delineated, so the whole species is generalised.
Data errors can expose RASD: erroneous coordinates outside a treatment polygon, scientific names in the wrong field (common in eDNA data with BIN numbers), and locality in the wrong field.
AI makes such errors easier to mine; an experimental ALA AI tool mining iNaturalist data exposed a sensitive species because locality was in the wrong field.

notable_claims.claim: The ALA applies obfuscations to over 184 million records.
Taxonomy is an absolute nightmare when implementing RASD based on species lists.
Erroneous coordinates outside a treatment polygon can leave RASD fully exposed.
AI makes it easy to mine and return information that was thought hidden or altered.

recommendations: Plan your approach: consider what is being restricted, the flow-on effects and the risks of each treatment.
limitations: Precautionary generalisation at higher ranks generalises many unnecessary records.
examples_case_studies: Subspecies flagged sensitive while the provider only supplies species-level data.
eDNA datasets with BIN numbers in the name field.
Experimental AI mining iNaturalist data exposing a misplaced locality.

representative_excerpt.text: So our principal take-home message that underpins all of these issues that we're going to raise is basically making sure you plan your approach.

notable_moments.description: Taxonomy as the biggest RASD implementation problem.
Three common taxonomic edge cases and how the ALA handles them.
Data errors and AI mining exposing restricted data.

title: Using wildlife trade data to support proactive RASD decision-making

programme.title: Using wildlife trade data to support proactive RASD decision-making
programme.session: SYM23 To see or not to see - that is the question. Managing restricted access data (RASD)
programme.abstract: The poaching of wildlife is a growing biodiversity threat, with online trade increasingly facilitating exploitation. Wildlife traders monitor publications, biodiversity repositories, and social media to identify desirable species, and trade activity reveals species being poached prior to formal conservation assessment. While biodiversity data are fundamental to conservation and research it can also increase exploitation of vulnerable taxa. A challenge for RASD frameworks is the time lag between species discovery, conservation assessment, and data restriction. During this period, biodiversity databases may expose species to collection pressure before threats are formally recognised. Current approaches to sensitive species data management are often reactive, relying on formal conservation status or legal protection. This issue is particularly relevant for terrestrial invertebrates, many of which are newly described, range-restricted, data deficient, and increasingly targeted in wildlife trade. Public occurrence datasets are often the only available locality information for these taxa. In Australia, the recent restriction of occurrence data for the trapdoor spider Moggridgea rainbowi following a suspected poaching incident demonstrates adaptive data governance and underscores the value of extending precautionary approaches to additional vulnerable wildlife taxa. We propose that wildlife trade data can function as an early-warning indicator for identifying species subject to poaching and exploitation, and for determining when occurrence data warrant precautionary restriction, prior to formal conservation assessment. Incorporating wildlife trade data into RASD frameworks supports proactive biodiversity data governance and can reduce exploitation risk from data accessibility.

actual.identification_notes: Introduced by the convener after slide problems; content matches the abstract.

summary: PhD researcher Charlotte Lassaline argued that RASD lists, which rely on formal conservation assessments, are biased towards well-studied vertebrates and miss poorly known, range-restricted invertebrates that are increasingly sought in wildlife trade. Using the Kangaroo Island pygmy trapdoor spider, whose public data were restricted within about two weeks of a reported poaching incident, she contrasted reactive and proactive approaches. She proposed a wildlife trade species sensitivity framework combining trade-demand measures with weighted biological sensitivity factors into a vulnerability index to flag species for data protection before formal assessment.
one_line_takeaway: Wildlife trade data can act as an early warning system to protect species' locality data before formal conservation assessments catch up.
why_it_matters: Offers a practical, evidence-based way to prioritise species for data restriction, particularly for invertebrates that formal lists overlook.
key_points: Wildlife trade is predicted to affect one in five species worldwide; poachers use public occurrence data to locate species.
RASD lists are largely informed by formal assessments (IUCN Red List, CITES, government lists) that are slow and data-hungry.
Only about 1.4% of insects and just over 1% of arachnids have been evaluated by the IUCN Red List, versus most vertebrates.
Invertebrates are often newly described, range-restricted and data deficient, yet increasingly desired by collectors; public occurrence data may be the only information on where they occur.
There is a 'window of vulnerability' between exploitation starting and formal recognition and legal protection.
Kangaroo Island pygmy trapdoor spider: nationally endangered after bushfires but data still public; a poaching incident reported to the ALA led to restriction within about two weeks (reactive).

Proposed framework: trade demand (number of adverts, individuals traded, market value) plus weighted biological sensitivity factors (distribution, population size, reproductive output, dispersal) produce a vulnerability index.
High-index species already protected should be considered for RASD listing; unassessed ones are candidates for investigation; data should be obscured not removed, available on request, and reviewed.
methods: vulnerability index from weighted sensitivity factors

notable_claims.claim: Wildlife trade is predicted to affect one in every five species worldwide.
Only 1.4% of insects and just over 1% of arachnids have had their conservation status evaluated by the IUCN.
After a reported poaching incident, the spider's data were restricted online in less than about two weeks.

recommendations: Use trade pressure as an early indicator of exploitation risk for RASD decisions.
Obscure rather than remove sensitive locality data, keep access by request, and review restrictions as research emerges.
examples_case_studies: Kangaroo Island pygmy trapdoor spider poaching incident.

representative_excerpt.text: So importantly, this means the trade pressure can be considered as an early indicator of exploitation risk. It doesn't necessarily tell us that a species is vulnerable, but it tells us that a species is being exposed to a pressure that may lead to it being threatened in the very near future.

notable_moments.description: IUCN Red List coverage gap for insects and arachnids.
Kangaroo Island pygmy trapdoor spider case.
The wildlife trade species sensitivity framework.
