title: A new standard for restricted access (sensitive) species data

programme.title: A new standard for restricted access (sensitive) species data
programme.session: SYM23 To see or not to see - that is the question. Managing restricted access data (RASD)
programme.abstract: There is growing concern among many organisations and researchers about so-called sensitive species or restricted access species data (RASD), that is, data that needs to be modified or withheld from the general public. This data is intrinsically difficult to share or display and the existing Darwin Core fields no longer give data managers the flexibility to deal with the diverse array of emerging issues that managers encounter. Following a workshop in 2023, a Darwin Core Task Group was established on sensitive species data. The Task Group has developed a suite of reasons and treatments and an underlying vocabulary that enables data managers to communicate what has happened to restricted data and why in line with FAIR principles. The data extension is intended to handle a wide range of reasons for restricted access and a similarly wide range of treatment options that can be applied to the data. This proposed data extension paths the way for institutions, regions or countries to develop a consistent approach to the management of restricted data. We will outline and discuss the new restricted access species data extension, including solutions for both Darwin Core Native and Darwin Core Data Packages.

actual.identification_notes: Introduced as 'Tanya Latey' (ASR) from the ALA; content matches the abstract.

summary: Tania Laity presented the work of the TDWG Sensitive Species Extension Task Group (convened by the ALA, GBIF and Gaia Resources), which arose from a 2023 Hobart workshop and is building on Arthur Chapman's work. The group has drafted hierarchical vocabularies of RASD reasons (privacy, sensitive location, harm, biosecurity, species attributes, usage restrictions, First Nations cultural significance) and treatments (coordinate obfuscation, attribute generalisation, date generalisation, withholding and embargo). She showed how treatments attach to records in Darwin Core Archives (as a star-schema extension) and Darwin Core Data Package (via join tables), walked through the treatment fields, and demonstrated a cave case study with a troglobitic spider, fossils and undescribed mites.
one_line_takeaway: A proposed Darwin Core extension would record why data were restricted and what treatment was applied, in a one-to-many way similar to MeasurementOrFact.
why_it_matters: Would give data users visibility of restrictions and reasons across providers and aggregators, supporting FAIR handling of restricted data; submission to TDWG was planned by end of year.
key_points: Task group first met in September 2024; conveners from ALA (Cam Slatyer, Tania Laity, Simon Sharon), GBIF and Gaia Resources; members from government, universities, data providers and aggregators in several countries.
The group prefers 'restricted access species data' over 'sensitive' because 'sensitive' makes people reluctant to share.

Reason vocabulary: personal information and privacy; sensitive species location; potential harm to people or property; biosecurity risk; species attributes (e.g. roosting or nesting sites); usage restrictions (legal contracts); First Nations cultural significance.

Hierarchical treatment vocabulary: coordinate obfuscation (truncation to grid, snapping to polygon centroid, randomising), generalising attributes (taxon level, locality text), generalising dates (month, year, decade), withholding records/attributes/datasets and embargoes.
A treatment needs a reason; one reason may need several treatments; a record may have several reasons - applied one-to-many like the MeasurementOrFact extension.
In Darwin Core Archive, treatments are an extension pointing to the core; in Darwin Core Data Package, a treatment class is joined to events or occurrences via join tables (e.g. event-treatment).

Treatment fields include target field, treatment reason, treatment type, free-text description, start and end dates (for embargoes), treatment organisation and a contentious 'treatment in effect' flag.
Draft documentation for the TDWG maintenance process was being prepared for submission by the end of the year.

entities.name: TDWG Sensitive Species Extension Task Group

methods: join tables in Darwin Core Data Package

notable_claims.claim: The task group arose from a workshop at the 2023 TDWG meeting in Hobart.
The group hopes to submit the draft standard for review by the end of this year.
The vocabularies apply in a one-to-many relationship with a Darwin Core record, similar to MeasurementOrFact.

limitations: The 'treatment in effect' field is contentious and may be dropped.
future_work: Submit draft documentation to TDWG for review and ratification by end of year.
examples_case_studies: Cave case study: troglobitic spider whose occurrence remarks reveal a cave (coordinates truncated to 10 km and remarks withheld), fossils attracting illegal collection, and undescribed mites under a one-year embargo until publication.

summary: Two panel Q&A sessions chaired by Cameron Slatyer: an impromptu one on the first four talks when the session ran ahead of schedule, and a longer one with all speakers after the final talk. Topics included the real cost of managing sensitivities (several FTE in Sweden, monthly list updates at the ALA, opportunity cost), breaches (none known), personal privacy of collectors, whether generative AI already exposes locations, obfuscation on request of data collectors (e.g. pest hunting and Indigenous datasets), taxonomic upscaling, names that reveal localities, correlated fields such as collector and date, historical data, informationWithheld usage, and the feasibility for global collections like the Smithsonian. It closed with the argument that much RASD reflects expert preciousness rather than real threat and that restriction should be justified formally.
one_line_takeaway: Restricting data is costly and imperfect; panellists argued for targeted, 'shrink-wrapped', well-justified restrictions handled centrally rather than blanket redaction.
why_it_matters: Captures practitioners' candid views on the costs, risks and unintended consequences of RASD, including the conservation harm of over-restriction and the new threat of AI mining.
key_points: Cost: Sweden has about three FTE handling access contracts; FinBIF sees a large hidden human cost and opportunity cost; the ALA updates RASD lists monthly but estimates about a million records came in only because RASD treatment was available.
No panellist knew of data breaches; Will Morris argued habitat loss, not knowledge of locations, is the main threat and 'security by obscurity' is a poor conservation tool.
Collector privacy (Kew question): Sweden requires contactable reporters but allows hiding observations; INBO sometimes attributes data to a team rather than individuals.
Generative AI (Gemini, ChatGPT) could already reveal where the Kangaroo Island spider lives because the data were mined years ago, though a long-restricted species was refused.
Entire datasets may be generalised as a condition of sharing, e.g. vertebrate pest data (to deter illegal hunters trespassing) and Indigenous datasets.

ALA generalises only records attached at genus level, not all species in a genus; privacy-obscured iNaturalist records not shared with government led to an area with a highly endangered species being cleared.
Names can reveal localities (e.g. a species named after Studley Park); the extension allows withholding the taxon name while keeping the record discoverable.
Obfuscation is a trade-off: related fields (collector, date, sequential identifiers) can re-identify localities; effort must stop somewhere.
No cutoff date for historical data according to the ALA (30% of ALA species' latest record is over 50 years old); mobile species like nesting birds differ.

Global collections can't annotate every record; in Australia collections rely on the ALA to generalise centrally. Cameron argued about 80% of restrictions stem from experts being precious about taxa (e.g. 2,000 sensitive orchids) while actually poached taxa go unprotected.
Many ALA and GBIF users don't realise generalised data exist; better ways to represent generalised data are needed.
questions: How much do organisations actually spend on handling sensitive data?
Is withholding data already too late given AI has indexed past data?
How can global collections with small staff decide what to restrict?
How can culture change so that data need not be redacted?

notable_claims.claim: Sweden has about three full-time staff handling restricted-data access contracts.
About a million records came into the ALA that would not have been public without its RASD system.
Security by obscurity is a really poor conservation tool; habitat loss is the number one threat.

recommendations: 'Shrink-wrap' restrictions as tightly as possible to keep data available for research and conservation.
Justify restrictions through formal processes rather than blanket precautionary redaction.
Develop better ways to show users that data are generalised.

q_and_a.question: How expensive is handling sensitivities, in any units?

q_and_a.question: Have there been data breaches and are escalation processes mature?

q_and_a.answer_summary: The extension allows withholding the taxon name while keeping the record discoverable.

q_and_a.question: Will the extension capture signed agreements restricting publication?
q_and_a.answer_summary: Yes, via a legal agreement treatment reason and the description field.

q_and_a.question: How far back should RASD rules apply to historical data?
q_and_a.answer_summary: ALA view: no cutoff date; others note mobile species like nesting birds change location.

q_and_a.question: Do you fill Darwin Core informationWithheld?
q_and_a.answer_summary: Yes, ALA does; INBO uses metadata too; many users don't realise data are generalised.

q_and_a.question: How can a global collection with limited staff mark 11 million records?
q_and_a.answer_summary: Not feasible record by record; rely on central exposure/generalisation (as the ALA does for Australian collections).

title: Open Digital Curation Needs: openness, interoperability, provenance

programme.title: Open Digital Curation Needs: openness, interoperability, provenance
programme.session: SYM13A Responsible AI, Open Digital Curation, and Round-Tripping for Biodiversity Data
programme.abstract: Moving toward open digital curation to make round-tripping possible, consider the necessary interplay of three facets: openness, interoperability, and provenance. Via open application programming interfaces (APIs), data becomes accessible to humans and AI. Given openness, interoperability becomes possible and offers opportunities to contribute and collaborate. We share three examples here: [iNaturalist (iNat)](https://www.inaturalist.org/), the [Catalogue of Life (COL)](https://www.catalogueoflife.org/), and the [Global Biodiversity Information Facility (GBIF](https://www.gbif.org/)). With iNat's open APIs, our researchers using [TaxonWorks (TW)](https://taxonworks.org/) can pull images and related data into TW. In the other direction, iNat curators submit or point their users to the specific gitHub repository to log taxonomic inquiries directly to those curating these data. This reduces steps (e. g. emails) needed to get to round-tripping. From TW, our collections data go straight to GBIF. We grab the GBIF-related ingestion feedback directly into TW to again reduce the human mental data curation burden and imagine future automated validation. Our taxonomic data flow interoperably between TW to COL via [Checklist Bank](https://www.checklistbank.org/). To do all of the above, we must decide on and use identifiers (e. g. [ORCiD](https://orcid.org/)s, [Wikidata Q numbers] (https://www.wikidata.org/wiki/Q43649390)) and the related metadata that helps us ensure we have a provenance trail. Understanding our data through these breadcrumbs provides the foundation for round-tripping. In TW, imagine extracting data from literature using large language models (LLMs). Our communities need software and APIs to vet the resulting data, along with robust provenance. We find it's these decisions, usually human-mediated, that are difficult to capture in context, for example, with the user interface. When we connect via our APIs for data exchange, what must we persist? What can be temporary?

title: Machine-Ready Botanical Data: Mapping Integrated Collections and Traits with Darwin Core Data Package

programme.title: Machine-Ready Botanical Data: Mapping Integrated Collections and Traits with Darwin Core Data Package
programme.session: SYM13A Responsible AI, Open Digital Curation, and Round-Tripping for Biodiversity Data
programme.abstract:
The Darwin Core Data Package (DwC-DP) provides a powerful foundation for representing biodiversity data in ways that are both AI-ready and round-trip capable. We present a DwC-DP concept mapping developed for the Missouri Botanical Garden (MBG) that integrates herbarium specimens, living collections, and trait (extended specimen) data within a unified framework. To our knowledge, this represents the first detailed cross-collection DwC-DP concept map in the botanical domain, demonstrating how heterogeneous institutional data can be aligned into a coherent, machine-actionable structure.

We identify key areas in the mapping where controlled vocabularies are needed to further define the standard within the relevant communities. In particular, traits and character states constitute a critical class of information for AI applications, such as taxon identification and ecological modeling. While DwC-DP provides a structural basis for integrating such data, practical use requires alignment with external ontologies. We discuss an approach under development at MBG to integrate a trait ontology with DwC-DP, building on an internal pilot system.

Furthermore, we examine a gap in the current design relevant to AI-readiness around identifications: the need to capture not only the data that informs a determination, but the evidentiary and procedural basis for the decision. We consider how such information might be modeled externally to the core design.

This work highlights both the immediate utility of DwC-DP for institutional integration and the collaborative work needed, particularly around shared vocabularies, to advance interoperable and AI-ready botanical data systems.

title: From Images to Structured Data: A Scalable AI Workflow for Natural History Museums

programme.title: From Images to Structured Data: A Scalable AI Workflow for Natural History Museums
programme.session: SYM13A Responsible AI, Open Digital Curation, and Round-Tripping for Biodiversity Data
programme.abstract:
Natural history museums worldwide face a major digitisation backlog. To unlock this critical bottleneck in research, the biodiversity informatics community is rapidly developing AI-based workflows to automate specimen label transcription and thus speed up the digitisation process. We present here a case study in which we describe an effective AI workflow for extracting specimen label data using Gemini 3.

The workflow combines batch processing with a two-stage Gemini large language model pipeline via API integrations. High-resolution specimen images are first processed to transcribe handwritten and printed labels. After post-processing to remove duplicate data, extract identifiers and fix common transcription errors, the cleaned transcriptions are resubmitted for data structuring using a predefined JSON schema aligned with collection management requirements.

A central design principle is provenance-aware, non-destructive integration of the data into the Finnish museum collection management system. Existing human-curated data are never overwritten. The workflow also records metadata describing which fields were generated by AI, while process-level provenance metadata are archived to support transparency, auditability, and reproducibility.

To support scalable quality assurance, the pipeline automatically generates validation reports from a random sample for human review. Our presentation discusses workflow architecture, provenance strategies, validation models, and lessons learned from deploying AI-assisted transcription at an institutional scale.

actual.identification_notes: Introduced as 'Anna Koivunen' (ASR).

summary: Anne Koivunen, head of digitisation at Luomus, described a pragmatic AI pipeline for tackling a backlog of 10 million undigitised specimens with fewer staff and a goal of full digitisation by 2045. Label images go to Gemini 2.5 for verbatim transcription, then again with a prompt and schema for structured data saved into the Kotka collection management system; for messy vascular plant and moss labels an 'intent' step asks the model what the writer meant. AI output never overrides human-transcribed fields, is flagged, and run metadata (model version, prompts) is stored. She stressed that winning collection staff's trust was harder than the AI itself.
one_line_takeaway: A simple 'just do it' AI transcription pipeline with schema prompts, an intent step and full provenance can make label digitisation scale.
why_it_matters: A realistic, production-oriented example from a mid-sized museum showing both technical choices and the organisational change needed to adopt AI transcription.

Scalability means variety as well as volume: taxon-specific label types, handwritten/typed, multilingual (Finnish, Swedish, Russian), corrections and differing collection traditions.

title: Closing the Loop: The DiSSCo Annotation Validation Framework for Trustworthy Data Round-Tripping

programme.title: Closing the Loop: The DiSSCo Annotation Validation Framework for Trustworthy Data Round-Tripping
programme.session: SYM13A Responsible AI, Open Digital Curation, and Round-Tripping for Biodiversity Data
programme.abstract:
The Distributed System of Scientific Collections (DiSSCo) represents a paradigm shift in specimen data infrastructure, moving from a "custodian-only" model to a distributed, community-driven data lifecycle. Central to this is the ability for human experts and artificial intelligence (AI) agents to enrich Digital Specimens through annotations. However, as AI-driven workflows scale up, there is a risk of specimens becoming annotated with hundreds of low-quality annotations, which threatens synchronization with the source data. Without robust governance, collection managers will face "annotation fatigue," stalling "round-tripping"-the flow of data enrichments back to Collection Management Systems (CMS).

This presentation introduces the DiSSCo Annotation Validation Framework, which went through an international public consultation process in mid-2026. For responsible open digital curation, it treats annotations as first-class digital objects with full provenance, persistent identifiers (Handles) and attribution.

At its technical core, the framework differentiates by the scientific impact of the proposed data change. It aims to find a balance between low-impact corrections, which can be processed efficiently through automated services and high-impact modifications such as taxonomic reidentifications or stratigraphic updates, which should trigger a curated peer-review workflow.

By filtering and prioritizing incoming enrichments, the framework ensures that data round-tripping to source CMS remains high-quality, manageable, and highly trusted. This mechanism effectively closes the loop between external research communities, AI annotators, and physical collection institutions, ensuring Digital Specimens remain dynamic, accurate, and reflective of the latest scientific consensus.

actual.identification_notes: Chair introduced 'Wouter Addink'; content matches the abstract.

summary: Wouter Addink, DiSSCo technical director, framed the problem of a curator swamped by thousands of AI annotations that could override records and lose provenance. DiSSCo's planned annotation validation framework runs machine annotation services centrally for all collections and places annotations in layers: an untouched institutional base layer, a community enrichment layer for unvetted annotations, and a curated consensus layer. Annotations pass automated technical validation, then are routed by type and impact: low-impact corrections are auto-promoted, medium-impact ones need a two-agent condition or a trusted agent, and high-impact ones (new identifications, type status, catalogue numbers) need managed expert review. A public consultation was extended to 16 October with an online meeting on 22 October.
one_line_takeaway: DiSSCo proposes impact-based, layered validation so trusted annotations are promoted automatically and only high-impact ones need expert review.
why_it_matters: Addresses how to absorb large volumes of human and AI annotations without losing institutional control or provenance, a key prerequisite for AI-assisted curation at scale.
key_points: Scenario: a museum builds an AI annotation service that produces thousands or millions of annotations; directly writing to the CMS loses sovereignty and provenance.
Machine annotation services run in the DiSSCo infrastructure so they can be applied to all participating collections; anyone with ORCID can annotate.
Layers of trust: institutional base layer (untouched), community enrichment layer (unvetted), managed review, and curated consensus layer holding the latest digital specimen version.

Validation flow: submission with persistent identifier and agent ID; automated technical validation (schema, content policies, e.g. no malicious content or exact locations of protected species); automated routing; promotion creating a new version.
All versions are stored, making the system resilient to errors in automated promotion.
Comments and quality flags go to the enrichment layer; delete proposals need administrator review.

Edits are assessed for impact: low (error corrections, measurements) auto-promoted; medium needs two agents agreeing or a trusted agent with a good track record; high (new identification, type status, catalogue number) needs expert review, where experts may also be trusted machines.

Three documents (general concept, technical specifications, governance/policy framework) are under public consultation, extended to 16 October; online meeting 22 October; finalisation by year end, then implementation.

notable_claims.claim: Low-impact annotations like error corrections can be automatically promoted to the consensus layer.
Medium-impact annotations require a two-agent condition or a trusted agent.
The public consultation was extended to 16 October with an online meeting on 22 October.

recommendations: Review the consultation documents, starting with the general concept.
future_work: Finalise the framework documents by end of year and start implementation.

title: Geonomia: Metadata and Community for Georeferencing

programme.title: Geonomia: Metadata and Community for Georeferencing
programme.session: SYM13A Responsible AI, Open Digital Curation, and Round-Tripping for Biodiversity Data
programme.abstract:
There has been considerable progress and investment into the digitisation of natural history collections, particularly among larger institutions that hold globally distributed specimen collections. These specimen records provide the “what, where, when” evidence used as the basis of much research. Data handling pipelines often include data cleaning steps which enhance our understanding of the core “what, where, when” and other attributes of the specimen record. Attributing these enhancements, along with acknowledging their source, to the digital specimen record is difficult due to the distributed nature of research tasks, many of which take place outside the holding institution of the specimen.

Distributed curation and management of digital specimen records are a necessary step in their use to support specific research interests and objectives, resulting in rich but fragmented, unusable data. Data are easily transferable, though trust in the data is essential for passive cross-institutional collaboration, particularly for subjective and ad-hoc tasks such as georeferencing.

With a focus on improving geographic coordinates or retrospectively adding new spatial data, attendees will be presented with the Geonomia project, which clusters GBIF-mediated specimen data to uncover field collecting patterns. The system includes a georeferencing application which will be demonstrated alongside community workshop outputs focussing on the digital curation of the georeferencing process and outputs. The aim of the project is to encourage the re-integration of comprehensive georeference metadata and continually improve the context of field collecting patterns.

Nicolson, N., Bachman, S. and Whittaker, A. (2026) Geonomia. Available at: https://github.com/geonomia (Accessed: 27/05/2026)

summary: Nicky Nicolson presented Geonomia, a Kew project to make specimens' textual localities computable. Only 13% of Kew's 6.3 million digitised specimens appear on GBIF maps, yet analysis of download predicates behind citations showed two-thirds of users filter spatially, discarding most of Kew's data. Using density-based clustering of collector number and date (collectors move forward in time and space), the team groups specimens into collecting trips across all herbaria's GBIF data, finds outliers, and passes trip-level batches to an LLM to summarise itineraries, habitats and regions, publishing results with Datasette. She argued collecting trips are a useful entity between GBIF's related records and Bionomia's collector careers, and that georeferencing should be shared community work.

title: From satellite embeddings to Darwin Core: an open, ensemble-AI workflow for Prosopis juliflora mapping and reusable training-dataset generation

programme.title: From satellite embeddings to Darwin Core: an open, ensemble-AI workflow for Prosopis juliflora mapping and reusable training-dataset generation
programme.session: SYM13A Responsible AI, Open Digital Curation, and Round-Tripping for Biodiversity Data
programme.abstract:
Prosopis juliflora is among the most consequential invaders of global drylands, drawing down groundwater, depressing crop yields, and displacing grassland and pastoral commons. In Kutch, Gujarat, where Prosopis has overrun gauchar lands and Banni grassland fringes, classifier outputs guide biomass sourcing for a pyrolysis facility at Anjar, so every update carries operational consequence.

The pipeline fuses three openly licensed inputs on Google Earth Engine. AlphaEarth embeddings provide a learned per-pixel representation. Sentinel-2 contributes NDVI and EVI. SRTM derivatives (slope, roughness, TPI) separate Prosopis from similar canopy on rocky slopes. A four-model ensemble (two Random Forests, GTB, CART) is trained on versioned polygons tagged by source: presences, absences, false-positive corrections, and positive refinements. The correction loop turns model errors into named, attributable training records rather than silently retraining over them. Ensemble accuracy reaches ~91% on held-out test data.

Layered masks (hills, water, road buffers) exclude implausible pixels; each is a named, recorded operation with justification and source, auditable downstream.

Every positive pixel becomes a Darwin Core occurrence with basisOfRecord=MachineObservation, coordinateUncertaintyInMeters from pixel geometry, and identifiedBy naming both human curators and model version. Ensemble probability is carried as a MeasurementOrFact extension. The dataset, training polygons (CC BY 4.0), mask metadata, and model artefact are structured for GBIF publication, closing the round-trip from human curation to AI enrichment to reusable training material.

summary: Pranav Jha described mapping the invasive Prosopis juliflora (Neltuma juliflora) across India, especially about 1.1 million hectares in Kutch, Gujarat, using satellite data and geospatial foundation model embeddings. The workflow combines Sentinel, hyperspectral and NISAR radar data with ground truthing, AlphaEarth embeddings, NDVI and slope checks, reaching about 91% accuracy, and uses 3 m hyperspectral signatures to distinguish Prosopis from similar natives. Ground teams validate predicted clusters through drop, curation and refined zones to build reusable training datasets, and the model is being extended to Lantana camara and mangroves.
one_line_takeaway: Satellite embeddings plus hyperspectral signatures and ground validation can map invasive Prosopis at scale and generate reusable, attributable training data.
why_it_matters: Links remote sensing AI to biodiversity data reuse, with a focus on transparent, reusable evidence for invasive species management.
key_points: Prosopis juliflora is among IUCN's top invasive species and has spread across APAC and sub-Saharan Africa; in Kutch it covers about 1.1 million hectares, harming native species and pastoral communities, and has spread to 20+ agroclimatic zones.
Satellite mapping is needed to understand invasion at scale, over time (multi-date imagery), where to look next and what it displaces.
Density is mapped at 10 m resolution to guide ground teams to hotspots.

Inputs: Sentinel, hyperspectral (e.g. AVIRIS and others), NISAR SAR data and ground truth; AlphaEarth geospatial foundation model embeddings train a classifier, followed by NDVI and slope/elevation checks.
Current accuracy about 91%; working with Google DeepMind to include it in Google Earth.
Prosopis resembles native Prosopis cineraria and acacias; 3 m hyperspectral spectroscopy separates them.
Ground workflow of drop, curating and refined zones produces reusable datasets; goal is transparent, attributable, reusable evidence.
Next: Lantana camara in northern India and mangroves in sub-Saharan regions.

The current model accuracy is 91%.

future_work: Extend to Lantana camara and mangroves.

title: Open Digital Curation and Round-Tripping Biodiversity Data Enhancements Across Collection Infrastructures: Six Years and 50 Million Links in Bionomia

programme.title: Open Digital Curation and Round-Tripping Biodiversity Data Enhancements Across Collection Infrastructures: Six Years and 50 Million Links in Bionomia
programme.session: SYM13B Responsible AI, Open Digital Curation, and Round-Tripping for Biodiversity Data
programme.abstract: Throughout the past 6 years, [Bionomia](https://bionomia.net) has supported open digital curation through machine-readable annotations, bidirectional synchronization workflows, and contributor attribution that preserves curatorial authority while enabling broader participation. Case studies will illustrate how annotations involving specimen linkages can be generated by humans and redistributed back to source repositories rather than remaining isolated within downstream aggregators. Bionomia’s data processing tools, services, and outputs enable lightweight integration with collection management systems while preserving institutional ownership and editorial control over incoming enhancements. Recently, the human name parsing tool was successfully ported to a high-performance Go package using Claude AI. The platform also exposes mechanisms for crediting contributors in ways that support professional recognition, reproducibility, and reuse. The continuous cycle of incremental enhancements has not been without its technical challenges, and these will be discussed in relation to Darwin Core and data exchange structures used by our community. By framing digital curation as an ongoing and collaborative process rather than a terminal publication event, Bionomia demonstrates how round-tripping infrastructures can strengthen resilience, trust, outreach, and long-term stewardship across biodiversity data ecosystems despite uncertainties about any one project's governance and sustainability.

actual.identification_notes: Virtual pre-recorded talk; the chair welcomed David Shorthouse, and the video initially played only as audio before being fixed.

summary: In a pre-recorded talk, David Shorthouse questioned calls for taxonomists to train AI identification models without credit, and highlighted that 60% of preserved specimens in GBIF lack any identifiedBy value. He reviewed six years of Bionomia: services for individuals (alerts when specimens are used in research, Zenodo archives with DOIs) and for organisations (frictionless data packages of CSV files, badges), and the potential of the collector social network for attribution suggestions. He identified unstable occurrence identifiers as the main barrier to round-tripping, noted no CMS can record third-party attribution provenance, and discussed the Darwin Core Data Package's agent terms, predicting recordedByID and identifiedByID will become obsolete and calling for a TDWG task group on an agent role vocabulary.

title: Type specimens in Wikidata

programme.title: Type specimens in Wikidata
programme.session: SYM13B Responsible AI, Open Digital Curation, and Round-Tripping for Biodiversity Data
programme.abstract:
Type specimens play a vital role in ensuring the correct application of scientific names. Recently a type specimen data model has been created for Wikidata. This data model results from work undertaken by participants of the [Wikidata:WikiProject Natural History Specimen Data Mode](https://www.wikidata.org/wiki/Wikidata:WikiProject_Natural_History_Specimen_Data_Model)l. The data model encourages the creation of type specimen Wikidata items that link to appropriately structured data. Several Wikidata properties were proposed and accepted by the Wikidata community to facilitate the formation of this data model. The data model also encourages the linking of institutional identifiers to appropriate type specimen items.

Documentation was produced to guide editors in the creation and linking of type specimen Wikidata items. This included an exemplar spreadsheet generated from an OpenRefine project creating Wikidata items for holotype specimens held in the New Zealand Arthropod Collection.

A data model for structured data on Wikimedian Commons was also proposed by the WikiProject. This is intended to apply to natural history specimen media files added to Wikimedia Commons. Again documentation was produced to assist editors to create or add appropriate structured data to natural history specimen image files.

One of the core aims of the WikiProject was to align specimen and type-material modelling across Wikimedia projects with existing biodiversity informatics standards. As a result crosswalk documentation was produced to illustrate the mapping between fields of the Wikidata type specimen data model and Darwin Core. Crosswalk documentation was also produced mapping Wikidata properties used to add structured data on Wikimedia Commons to media files and equivalent Darwin Core terms.

title: Here, There, and Everywhere: Modelling Research Expeditions in Wikidata

programme.title: Here, There, and Everywhere: Modelling Research Expeditions in Wikidata

programme.abstract:
Research expeditions are major sources of natural history collections and connect distributed cultural heritage across institutions and countries. However, expedition data remain fragmented, inconsistently modelled, and often lack stable identifiers. This hampers discoverability, interoperability, and provenance tracking, while also limiting efforts to contextualise collecting events and practices within their broader historical context. The TDWG Task Group “Modelling Research Expeditions” developed recommendations for modelling and linking of expedition data, working towards a shared terminology, a reusable data model and schema, and best practices for publishing expedition metadata as Linked Open Data.

The presentation proposes recommendations for an expedition data model connecting both historical and contemporary collecting events with specimens and other objects, participants, institutions, localities, itineraries, publications, and archival records. Particular emphasis is placed on interoperability with Darwin Core, the use of Wikidata identifiers, and collaborative community curation of expedition metadata as a complement or even replacement for the round-tripping of data back into collection databases. The recommendations aim to improve data quality, facilitate cross-institutional linking, annotation and validation workflows, and transparency regarding the historical context of collecting activities. By enabling machine-readable and multilingual representation of expedition data, the proposed model contributes to making collection data more FAIR and supports broader reuse in e.g., knowledge graphs, visualisation tools, and digital humanities research.

title: Digital curation across the biodiversity data lifecycle, at the node level (SiB Colombia), aggregator level (GBIF) and how to incorporate user feedback

programme.title: Digital curation across the biodiversity data lifecycle, at the node level (SiB Colombia), aggregator level (GBIF) and how to incorporate user feedback
programme.session: SYM13B Responsible AI, Open Digital Curation, and Round-Tripping for Biodiversity Data
programme.abstract:
Digital curation should be a continuous process through the biodiversity data lifecycle. Within the GBIF ecosystem, it starts at the publishing level facilitated by GBIF nodes, continues with quality checks done automatically by GBIF Data Processing and incorporates user feedback provided through GBIF.org or when publishers are contacted directly.

Here we will explain how the data curation is done at SiB Colombia as one example of a GBIF node. Using a publishing support model called “acompañamientos”, where a dedicated helpdesk team reviews some prioritized DwC elements and provides feedback to publishers before publication. With the main goal of facilitating data mobilization by ensuring the data is as complete as possible, meets quality requirements and is free of consistency errors.

The next step is the data processing done automatically by GBIF pipelines before ingestion, addressing some of the most common and relevant elements for users, such as dates, coordinates, controlled vocabularies, etc. These quality flags allow publishers and users to review and improve their data.

The next section covers how the user feedback is currently handled on GBIF, for taxonomic issues that are handled with a human/AI approach, where an AI agent generates JSON tags that are later reviewed by a human team that ensures results are correct and there are no hallucinations.

We also present an overview of user feedback related to occurrence records, covering how much feedback arrives at GBIF, how often publishers respond, and whether they are willing to correct their data.

Finally, we will explore how things can be improved on all fronts to have better data curation and round tripping in the long run for GBIF mediated data.

GBIF interprets names and other fields and exposes flags through the Data Validator and annotated downloads. title: Closing Gaps in Specimen Metadata: A Collaborative Annotation and Feedback Platform for Natural History Collections

programme.title: Closing Gaps in Specimen Metadata: A Collaborative Annotation and Feedback Platform for Natural History Collections
programme.session: SYM13B Responsible AI, Open Digital Curation, and Round-Tripping for Biodiversity Data
programme.abstract:
While the digitization of natural history collections is accelerating globally, GBIF data trends reveal a critical bottleneck: a persistent gap in the completeness of digitized specimen records. Many records still lack essential metadata, specifically accurate taxonomic classifications, precise geospatial coordinates, and explicit collection dates. Bridging these gaps requires a systematic, scalable annotation mechanism.

Inspired by collaborative frameworks such as the European DiSSCover initiative, we developed an annotation platform tailored for digital specimens. The platform ingests natural history collection data from the Taiwan Biodiversity Information Alliance (TBIA). The platform allows users to query target specimens by data completeness or holding institution through filtering functions. To optimize the workflow, it pairs an intuitive manual interface with AI-assisted data extraction, enabling users to verify and adjust AI-generated transcriptions to increase processing efficiency.

Aggregated annotations form a trackable feedback loop, allowing enriched records to be returned to the original data providers for review and merging into their primary databases. This continuous cycle improves the quality of open data while lowering the barrier to participation for smaller institutions. Collections from institutions without sufficient staff often fail to transcribe labels fast enough to keep pace with imaging; the platform lets them publish specimen images early and recruit public contributors to fill in the data, increasing the usability of their holdings and encouraging institutions with un-digitized collections to join the biodiversity informatics community.

title: Responsible and GreenAI: Does our community need Gigantic Data Centers to deliver?

programme.title: Responsible and GreenAI: Does our community need Gigantic Data Centers to deliver?
programme.session: SYM13B Responsible AI, Open Digital Curation, and Round-Tripping for Biodiversity Data
programme.abstract: Both the public and private sectors invest billions in AI. Key players notably in the US, China and the EU try to outcompete each other by releasing the fastest and most powerful Large Language Models (LLMs) and building the largest data centers to cope with the increasing demand for computational power. AI Factories are end-to-end systems that continuously turn data into AI models and AI-powered services at scale. For example, in February 2025, the EU launched the InvestAI initiative to mobilise €200 billion in broader AI investment, including a dedicated €20 billion European fund for AI Gigafactories. In the US, figures around 500 billion US$ invested in AI infrastructures are cited, with similar figures being estimated from China. Looking at the global scale, with the digitisation efforts and open science policies, billions of data points and media resources around biodiversity are made available and potential candidates for AI applications. One may argue that our discipline is actually in need of such large resources to deliver. When sizing down to specific taxon levels or smaller geographic areas, training datasets of several 100 000 to less than 1 Mio of records managed to deliver accurate AI models for automated species recognition based on images or sounds. When consulted, researchers often answer that they can run the algorithms on their local servers, even local computers, without being in need of heavy computing power from large data centers. Could Small Language Models (SMLs) dedicated to a specific discipline or question, including fact-checking, taking into account ethical and legal aspects, do the job and become a model for a greener and more rational use of AI?

title: Agentic AI Systems for Specimen Interaction and Camera-Based Observation

programme.title: Agentic AI Systems for Specimen Interaction and Camera-Based Observation
programme.session: LT17 Bots, Bits, and Biodiversity
programme.abstract: The study, recording and interpretation of natural history specimens is a highly contextual activity, drawing on curatorial expertise, published literature, collections data and comparative knowledge across taxa. In many cases, working with specimens is also a physical process, requiring observation, annotation, transcription, imaging and careful handling. These activities are time-consuming and can limit the number of specimens that can be examined, recorded or reinterpreted at scale. This presentation explores the development of an agentic AI system capable of interacting with physical specimens through a dedicated imaging and specimen observation platform. Operating on local/on-device hardware, the system integrates large language models, computer vision, camera control and hardware control to support direct observation and interpretation of specimens within collections environments. The system uses a camera-based platform to capture visual data from specimens and incorporate this information into the model’s reasoning process. By combining visual input with collections data and relevant literature, the agent can support tasks such as specimen inspection, metadata verification, annotation and morphological interpretation. Through the integration of RAG, the system links observed specimens to contextual knowledge, enabling more informed and interactive analysis. This establishes a foundation for embodied AI within museum settings, where models can move beyond static datasets and engage more directly with physical collections. Live demonstrations will show how such systems can support curatorial and research workflows, providing a new interface between researchers, AI systems and physical specimens while maintaining local control over data, models and processing.

title: Rediscovering Archives - Using LLM's for the Transcription and Extraction of Ecological Data from Historical Archives

programme.title: Rediscovering Archives - Using LLM’s for the Transcription and Extraction of Ecological Data from Historical Archives
programme.session: LT17 Bots, Bits, and Biodiversity
programme.abstract:
Historical archives held by museums and research institutions contain vast quantities of material that remain underutilised due to limitations in accessibility, readability, and searchability. Recent advances in multimodal large language models (LLMs) present new opportunities for improving access to these collections, particularly for complex historical documents that challenge conventional optical character recognition (OCR) and handwritten text recognition (HTR) approaches. This is especially relevant within natural history archives, where materials range from structured to unstructured, often containing handwritten and typed text alongside historical terminology.

This project investigates the use of multimodal LLMs for the transcription and interpretation of historical archival documents, with a focus on prompt engineering and schema-guided extraction to produce structured, machine-readable outputs. We focus on natural history collection materials such as those housed at Natural History Museum, UK, and Zoological Society London, as well as publicly available datasets such as the India Office botanical records from the British Library. Our study evaluates transcription performance - measured by Levenshtein distance, word error rate, and character error rate - across mixed-format, handwritten documents against ground truth transcriptions. By examining how multimodal LLMs perform on ecologically and historically relevant archival materials, this work contributes to emerging research on AI-assisted archival accessibility and explores how historical collections can be transformed into structured digital resources suitable for biodiversity and historical research.

summary: Phoebe Santos presented master's research (NHM, ZSL, UCL) testing whether a single LLM transcription approach generalises across different historical record types. title: KakraCards: An AI-Assisted Pipeline for Liberating Six Decades of Seabird Heritage Data

programme.title: KakraCards: An AI-Assisted Pipeline for Liberating Six Decades of Seabird Heritage Data
programme.session: LT17 Bots, Bits, and Biodiversity
programme.abstract: The continuous monitoring of the Common Gull (Larus canus) breeding colony on Kakrarahu islet in the Baltic Sea, Estonia, is one of the region's longest-running ecological research projects, dating back to 1962. With continuous breeding success data collected since 1968 and ringing and age data since 1971, this project holds a vast repository of longitudinal population dynamics data. Historically, these data were recorded in field notebooks, systematized on catalogue cards, and later partially transferred to spreadsheets. Modern data collection has now transitioned to a specialized mobile application for real-time field use. This work-in-progress project outlines the ongoing effort to rescue and digitize this extensive legacy dataset using a hybrid approach of manual data entry and novel AI-based digitization techniques and store it together with the latest field data. Because the monitoring methodology has remained constant over the decades, the recovered data holds immense value for understanding long-term population dynamics. The primary goal of this initiative is to make these unique ecological data widely available following FAIR principles. While multiple open-access publication approaches will ultimately be utilized, this presentation focuses on one particular pathway. By utilizing PlutoF, a comprehensive common data space for biodiversity developed by the University of Tartu, we establish a pipeline to structure, store, and publish the historical dataset to the Global Biodiversity Information Facility (GBIF). This workflow demonstrates an effective framework for rescuing legacy mass-monitoring data and ensuring over six decades of ecological observations become globally accessible.

programme.title: Data Quality in Focus: Bridging the Biodiversity Data Gap for Sustainable Finance
programme.session: LT17 Bots, Bits, and Biodiversity
programme.abstract:
Sustainable finance increasingly demands biodiversity data and metrics, yet these are only credible when underlying data are traceable, quality-assessed, and explicit about uncertainty. Currently, the financial sector faces a "biodiversity data gap": existing datasets are sparse and taxonomically biased, and often lack the depth needed for reliable risk assessments. Without robust data standards, investors cannot reliably evaluate the local impact of their portfolios or meet emerging nature-positive targets.

Drawing on insights from the Mistra FinBio program, we identify critical roadblocks in biodiversity reporting and propose a key improvement: a "data quality hierarchy." By mapping data and model outcomes to quality tiers and standardized metadata, it would enable AI-ready data for financial risk models, turning observations into trustworthy, decision-ready inputs.

The TDWG community is invited to collaborate on closing this data gap, focusing on improving data quality standards. Biodiversity data should not just be collected, but made interoperable, machine-actionable, and ready for the next generation of sustainability reporting.

title: Robots Rapidly Writing Records: Machine Annotations at Scale with DiSSCo

programme.title: Robots Rapidly Writing Records: Machine Annotations at Scale with DiSSCo
programme.session: LT17 Bots, Bits, and Biodiversity
programme.abstract:
In the face of the biodiversity crisis, digitization efforts in natural science collections need to rapidly increase. Scaling up these efforts requires the support of the community - and machines. DiSSCo, the Distributed System of Scientific Collections, enables this through annotation and harmonization of the data.

When natural science collection datasets are ingested into DiSSCo, specimens are transformed into Digital Specimens, assigned a Persistent Identifier, harmonized to a shared data model, and become and become fully actionable by machines as discrete knowledge units.

Through this process, DiSSCo enables community curation through annotations by humans and machines. With Digital Specimens harmonized to one data model across host institutions, DiSSCo is uniquely situated to host “plug and play” machine services to act on any specimen in the DiSSCo infrastructure. Instead of being confined to a single dataset they were designed for, Machine Annotation Services (MAS) adapted for DiSSCo can act on any Digital Specimen, breaking institutional silos and furthering collaboration.

For the first time, DiSSCo MASs have been tested at scale, running on all digital objects in a dataset as they are ingested into the DiSSCo infrastructure. These pilot services link all Digital Specimens in a given dataset to counterparts that can be found in GBIF, ENA, or BOLD. With the pilot successful, there is now an opportunity to run more complex services (such as label transcription using large language models) at scale on natural science collection data in DiSSCo.

This lightning talk gives an overview of the MAS-on-Ingestion feature in DiSSCo and what that means for transforming collection data.

title: From Collection Drawers to AI - A One-Week Recipe

programme.title: From Collection Drawers to AI - A One-Week Recipe
programme.session: LT17 Bots, Bits, and Biodiversity
programme.abstract:
Over 724 million entomological specimens exist worldwide. The collection at the Norwegian Institute of Bioeconomy Research (NIBIO) holds approximately 200,000 partly databased specimens, highlighting the urgent need for digitisation with high-quality images and structured metadata to support research and outreach.

We asked: what can be built in one week to initiate digitising a small collection, and how can AI enhance the process?

During a joint visit between NIBIO (Division of Biotechnology and Plant Health) and the Natural History Museum UK (AI & Innovation), we developed a functional, low-cost imaging setup using recycled office materials, simple LED lighting, and two borrowed cameras (Nikon Z7 and Z7 II). The aim was not perfection, but speed, accessibility, and replicability. We focused on Scolytinae (bark beetles), a group central to NIBIO’s research. Specimens of varying sizes were imaged in dorsal and lateral views and filmed in 360° rotation. In total, several hundred specimens were captured, producing a compact but versatile dataset. This dataset was used in three AI pipelines: (1) CNNs trained for species classification; (2) 3D reconstruction from video to generate interactive models for outreach; and (3) combined CNN and LLM approaches to extract specimen label data directly from videos. Together, these experiments demonstrate that rapid, low-cost digitisation can meaningfully support AI-driven classification, data extraction, and engagement, providing a scalable entry point for modernising biological collections.

title: Semantic Governance and Knowledge Organization in AI-Augmented Biodiversity Infrastructures

programme.title: Semantic Governance and Knowledge Organization in AI-Augmented Biodiversity Infrastructures
programme.session: LT17 Bots, Bits, and Biodiversity
programme.abstract:
As artificial intelligence becomes increasingly integrated into biodiversity data infrastructures, AI-generated annotations, classifications, and metadata are reshaping how biodiversity knowledge is organized, interpreted, and governed. While large language models and other generative AI systems create new opportunities for metadata enrichment, semantic integration, and data discovery, they also introduce challenges related to interpretability, semantic consistency, provenance, and institutional trust. This presentation examines biodiversity infrastructures from a knowledge organization perspective, focusing on how probabilistic AI outputs interact with structured biodiversity standards, controlled vocabularies, and long-standing cataloguing practices. The talk will explore emerging challenges surrounding semantic ambiguity, machine-generated biodiversity knowledge, and the governance of AI-assisted curation workflows within biodiversity repositories. Particular attention will be given to the need for provenance-aware, semantically transparent, and interoperable approaches that align AI-generated outputs with community standards and reproducible biodiversity data practices. By framing AI integration as both a technical and governance challenge, this presentation highlights opportunities for TDWG to support the development of shared semantic frameworks and best practices for AI-augmented biodiversity infrastructures.

Keywords: knowledge organization; semantic governance; biodiversity informatics; large language models; provenance; metadata; semantic interoperability; AI-generated annotations; biodiversity standards; AI-assisted curation

title: kabr-tools: A Modular Workflow for Automated Video-Based Behavioral Monitoring Across the Autonomy Spectrum

programme.title: kabr-tools: A Modular Workflow for Automated Video-Based Behavioral Monitoring Across the Autonomy Spectrum
programme.session: LT17 Bots, Bits, and Biodiversity
programme.abstract: Quantifying animal behavior from video footage is central to conservation and welfare assessment, but drone and camera-trap deployments now generate datasets that are too large to process manually. Existing tools support individual stages of video-to-behavior processing, yet ecologists lack practical guidance on which stages can be reliably automated and which require manual review. We present kabr-tools, an open-source modular workflow for video-based behavioral monitoring that supports a spectrum of autonomy, from fully manual annotation to fully automated processing. Components for detection, tracking, and classification are interchangeable and taxon-agnostic, producing structured outputs that align with biodiversity data standards. We evaluate the workflow against expert annotation at each pipeline stage and trace how errors propagate into downstream behavioral estimates, using drone footage of Grevy's zebras, Plains zebras, and reticulated giraffes at Mpala Research Centre, Kenya, and drone and camera trap footage of African wild dogs at The Wilds, Ohio. Detection is the primary bottleneck in both systems, since once individuals were reliably detected, tracking and classification added limited additional error for common behaviors. Automated classification achieved 91.3-F1 for the three most frequent ungulate behaviors, declining to 50.3-F1 for rare categories. A camera-source ablation confirmed that tail-class failure reflects insufficient training examples rather than a modality-specific limitation. This error characterization positions animal behavior studies on the autonomy spectrum, given their research question and required precision, and highlights where standardized, machine-actionable behavioral outputs depend on targeted human review.

title: A community-curated controlled vocabulary for fossil collections using dwc:materialEntityType

programme.title: Developing a community-curated controlled vocabulary for fossil collections using the term dwc:materialEntityType
programme.session: SYM06 Rocks, Minerals, and Metadata: Integrating Earth Sciences into the TDWG Community
programme.abstract:
Data about fossil specimens are not always easy to distinguish from that related to modern material, especially when aggregated in broadly scoped platforms such as the Global Biodiversity Information Facility. While fossil specimens have traditionally relied on the dwc:basisOfRecord term to distinguish themselves, this needs to be reconsidered given the recent ratification of a conceptual model for Darwin Core, and the associated Darwin Core Data Package. With these, the terms dwc:materialEntityCategory and dwc:materialEntityType are expected to functionally replace dwc:basisOfRecord in the evolution of publishing data using the Darwin Core standard. The term dwc:materialEntityCategory aims to define a broad category identifying the nature of a dwc:MaterialEntity with a tightly controlled vocabulary including the value "fossil" or "fossilized." dwc:materialEntityType is a narrower concept for which we expect controlled vocabularies to be more discipline-specific.

We have been coordinating members of the paleontological research and collections communities to build consensus around a controlled vocabulary that fossil collections can use with dwc:materialEntityType. This vocabulary would streamline research requests and facilitate collections management workflows by enabling users to gain a better understanding of the physical material represented by the digital record. For example, looking at two current records of fossil insects without images, it would not be obvious if one was preserved in amber and another was a compression fossil on a slab. We propose an initial controlled vocabulary focused on a relatively small set of concepts, potentially to be expanded to sub-concepts in a future proposal. Here we present the process and our preliminary proposed vocabulary.

Using examples (insects in amber versus compression fossils, bivalves in matrix, forams as bulk samples, picks, slides or macrofossils, trilobite mass-mortality slabs) she showed that early values such as macrofossil/mesofossil/microfossil are too coarse for search, research and imaging planning. The group proposes a first-level controlled vocabulary drawn from terms collections already use, with an informal second level, and is seeking community feedback via a QR-linked document before formal proposal to Darwin Core.

title: Extending Specify 7 for geological collections (GeoSpecify)

programme.title: Extending Specify 7 for Geological Collections
programme.session: SYM06 Rocks, Minerals, and Metadata: Integrating Earth Sciences into the TDWG Community
programme.abstract:
For 25 years, Specify has provided biological research museums and genetic repositories with software and technical services for curating, integrating, and publishing collections information. With funding from the Swiss Academy of Sciences (SwissCollNet initiative) and in collaboration with four Swiss natural history museums (Basel, Bern, Lausanne, Geneva), the Specify Collections Consortium (SCC) extended Specify to support geological collections.

Geocollections database requirements are similar in many ways to those of biological collections, however their unique properties and cataloging protocols challenged us to extend Specify concepts and capabilities. In addition to adding new tables, such as Absolute and Relative Age, and a new tree, Tectonic Unit, Specify added support for new protocols, most notably, Collection Object Groups (COGs), Components, and Collection Object Types (COTs).

In this presentation, SCC staff will discuss and demonstrate the new tables, tree, and features added to the Specify schema in order to support Geology Collections and their unique needs. These new features were designed to also support functionality required by Natural History Collections, the backbone of our membership.

The SCC is an open-source, collections community collaborative governed, funded, and sustained by its member institutions. Our software and technical support priorities address member data and system infrastructure needs. With Specify’s extension into the earth sciences, natural history museums will now be able to curate, integrate, and publish data from a robustly engineered single platform for both biological and geological collections.

summary: Theresa Miller presented GeoSpecify, the SwissCollNet-funded collaboration (Natural History Museum Bern, Specify Collections Consortium, Ben Norton) that extended the existing Specify 7 data model for geology rather than building a separate system. After requirements gathering with Swiss museums and an advisory committee, Specify gained an improved chronostratigraphy tree with start/end ages and biostratigraphy flags, a tectonic unit tree, an extended Geologic Context table, one-to-many relative and absolute age tables, and an 'extended age query' that searches all age fields by name or numeric range with strict or non-strict matching. Collection object types, discipline default forms, collection object groups (discrete, consolidated, drill core) and components allow mixed rock, mineral and fossil collections in one system, with Darwin Core Archive export planned to include the mineralogy extension.

why_it_matters: Institutions with mixed biological, paleontological and geological holdings can manage them in one standards-aligned system and publish geology data via Darwin Core.

title: Improving access to Earth science collections data via GeoCASe and the European Open Science Cloud (GeoDARA)

programme.title: Improving Access to Earth Science Collections Data via GeoCASe and the European Open Science Cloud
programme.session: SYM06 Rocks, Minerals, and Metadata: Integrating Earth Sciences into the TDWG Community
programme.abstract: Earth Science collections curated by natural history museums and research institutions contain critical records documenting past climates, environmental change, natural hazards, biodiversity dynamics, and geological processes across deep time. Despite their considerable scientific and societal value, these data have often remained fragmented, inconsistently described, and difficult to integrate with other Earth observation datasets. The CETAF Earth Science Group (ESG) is working to improve the discoverability, interoperability, and reuse of Earth Science collections data across Europe. ESG is leading the further development of GeoCASe (https://geocase.eu), a data network, aggregation service, and web portal for geoscientific collections data. The recently launched EOSC-Gravity project “Geodera” aims to integrate geological specimen-and sample-level data within the European Open Science Cloud (EOSC) through their Data Terra thematic node. Geodera will use representative case studies from different branches of geology to analyse and identify researchers’ data service needs, and to evaluate the usefulness of collections-based records for scientific applications and cross-domain research. Particular attention will be given to metadata harmonisation with external research platforms and datasets, including Earth observation data services within EOSC and Data Terra. This work includes assessing existing TDWG community standards, such as ABCD and Darwin Core, together with their geoscience extensions, as well as emerging concepts such as digital specimens. The project will identify gaps in current metadata schemas, provide training and practical guidelines to improve data quality, expand the GeoCASe consortium, and strengthen interoperability across the Earth Sciences domain.

Three case-study datasets (Quaternary pollen records from Estonia, 7,500-year tree-ring isotope records from the University of Helsinki, and HMS Challenger foraminifera from NHM London) are being used to assess metadata such as object type, taxonomy, origin, age, depositional environment and provenance. title: Improving geospecimen provenance and findability in the National Museums Scotland Scottish mineral collection

programme.title: Improving geospecimen provenance and findability in the National Museums Scotland Scottish mineral collection
programme.session: SYM06 Rocks, Minerals, and Metadata: Integrating Earth Sciences into the TDWG Community
programme.abstract: Geospecimen metadata is only as valuable as it is findable. Specimens can be located through a variety of properties - for example by species, donor, location in the museum or provenance in the field. Unfortunately, place names are not always unique and historic descriptions are often ambiguous, inconsistent, and difficult to georeference at scale. Therefore, grid references are better but how many curators have time to look this up manually? We present a curatorial workflow using the National Museums Scotland collection of Scottish minerals - about 18000 specimens collected over 200 years, with variable quality and certainty of provenance. It reconciles legacy mineral names, standardises locality information, and where possible, links specimens to structured localities and coordinates from external resources such as Mindat API. Provenance is treated not as a single point on a map, but as a spectrum of certainty and scale, ranging from a specific named mine shaft to a whole district or county. Museum documentation can therefore preserve uncertainty and locality granularity that are often flattened in external resources. Linking collection records with Mindat can strengthen locality data through grid references and occurrence context, while the museum record retains curatorial detail. This process improves discovery by enabling specimens to be found by searching at any scale, from broad region to specific locality. Museums can not only draw on external data but also use internal collection records to identify missing or faulty data. Moreover, minerals in the collection not yet recorded from Scotland in Mindat are readily identified. This enriches both information sources, and demonstrates geocollections as active contributors to data infrastructure development.

summary: Sarah Stewart, a computational chemistry PhD student, reported on a two-month internship improving provenance for the roughly 18,000-specimen Scottish mineral collection at National Museums Scotland. She merged transcribed historical ledgers with modern museum records, parsed locality strings into hierarchical levels, standardised names to IMA species and Dana/Strunz classes, and matched unique localities to Mindat to add coordinates, using Python scripts plus manual review. The pipeline exposed record problems (26,000 records for 18,000 specimens, about 1,000 without IDs, 15,000 duplicates needing triage) and resulted in 16,000 validated specimens, while the museum contributed new species occurrences and almost 2,000 new localities back to Mindat.

title: Bridging domains: how SESAR supports Earth and biodiversity digital extended specimens

programme.title: Bridging Domains: How SESAR Supports Earth and Biodiversity Digital Extended Specimens
programme.session: SYM06 Rocks, Minerals, and Metadata: Integrating Earth Sciences into the TDWG Community
programme.abstract:
SESAR, the System for Earth and Extraterrestrial Sample Registration has served as a repository of Earth science specimen metadata since 2004. Scientists and collection managers “register” their specimen with SESAR, and SESAR provides them with a stable landing page containing metadata describing their sample, and a persistent identifier (an IGSN, or International Generic Sample Number, now managed by DataCite). Though originally focused in the Earth and geological science community, SESAR has gradually expanded to additional domains such as archaeology, paleontology, and environmental sciences. SESAR currently supports 1000+ individual researchers and dozens of collections, globally, in making their sample records publicly accessible, providing an open, global catalog and discovery platform for researchers to find samples and specimens. In this presentation, we provide an overview of SESAR and present the outcomes of a five-year database migration and modernization project, focusing on the ways in which we have integrated and formalized our adoption of broader community vocabularies and standards, such as GeoSciML, and our ongoing efforts to support Darwin Core. We share ways the new database enables greater flexibility in incorporating new community vocabularies and in better supporting the unique needs of organizations and curated collections. We conclude by sharing how SESAR supports the community vision of a “digital extended specimen.”

Corresponding author

Natalie Raia University of Arizona, College of Information Science

She previewed a major migration under way that week: a redesigned search portal, sample landing pages with maps and sample 'family' links, an improved Workbench, and adoption of an application profile of the iSamples Earth and environmental material vocabulary (thousands rather than hundreds of terms). SESAR supports digital extended specimens by storing IGSNs, other identifiers and semantically rich links to related resources that propagate to DataCite Commons, and is developing a Darwin Core crosswalk and profiles for other communities.

title: Developing and implementing a relational mineral taxonomy model in EMu for Museums Victoria's mineral collection

programme.title: [Skipped talk] Developing and implementing relational mineral taxonomy model in EMu for Museums Victoria's Mineral Collection
programme.session: SYM06 Rocks, Minerals, and Metadata: Integrating Earth Sciences into the TDWG Community
programme.abstract:
Mineral identification and classification data in Museum’s Victoria’s (MV's) EMu CMS have until recently been stored within individual specimens’ catalogue records and managed as part of a series of shared hierarchical look-up-lists. This is unlike MV's biological taxonomic data, which have made use of a one-to-many relational structure between taxonomy and catalogue records at least since the implementation of EMu in the late 1990’s. Disadvantages of the model previously applied to mineral data include difficulties making changes following nomenclature revisions, an inability to capture incomplete taxonomy (eg. cataloguing specimens only identified to the level of a group or solid solution series), and a limited ability to query the database on mineral properties, chemistry or classification schemes.

I report on the development and implementation of a relational mineral taxonomy model in EMu over 2025-26. This model captures a hierarchy of mineral taxonomy; subgroup, group and supergroup as formlised by the International Mineralogical Association (IMA) in 2009, the Dana and Strunz classification systems, ideal chemical formula and elements, and IMA approval status. It also allows use of some existing functionality for zoological taxonomy, capturing the history of identification and linking taxonomy records to publications in which species were described or revised. Data to populate 6,125 taxonomy records for IMA approved mineral species were extracted from Mindat.org via their API. A further 162 taxonomy records for invalid, as yet undescribed, or incompletely classified specimens were created and manually populated. These 6,287 taxonomy records have been linked to the 56,792 catalogue records containing mineral identification data in MV's database.

summary: Oskar Lindenmayer described moving Museums Victoria's 57,000-specimen mineral collection (about 2,500 species, 131 type specimens) from classification stored locally in each EMu catalogue record to shared mineral taxonomy records in EMu's taxonomy module. The model adopts IMA hierarchy terms (species, subgroup, group, supergroup, plus other rank/value), keeps Dana class/code for legacy while adding Strunz-Mindat classes, handles solid-solution series such as wolframite via a multi-valued series field outside the hierarchy, and separates ideal formula and ideal elements. Catalogue records were linked to shell taxonomy records holding Mindat IDs before the new fields existed, then populated rapidly via the OpenMindat API, with about 150 non-standard records created manually.
one_line_takeaway: Linking catalogue records to shared, Mindat-populated mineral taxonomy records makes mineral identification data consistent and queryable.
why_it_matters: Gives mineral collections a template for relational, standards-aligned classification data in a common CMS, reusing infrastructure built for biological taxonomy.

title: Understanding geological specimen use for effective digitisation strategies

programme.title: Understanding Geological Specimen Use for Effective Digitisation Strategies
programme.session: SYM06 Rocks, Minerals, and Metadata: Integrating Earth Sciences into the TDWG Community
programme.abstract:
Without representation on major international platforms like GBIF, geological collections are currently much less digitally accessible to user communities than digitised biological specimens. Improving the access of users requires the digitisation of more geological and mineralogical specimens and the appropriate representation of their associated data. Forthcoming standards like the TDWG Mineralogy Extension and Minimum Information for a Digital Specimen (MIDS) will provide a framework with new fields that will enable the sharing of expressive top-level data, but there is a clear need for a better understanding what the audiences for these collections need from this data as we plan how to digitize and share collections data.

Here we present the preliminary longitudinal study of the users and use cases of geological and mineralogy specimens in museums, especially in three long-established well-known collections - the Smithsonian Institution, Natural History Museum of London, and National Museums Scotland. We analyze use of our specimens recorded in the published literature (including journals), loan forms, audience demographics, and web search. These data enable us to better understand the granularity of kind of data our audiences need and to develop more effective strategies about what and how to digitise.

summary: Rachel Walcott presented early results from pooling data from three institutions (National Museums Scotland, Smithsonian Mineral Sciences and NHM London) to quantify how abiotic geological collections are used, as input to digitisation priorities. Smithsonian inquiry forms show MIDS-level basics dominate searches but subcollection-specific fields have a substantial long tail; loans show meteorites and minerals are heavily sought while rocks decline over time; NHM loan purposes show about 40% 'predicted' uses (exhibition, outreach) and a wide variety of others, with very little for climate change. She concluded that images are used more than expected, MIDS elements are essential, and geological context (e.g. hydrothermal veins, pegmatites) is a key subject-specific element the mineralogy extension should support.

why_it_matters: Provides rare quantitative evidence for prioritising what to digitise in abiotic geology collections, including challenging the assumption that climate research is a major user.

title: The United States contribution to the global taxonomy of the Catalogue of Life in the first quarter of the 21st century
