programme.session: CO1 National & Global Taxonomic Backbones
programme.abstract: In 1996, the Catalogue of Life (CoL) was planned as a comprehensive inventory of all valid species known to biological science globally. Creating this list required a coherent classification and representative synonymy. The first edition of CoL was published on CD in 2001.The Integrated Taxonomic Information System (ITIS) became a major data provider, contributing over half of the species in the first edition (incl. mammals, birds, and many other groups). Crucially, ITIS also provided the global hierarchy that served as the CoL Management Classification for many years. The Species Files, another big US contributor, joined CoL in 2004, gradually adding global checklists for Orthoptera, Blattodea, Phasmida, Aphidomorpha, Mantodea, Plecoptera, Embioptera, Coreoidea, Psocodea, Dermaptera, Lygaeoidea, Isoptera, etc. Over 25 CoL annual editions, other US-based global databases have participated in CoL: Hexorallians of the world (2002-2017); ICTV (2002-); Moss TROPICOS (2002-2022); Systema Dipterorum (2005-); LecyPages (2007-2017); LDL Neuropterida (2009-); Brassicaceae (2010-2023); Early Land Plants Today (2010-2022); 3i Auchenorrhyncha (2011-); Membracoidea of the World Database (2011-2024); Entiminae (2016-); PBI Plant Bug (2016-); The World List of Cycads (2016-); PaleoBioDB (2017-); Gymnodinium (2018-); Jewel Beetles (2018-); StaphBase (2019-); Sepidiini tribe (2021-); World Catalogue of Opiliones (2021-); Global Lepidoptera Index (2022-); Bryonames (2023-); LWS fleas (2023-); The World Odonata List (2023-); AntCat (2025-). By 2025, US-based and expert-curated databases contributed 793,339 species, or 36% of the entire 2.2-million-species CoL base release. Also, US experts support CoL, making significant contributions to various biodiversity projects worldwide.

title: A knowledge organisation system for taxonomic data

programme.title: A Knowledge Organisation System for Taxonomic Data
programme.session: CO1 National & Global Taxonomic Backbones
programme.abstract:
With the Taxon Concept Standard (TCS) now ratified, the community has a framework to better organize taxonomic data. While often designed for specific Floras, these models can serve as reference implementations for TCS and broader Knowledge Organisation Systems (KOS). This presentation introduces a model developed for VicFlora that is oriented around the Taxon Concept as the core of the system, with all other data layers acting as supporting components.

The model is structured across six key layers:

Semantics: Taxon Concepts and mappings Syntax: Names, relations, usages, and typification Governance: Taxon trees and versioned nodes Authority: Provenance (references) and attribution (agents) Narrative: Profiles and descriptions Identity: External identifiers.

To manage complexity, we employ a "sidecar" pattern. Extension sidecars manage name types and reference roles, while functional sidecars allow Taxon Concepts to remain immutable, while their context can change. By decoupling these, we can update classifications (via Tree Nodes) or modify descriptive content (via Profiles) without redefining the concept itself. The Profile serves as the primary extension point, bridging internal models with other TDWWG standards like Plinian Core, Darwin Core, and SDD.

We distinguish between narrowly defined relationships and polymorphic ones-such as provenance and attribution-which require flexible handling. This architecture provides a blueprint for building taxonomic systems that are theoretically sound under TCS and functionally agile, demonstrating how a concept-centric KOS can effectively integrate keys, maps, and occurrences.

actual.identification_notes: Name transcribed 'Niels/Nils'. The speaker said he discarded his prepared talk and ad-libbed after discussions at the Living Atlas meeting.

summary: Niels Klazenga argued that problems with taxonomic checklists are data-quality issues that are fixable, and presented a layered data model developed as a reference implementation for his flora following ratification of TCS 2 (Taxon Concept Schema) last December. The model separates concerns into semantics (taxon concepts), syntax (names, typification, usages), authority (references, agents), governance (taxon trees and revisions) and narrative (profiles), plus identity, infrastructure and extension layers, using 'sidecar' patterns to keep taxon concepts immutable. He mapped layers to TCS, Plinian Core and Darwin Core, noted that governance is not covered by any standard, and proposed a conceptual model for taxon data developed with the Darwin Core maintenance group.
one_line_takeaway: Separating taxon data into layers with immutable taxon concepts at the centre gives a practical path to implementing TCS and fixing checklist quality problems.
why_it_matters: Offers a concrete reference architecture for taxon-concept-based systems and identifies gaps (governance, conceptual model) in current TDWG standards.
key_points: TCS was ratified last December; reference implementations are needed for uptake.
Taxon concepts (scientific hypotheses) are central; names sit in a separate syntax layer, following David Remsen's distinction between syntax and semantics.
Authority (references, agents) links to all layers; governance holds taxon trees, nodes and revisions; narrative holds profiles and most flora content.
Identity (external IDs such as IPNI, Tropicos, MycoBank), infrastructure and extension layers support the system.
Sidecar extensions (name types, reference roles) and functional sidecars (tree node, profile) keep taxon concepts immutable.
Maps (name usages, relationships) are used in tabular data but are not entities with identifiers.
Phylogeny had to be core rather than an extension since it expresses domain semantics.
The Darwin Core Taxon class tries to shoehorn a whole domain into a single entity.

notable_claims.claim: Problems with checklists are a data quality issue that can be fixed, and fixing them is not all that hard.
Governance of taxon trees is not covered by any existing standard.
The Darwin Core Taxon class is problematic because it tries to shoehorn an entire domain into a single entity.

future_work: Develop a conceptual model for taxon data and work with the Darwin Core maintenance group on interfaces between the models.
Implement the phylogeny layer.

q_and_a.question: Dima (online) asked how alternative taxon concepts would be organised.
q_and_a.answer_summary: Handling differing taxonomic views and versions is exactly what taxon concepts are for, since meaning lies in the concept not the name.

q_and_a.question: An audience member asked how species intergrades or complexes would be handled, given the hybrid module.
q_and_a.answer_summary: The hybrid formula is for names; species aggregates are a taxonomic problem and difficult.

q_and_a.question: Yury Roskov commented that a taxon concept is defined by the set of specimens included by its author.
q_and_a.answer_summary: Klazenga responded that this is more like circumscription; they agreed to discuss later.

representative_excerpt.text: The problem with the taxon data, they're definitely fixable if you take care of our semantic blind spots, our conceptual blind spots, and make the right infrastructure or the right systems for it.

notable_moments.description: Walkthrough of the layered model centred on taxon concepts.
Mapping layers to TCS, Plinian Core and Darwin Core.

title: Managing observations when taxonomy changes: the case of Artportalen and Dyntaxa

programme.title: Managing observations when taxonomy changes: the case of Artportalen and Dyntaxa
programme.session: CO1 National & Global Taxonomic Backbones
programme.abstract:
In the Swedish taxonomic database Dyntaxa (www.dyntaxa.se), updates are published continuously. This taxonomy is used by the Swedish citizen observatory Artportalen (www.artportalen.se). However, while about one million observations are added to Artportalen every two months, updates of taxonomy are only made once during this time.

In Dyntaxa, the taxon, with its corresponding taxonID, is the basis. The name for such a taxon can change without changing taxonID. Lumps are easy to deal with by pointing an unaccepted taxon (with its taxonID) to the accepted one. Technically, splits can also be dealt with automatically by keeping all observations on the old (sensu lato) taxon, even though it is no longer considered a species but essentially a collective taxon. However, this is usually unsatisfactory. When there is more information about the split you might be able to move observations to one or several of the new species. In Sweden, these cases are relatively few despite the volume of observations.

Another way is to inform the reporter of such observations of these changes. They will be presented with the option to move them if they now know what new species they observed.

The Dyntaxa data model can handle not only these relations between taxa, such as splits and different kinds of lumps, but also convey the reason for them and the statuses of the taxa involved. When an editor is working in Dyntaxa, lumping a species with another, an automated text is generated. This text summarizes which taxonIDs were involved and that, e.g., taxonID 25 was merged into taxonID 42. This is also stored in a machine-readable format in the database.

We show examples where automation works fine, and some where we currently assess them manually but could possibly automate more in the future.

actual.identification_notes: Speaker introduced as Johan; the taxonomic database is described but not named (Dyntaxa) in the transcript.

summary: Johan Liljeblad explained how Sweden's 26-year-old citizen observatory Artportalen stays aligned with the national taxonomic database (Dyntaxa, started 2004), which uses stable taxon-concept identifiers rather than names. Taxonomy is published continuously and harvested nightly, but Artportalen applies changes every two months with news notes: name changes need no action, lumps move observations to the new taxon ID, and splits keep observations on a 'collective taxon' unless information (e.g. geography or phenology) allows assignment to one segregate. Edge cases include chained lumps, excluded taxa and fully revised concepts, so the process remains semi-manual with expert review, which is manageable at about 100 new taxa and 10-15 reassignments per cycle.
one_line_takeaway: Concept-based taxon IDs with traceable history let a large observation system absorb taxonomic change pragmatically.
why_it_matters: A working national model for keeping millions of observations consistent with an evolving taxonomy, relevant to any portal linked to a changing backbone.
key_points: Every taxon has an ID and at least one recommended name; the ID stays stable to the concept while names change, and changes are traceable.
Taxonomy is harvested nightly (Darwin Core file) but applied to Artportalen every second month to manage changes and inform users.
Not every taxon in the database is reportable; a filter controls what can be reported.

Complications include multi-step lumps, taxa later excluded from Sweden, and totally revised concepts with no single target.

Sweden has about 60,000 species in the database and observations of about 40,000.

About 100 new taxa and 10-15 taxon ID reassignments arise every two months, which is manageable for a country like Sweden.

limitations: The model does not record which name the observer originally used.
The current Artportalen, launched in 2014, is old technology not built for smartphones.
future_work: A new version of Artportalen is being built with modern technology.
Log more change information, including the originally reported name.

q_and_a.answer_summary: IT staff identify taxa changed since the last update; name changes are simple, while exclusions and category changes are reviewed with experts for each organism group.

q_and_a.answer_summary: Taxon history is traceable in the taxonomic database; more could be logged, e.g. the name originally used by the observer.

title: Modernizing Brazil's taxonomic backbone: how ChecklistBank supports biodiversity and genetic heritage systems

programme.title: Modernizing Brazil’s Taxonomic Backbone: How ChecklistBank Supports Biodiversity and Genetic Heritage Systems
programme.session: CO1 National & Global Taxonomic Backbones
programme.abstract:
Brazil, has made major advances in organizing and managing taxonomic information. It is one of the few countries with two official and continuously maintained national species catalogues: one for Flora and Funga and another for Fauna, curated by more than 800 taxonomists.

Both lists are published monthly using IPT and shared with GBIF and ChecklistBank. Taxonomy is the essential backbone for biodiversity information systems, since taxonomic updates require continuous reprocessing of species occurrence records.

Brazil operates two major systems dependent on an updated taxonomic backbone: SiBBr - Brazilian Biodiversity Information System), a Living Atlases platform and SISGEN, the Brazilian Genetic Heritage Management System, where all research involving genetic heritage must legally register activities and outputs.

ChecklistBank has played a key role in strengthening Brazil’s biodiversity taxonomic backbone. Initially, it supported detailed quality assessment of the official lists, identifying duplicated names, typographical errors, inconsistencies in Portuguese Darwin Core terminology, and other standardization issues. More recently, it enabled the construction of a unified Brazilian taxonomic backbone by integrating the two official catalogues, incorporating invasive species, generating identifiers for taxonomic tree construction, merging extensions, and producing a Darwin Core Archive (DwC-A) directly consumed by national systems.

Previously, this workflow in SiBBr required extensive technical effort to clean, harmonize, and generate updated taxonomic files. With ChecklistBank and the support of its technical team, the process became more efficient, transforming a complex operation into a routine update performed every six months.

summary: Clara Baringo Fonseca described how GBIF Brazil uses ChecklistBank to build a single taxonomy for three national systems: the legally mandated genetic heritage and traditional knowledge system (SisGen), the national biodiversity portal and the protected-area research permit system. The monthly-updated Flora and Funga of Brazil (since 2010, 700+ specialists) and the Taxonomic Catalogue of the Brazilian Fauna (since 2015, 800+ specialists) are cleaned, merged with invasive species, Catalogue of Life microorganisms and GBIF fungi in ChecklistBank projects, and exported as Darwin Core Archives, some with and some without microorganisms. The taxonomy drives processing in the Living Atlas Brazil portal, versioned republication with DOIs in the IPT, and data-gap maps relevant to Global Biodiversity Framework targets 20 and 21.

title: Building a taxonomic reference authority for conservation: the Digital Catalogue of Biodiversity of Poland

programme.title: Building a Taxonomic Reference Authority for Conservation: The Digital Catalogue of Biodiversity of Poland
programme.session: CO1 National & Global Taxonomic Backbones
programme.abstract:
The Digital Catalogue of Biodiversity of Poland (DCBP) is a comprehensive inventory of all confirmed eukaryotic species and Cyanobacteria within Poland's administrative borders. The content is divided into taxonomic chapters managed by expert authors responsible for validating species composition and taxon attributes. These attributes cover occurrence status, threat categories, invasiveness, and other expandable characteristics. Each species entry is backed by a published reference or expert opinion documenting its presence in the country.

Currently, the DCBP comprises 100+ chapters published as individual GBIF checklist datasets and integrated into the Biodiversity Map (BioMap) portal, developed by the Polish GBIF Node. The total repository contains 73K species, including 36.7K animals, 19.9K fungi, 9.9K plants, 4.9K chromists, 0.5K protozoans, and 0.9K bacteria.

DCBP taxa belong to the taxonomic tree of the BioMap database, built on a PostgreSQL relational framework. This architecture connects checklists, species occurrences, datasets, collections, publications, and authors. The BioMap portal enables authors to manage their respective lists, edit or add new taxa, and update literature sources. Furthermore, the DCBP maps Catalogue of Life (CoL) taxon identifiers to facilitate external interoperability. We aim to establish the DCBP as the primary reference authority supporting Polish biodiversity research and conservation. Alongside other European national checklists, the Catalogue may serve as a valuable foundation for regional initiatives.

Each chapter is published to GBIF and synchronised to ChecklistBank; a portal offers interactive summaries and graphical views, and plans include DNA barcodes, printed publications and a Europe-wide network of comparable national checklists.

title: National Biodiversity Information Action Campaign production process: a case study of Taiwan

programme.title: National Biodiversity Information Action Campaign Production Process: A Case Study of Taiwan
programme.session: CO1 National & Global Taxonomic Backbones
programme.abstract:
With the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework (K-MGBF), a robust biodiversity information infrastructure is essential for Taiwan’s conservation goals. Since 2021, the Taiwan Biodiversity Information Alliance (TBIA) has implemented a national biodiversity data integration initiative through the 2021-2025 Action Campaign, focusing on species occurrence data, a Biodiversity Database Portal, inter-agency collaboration, and data standardization.

Building on this foundation, the 2026-2030 Campaign shifts toward long-term system resilience and operational sustainability. The Campaign was co-developed by an inter-agency working group, drawing on five years of experience while highlighting challenges in cross-domain coordination and staffing capacity.

Despite progress, key challenges remain in cross-domain governance, data circulation, integration of long-term monitoring needs such as Essential Biodiversity Variables (EBVs), and sustainable institutional and financial support.

In response, the Campaign defines five strategic directions: enhancing data openness and quality; strengthening interoperability via APIs and taxonomic checklists; building a comprehensive public-private network with stable funding; facilitating inter-agency technical exchange; and enhancing data usability through improved validation and citation practices. These strategies address governance, technical, data, and financial dimensions of infrastructure resilience.

This framework serves as an implementation-oriented synthesis, translating strategy into actionable guidance. This case study illustrates how biodiversity data infrastructures can evolve toward greater resilience, offering a reference for similar global initiatives.

title: Metadata matters: perceptions on the implementation of Darwin Core in the biocollections cyberinfrastructure

programme.title: Metadata Matters: Perceptions on the Implementation of Darwin Core and Other Considerations in the Biocollections Cyberinfrastructure
programme.session: CO2 Digitizing Collections & Legacy Data
programme.abstract: Bio-and geo-collections inform scientific discovery, advance knowledge, influence policy decisions, and serve as educational resources. Aggregating biocollections data requires several steps from curation of physical items, data capture and digitization, and creating DarwinCore (DwC) compliant metadata to allow for discoverability in institutional, discipline-specific, and data repositories such as GBIF. With differing curation practices over time, technological and methodological advancements, and evolving funding priorities, the physical research objects, their associated metadata, and derived data and media create a complicated cyberinfrastructure. This survey of curators and collection managers was conducted to better understand their perspectives on the data curation of biocollections. The survey focused on the characteristics of collections professionals, their data storage, access, and reuse practices, challenges to DwC metadata implementation, and who their anticipated users are. Recruitment through TDWG, iDigBio, SPNHC, and discipline-specific listservs led to 60 usable responses. Half of respondents held doctoral degrees, had been in their roles for more than 10 years, and 75% worked at academic institutions. Many themes emerged in relation to perceived roadblocks when mapping to data standards, such as data complexity and representing linked or derived data, gaps in standards development and community implementation guidelines as well as discipline-specific data practices, capacity and technical challenges, and a need for continued support and education around implementing standards and communicating changes or new terminology. The results can inform the building of a robot-ready cyberinfrastructure to increase data access and reuse.

actual.identification_notes: Introduced as 'Wade Bishop'. The moderator used the gap while the next virtual talk was set up to continue the discussion about Darwin Core community guidelines raised in this talk.

title: Pinned insect digitization conveyor: image and data transcription workflows

programme.title: Pinned Insect Digitization Conveyor: image and data transcription workflows
programme.session: CO2 Digitizing Collections & Legacy Data
programme.abstract: The Smithsonian National Museum of Natural History (NMNH) is currently digitizing pollinating insects using a Pinned Insect Digitization Conveyor developed by Picturae. The digital workflow, developed by the Smithsonian Office of Digital and Innovation, the NMNH Informatics and Data Science Center, and the Department of Entomology, are reviewed here. Insects and labels are placed on the conveyor and up to 1,500 specimens are processed daily. Four images are captured of each insect - one of labels and three focus-stacked images of the specimen. Conveyor images are run through a technical review process and are screened by Picturae before delivery to Smithsonian. Files are organized into a folder system which hold all specimen images from an insect drawer. A second technical check, using the Smithsonian system, Osprey, is followed by review of random images by an individual. Imaging errors may include issues related to automated focus stacking and specimens being captured at the wrong resolution for their size. When a drawer has passed QC, images are delivered to the institutional DAMS. A script then picks up the images for inclusion into the NMNH database of record, EMu. Stub records are created, images are attached, and the record is then published. Label images are submitted to a different vendor for data transcription. Transcribed data are run through Osprey where a review of randomly selected data is checked for accuracy. When a drawer has passed QC, data is transformed for bulk import back into EMu. Data is appended to the original stub records and images are made available for Open Access (CC0), if applicable. The current project goal is the digitization of 365,000 specimens of pinned insects of which the majority are pollinating insects.

title: X-raying wild plant seeds: preparing images for future AI-driven global biodiversity research

programme.title: X-raying wild plant seeds: Preparing images for future AI-driven global biodiversity research
programme.session: CO2 Digitizing Collections & Legacy Data
programme.abstract: X-ray imaging is an effective non-destructive method for assessing seed quality in seed banks, enabling the identification of full, empty or damaged seeds when estimating the proportion of potentially viable seeds within a sample. This method is routinely used at the Millennium Seed Bank, RBG, Kew, as an alternative to destructive cut-testing for evaluating seed lot quality. Over the past 25 years, more than 100,000 seed x-ray images have been captured, providing a valuable resource for documenting seed traits in wild plants (e.g., shape, size, length, width, and internal features). Here, we describe the processing of these images to generate a corresponding image with a structured grid overlay and standardised measuring scale, to support future AI-driven research to measure features. The image-processing script is Python-based and uses Pillow for standard image manipulation and pydicom for parsing medical-grade X-ray metadata. Script converts digital pixel data into a calibrated physical reference through a three-step mathematical transformation: (1) metadata extraction identifies image resolution from file headers by reading dots per Inch (DPI); for standard JPEGs, this is obtained via Pillow, while for DICOM files, resolution is derived from pixel spacing or equivalent tags using pydicom; (2) pixel-to-metric conversion computes pixels per centimetre using standard conversions, enabling grid intervals according to image resolution; and (3) grid placement generates an evenly spaced coordinated sequence across image dimensions. Scale accuracy is validated against physical seed length measurements from a representative sample. This workflow standardises legacy and newly acquired x-ray images, enabling downstream computational and AI-driven global biodiversity research.

title: Next-generation digitization: integrating spectral reflectance into the online mobilization of herbaria

programme.title: Next-Generation Digitization: Integrating spectral reflectance into the online mobilization of herbaria
programme.session: CO2 Digitizing Collections & Legacy Data
programme.abstract: Spectral reflectance is emerging as a prime candidate for next-generation herbarium digitization, as spectra provide non-destructive information on taxonomic identity and functional traits. We have operationalized digitization of spectral reflectance in the Missouri Botanical Garden Herbarium (MO) using a pipeline that runs in parallel to our specimen imaging and transcription workflow. Spectral measurements follow the protocol of the International Herbarium Spectral Digitization (IHerbSpec) working group - ensuring reproducibility and interoperability of spectra across the world’s herbaria - and are linked by keying on specific metadata with their corresponding specimen records in the collection management system, Tropicos. To date, our pipeline has resulted in >60,000 spectral measurements taken on >10,000 herbarium specimens (and counting), focusing on groups in which MO curators have taxonomic expertise. We are using these spectral measurements for research applications ranging from taxonomy to ecology, including, but not limited to, using spectra to detect misidentified specimens, predict ploidy, and evaluate how Amazonian trees have responded to climate change.

summary: Matthew Austin described how Missouri Botanical Garden, with philanthropic support to digitise its roughly eight million herbarium specimens, is adding spectral reflectance as a 'third layer' of digitisation alongside images and transcribed labels. After imaging and barcoding, a spectral team takes three point measurements per leaf surface on selected specimens (leaves liftable onto a black background, free of glue or pathogens, woody taxa with in-house curatorial expertise), recording rich per-scan metadata under the protocol of iHerbSpec, a 30+ institution working group. Data are linked in Tropicos by barcode; about 1.55 million specimens have been imaged and 16,000 have spectra, and clade-specific species identification models trained on expert-identified spectra achieve accuracies around the 90s, even identifying sterile specimens.

why_it_matters: Extends the digital extended specimen with chemistry/phenotype data and shows a standardised cross-institution protocol for making it reusable.
key_points: Spectral reflectance encodes chemical and physical properties and can infer functional traits and aid identification.

title: Experience of collaborative management of the World Auchenorrhyncha Database in TaxonWorks

programme.title: Experience of collaborative management of the World Auchenorrhyncha Database in TaxonWorks
programme.session: CO2 Digitizing Collections & Legacy Data
programme.abstract:
The World Auchenorrhyncha Database (WAD) initially began as a series of smaller projects managed using the 3i software platform (http://dmitriev.speciesfile.org). The 3i system was based on an MS Access database linked to custom web interfaces and was designed to provide detailed information on species taxonomy, nomenclature, distribution, biological associations, bibliography, and identification tools, including interactive and dichotomous keys.

Eight years ago, all Auchenorrhyncha-related projects were merged into a single database, and the data were migrated to TaxonWorks (https://taxonworks.org), an open-source biodiversity information workbench developed to replace three previously available platforms: 3i, mx, and SpeciesFiles. Migrating data from legacy databases into TaxonWorks created numerous opportunities for collaborative data entry and management.

Following the migration, the number of curators and users with extended access rights increased substantially, from only one or a few individuals to more than 65 contributors. In addition to implementing global nomenclatural changes within the group, curators now focus on more applied goals, such as adding species images, developing interactive and dichotomous identification keys, and refining distributional data to produce comprehensive regional species checklists.

Although many users are not directly involved in data editing, they continue to contribute significantly by commenting on nomenclatural and taxonomic issues and by sharing bibliographic resources and photographs. The global coverage of the WAD currently exceeds 48,150 valid species (https://hoppers.speciesfile.org), and its data are shared across major global biodiversity initiatives, including Catalogue of Life, GBIF, iNaturalist, Global Names.

title: Digitising heritage for science: the Medical Entomology Museum as a platform for entomological biodiversity research and vector-borne disease surveillance

programme.title: Digitising heritage for science: The Medical Entomology Museum as a platform for entomological biodiversity research and vector-borne disease surveillance
programme.session: CO2 Digitizing Collections & Legacy Data
programme.abstract: The Medical Entomology Museum (MEM) integrates heritage and science by maintaining one of Africa’s significant collections of arthropods of medical importance. Established primarily to support malaria and vector-borne disease research, the museum houses specimens collected over the past century. These collections serve as an important resource for species identification, biodiversity studies, and monitoring ecological and environmental changes that influence public health. This presentation highlights the museum’s role as both a historical archive and a dynamic research resource supporting FAIR (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, and Reusable) biodiversity data standards. Ongoing digitisation efforts aim to convert legacy specimen records, including type material, archival collections, and historically under-curated or orphaned datasets, into structured, machine-readable formats suitable for integration into global biodiversity informatics systems. These outputs support biodiversity research and strengthen vector-borne disease surveillance through improved accessibility, interoperability, and analytical readiness. The digitised collections also provide baseline data for malaria and vector surveillance, enabling historical comparisons and trend analysis. Beyond its scientific contribution, the museum provides insight into the history of medically important insect research in southern Africa and the development of public health interventions. It also promotes public awareness by transforming preserved collections into accessible tools for learning and engagement. In this way, the MEM demonstrates how heritage institutions contribute to science, biodiversity data innovation, and stronger public health systems.

title: How is digitisation doing? Monitoring the increase in digitised collections using MIDS

programme.title: How is digitisation doing? Monitoring the increase in digitised collections using MIDS
programme.session: SYM22 State of the Collections Description Interest Group. What's Happening and What's Not!
programme.abstract: The Minimum Information about a Digital Specimen (MIDS) standard has been under development by the TDWG MIDS task group for several years and entered expert review in early 2026. It provides a framework for automatically and reproducibly assessing the digitisation level achieved by a specimen, based on its provided data properties. Applying the MIDS level calculation to historical and recent GBIF specimen data snapshots, we shed light on the growth of digitised specimen collections in recent years and investigate patterns across the dimensions of taxonomy, preservation type, location, and age.

title: The Latimer Core standard and the Global Registry of Scientific Collections

programme.title: The Latimer Core standard and the Global Registry of Scientific Collections
programme.session: SYM22 State of the Collections Description Interest Group. What's Happening and What's Not!
programme.abstract:
The Global Registry of Scientific Collections (GRSciColl) aims to catalogue physical scientific collections, their content, location, associated staff and institutions. GRSciColl was originally developed before the Latimer Core (LtC) Standard became ratified. It has its own model, terms and associated vocabularies. The information can be stored in different types of entities: Institution and collection entries, which contain a lot of textual descriptions. Specimen occurrence records shared on the Global Biodiversity Information Facility (GBIF) platform and linked to GRSciColl institution and collection entries. Semi-structured tables called “collection descriptor groups”. They are used to describe collection content and are associated with collection entries. In this presentation, we will show where and how GRSciColl is integrating the LtC standard: GRSciColl entries can be accessed as well as uploaded in the LtC standard. GRSciColl collection descriptors groups use the LtC terms and suggested vocabularies. The objectClassificationName term is particularly useful when capturing information about subcollections corresponding to polyphyletic groups. It allows for example to find collections containing algae: https://scientific-collections.gbif.org/collection/search? objectClassification=Algae The use of LtC standard in training material for modelling of collection data.

We will also highlight some of the challenges of this integration.

summary: Marie Grosjean explained how GRSciColl, the community-curated registry of scientific collections and institutions maintained by GBIF, uses Latimer Core. Collection descriptors are flat tables that fill the gap between textual collection descriptions and specimen-level occurrences, using Darwin Core (dwc:) or Latimer Core (ltc:) headers; GRSciColl currently indexes Latimer Core biome type and object classification name, enabling searches such as marine algae collections by country. Latimer Core is also used as an import/export format and in editor training, but limitations include GRSciColl fields without Latimer Core equivalents (forced into measurementOrFact) and missing descriptors in exports, which will be revisited as Latimer Core's structure is formalised.
one_line_takeaway: Latimer Core gives GRSciColl a common language and exchange format for describing collections between free text and specimen records.
why_it_matters: Collection-level description lets undigitised or geological collections become discoverable, and GRSciColl is a key real-world implementation of Latimer Core.
key_points: GRSciColl registers collections, institutions, codes and identifiers, curated by 70+ editors with Index Herbariorum as a main source; it has an API and can be embedded in GBIF hosted portals.
Collection descriptors capture lists of taxa, collectors, statistics etc. and can include unmapped columns that are displayed but not indexed.

title: Once and future Latimer Core: status update and open conversation

programme.title: Once and Future Latimer Core: Status update and open conversation.
programme.session: SYM22 State of the Collections Description Interest Group. What's Happening and What's Not!
programme.abstract:
Latimer Core (LtC) is the TDWG standard intended to support description and exchange of information about collections and their associated organizational, and preservation contexts. Over the past year, the Maintenance Group has focused on improving its conceptual model, refining documentation, and exploring practical serialization and interoperability patterns that help long-term sustainability and implementation across diverse collection-management environments.

This presentation will provide an overview of the current state of LtC, summarize the work undertaken during 2025-2026, and introduce some implementation examples, including draft JSON and RDF/XML exchange formats. Together, these examples aim to illustrate both the flexibility of the LtC conceptual model and the unresolved questions surrounding structure, identifiers, and semantic interoperability.

The presenters will invite discussion of larger questions that extend to other TDWG efforts: How do we make standards understandable and maintainable for people across different domains of expertise? How should TDWG approach controlled vocabularies and governance? How should we model relationships between terms, and structure their identifiers (IRIs)? How do we document dataset creation, generation, or AI-assisted workflows? What happens when our standards depend on concepts borrowed from outside the TDWG ecosystem?

This session embraces the messier reality of standards work: balancing flexibility and structure, interoperability and usability, technical rigor and human comprehension. The goal is to share where LtC stands today, and invite discussion. How can TDWG standards remain useful, maintainable, and adaptable as biodiversity data practices continue to evolve?

title: Assessing record quality and completeness in geoscience collections

programme.title: Assessing record quality and completeness in geoscience collections
programme.session: SYM22 State of the Collections Description Interest Group. What's Happening and What's Not!
programme.abstract: The Minimum Information about a Digital Specimen (MIDS) standard allows collections to assess digitization progress using a numeric, discipline-specific score. Here we describe efforts to assess this type of data quality score in collections of geological specimens at the Smithsonian National Museum of Natural History (NMNH). We examine MIDS scores for subsets of the collection and compare them to established, internal record quality scores from the Smithsonian's Collections and Digitization Reporting System (CDRS). Our goal is to determine how to best implement MIDS, while also reviewing potential updates to CDRS. MIDS scores can range from 0 (Bare) to 3 (Extended). Most records from the geology collections score 1 (Basic) or 2 (Intermediate). No records score above 2. Low scores largely reflect 1) a lack of detailed metadata for older specimens and 2) incomplete data from ongoing digitization projects. Certain subcollections have more complete data but recently acquired collections score similarly to older collections. CDRS scores are calculated in the collections database using discipline-specific rulesets. Like MIDS, CDRS assesses digitization progress, but it differs from MIDS in four key ways: 1) it includes elements for physical collections management, like storage location and accession status; 2) it excludes some properties that appear in MIDS; 3) it may include data quality checks, which were omitted from MIDS by design; and 4) inconsistent rulesets make comparisons between disciplines difficult. We expect MIDS to be most useful for improving the completeness of published datasets and allowing comparisons between organizations, whereas CDRS scores will better capture internal data quality and collections management concerns.

title: Sustainability and collaboration in a time of uncertainty

programme.title: Sustainability and collaboration in a time of uncertainty
programme.session: SYM38 Sustaining the Geo- and Biodiversity Data Ecosystem: Standards-Driven Approaches to Long-Term Resilience
programme.abstract:
Over the past several decades, geo-and biodiversity sciences have been reshaped by digitization, data mobilization, and data integration efforts, giving rise to the community-developed Digital Extended Specimen as a unifying framework. These initiatives have produced substantial infrastructure, new tools and workflows, and a more connected global community. However, as funding cycles conclude, urgent challenges remain, including sustaining social, physical, and digital infrastructure; maintaining and aligning software and data quality work across networks; retaining expertise; coordinating governance; and supporting workforce development.

This presentation frames geo-and biodiversity data infrastructure as a distributed socio-technical system in which semantically structured and linked data, standards development, and data harmonization enable coordination, reduce duplication, and support research. It emphasizes that achieving machine-actionable, FAIR-and CARE-compliant data depends on sustaining a standards-based ecosystem of data providers, aggregators, platforms, repositories, and users.

Drawing on current efforts within the networks of the International Partners for the Digital Extended Specimen and the Biodiversity Collections Network, along with the broader community, this talk explores how coordinated approaches and research-and machine-ready standards can better align social, physical, and digital infrastructures needed to support community goals. It highlights opportunities to leverage economies of scale, strengthen governance and collaboration, and expand the relevance of biodiversity data across domains, offering a forward-looking perspective on building a more sustainable and integrated data ecosystem.

programme.abstract: This year GBIF celebrates its first 25 years. GBIF has grown from a big idea to a highly productive global network and biodiversity infrastructure. GBIF originated from the natural history museum community as an infrastructure to share data from specimens. GBIF now mediates data from over 285 million specimens and GRSciColl contains information from nearly 11,000 collections around the world. This success is due to the global GBIF network of over 2,600 data publishers and national nodes. The integration of data from different sources allows connection to related data with images, DNA sequences and even phylogenies. This data sharing allows reuse for many scientific applications beyond taxonomy and systematics such as conservation, invasive species research and climate change. At GBIF we track data usage and confirm the use of collection data in strategic documents that inform policy such as the IPBES assessment on invasive species. GBIF users link their GBIF-enabled research to achieving UN Sustainable Development Goals. Perhaps most importantly the easy access to shared digitized data is immediately available to national reporting and the CBD Global Biodiversity Framework. GBIF has succeeded by providing needed support for the nations that require. GBIF sustainability has benefited by its unique governance structure and community engagement. This collaboration will be even more important as move forward together for the next 25 years.

title: Unifying Natural Heritage for a Resilient Future

programme.title: Unifying Natural Heritage for a Resilient Future
programme.session: SYM38 Sustaining the Geo- and Biodiversity Data Ecosystem: Standards-Driven Approaches to Long-Term Resilience
programme.abstract:
In an era defined by rapid environmental shifts and global instability, the mobilization of biodiversity data is no longer a luxury-it is a necessity for informed survival. DiSSCo (Distributed System of Scientific Collections) represents a transformative response to this uncertainty, transitioning fragmented physical collections with specimens into a synchronized, FAIR-compliant digital ecosystem built on the Digital Extended Specimen concept.

This presentation explores how DiSSCo fosters collaboration by unifying over 1.5 billion biological and geological objects across hundreds of institutions. At the heart of this infrastructure is the open Digital Specimen, using a FAIR Digital Object compliant architecture that enables researchers and collection curators to link, analyze, and enrich collection data with the help of machines at an unprecedented scale.

By harmonizing institutional efforts, DiSSCo ensures the long-term sustainability of scientific assets, providing the evidentiary base required to tackle climate change, biodiversity loss, and emerging health risks. We will discuss the technical and organizational frameworks that allow DiSSCo to bridge the gap between isolated silos and a shared knowledge base. Ultimately, DiSSCo demonstrates that through integrated digital infrastructure and collaborative governance, natural heritage can pivot from a state of fragmented, fragile silos to a future of data-driven resilience.

title: Requirements of Sustainability Models for Geo-Biodiversity Data Cyberinfrastructure

programme.title: Requirements of Sustainability Models for Geo-Biodiversity Data Cyberinfrastructure
programme.session: SYM38 Sustaining the Geo- and Biodiversity Data Ecosystem: Standards-Driven Approaches to Long-Term Resilience
programme.abstract:
The sustainability of cyberinfrastructure (CI) for Geo-Biodiversity (GB) research depends on the existence of a sustainable GB community of entities (aka ecosystem) which includes data providers, data aggregators, users, professional organizations and others. Conversely, a healthy progressive GB ecosystem also needs a sustainable CI for its own sustainability. This interdependence originates significant CI requirements which fall into three categories, namely, functional requirements, operational requirements and economic-model requirements. Functional requirements relate to the research activities that the CI must support such as biodiversity data management, data analytics, FAIROS practices, educational tools and workforce training. Operational requirements follow from the need for efficiency, scalability, security and resiliency of CI services. Economic-model requirements relate to tracking usage of resources (including data) and associated costs, generation and allocation of revenue, and accounting to funding sources and stakeholders.

This presentation reviews the possible funding models for scientific CI in the context of the GB ecosystem and discusses the CI features that they require, elaborating on the nature of these requirements and possible solutions. These requirements need to be addressed in the context of existing software , design patterns and data standards for economic activities in cyberspace. While paid commercial solutions are provided, open-source solutions that can be adopted and integrated with relevant standards are also possible. This presentation will also provide an example of how a prototype agentic system for biodiversity data exploration, integration and analytics, called iChatBio, could be extended to address some of these requirements.

title: From preservation to perseverance: bridging disciplines for data resilience

programme.title: From preservation to perseverance: bridging disciplines for data resilience
programme.session: SYM38 Sustaining the Geo- and Biodiversity Data Ecosystem: Standards-Driven Approaches to Long-Term Resilience
programme.abstract:
Since 2025, major federal funding cuts in the US have put multiple scientific data infrastructures at risk, including many in the Earth and environmental sciences. For example, multiple data resources managed by NOAA, USGS and other federal agencies have been taken offline, typically without plans for replacement or restoration. Many NASA science programs have been cut, and multiple NSF programs for research and infrastructure in the Earth sciences are canceled or rumored to be canceled. The funding programs that remain are increasingly skewed toward AI and partnerships with industry. Earth science data infrastructures are having to quickly pivot to alternative funding models, and are discussing worst case scenarios in case of closure.

The Earth and biodiversity sciences have much to gain from coordination and partnership in this increasingly uncertain funding landscape. In this talk, I’ll share sustainability efforts taken by data infrastructures in the Earth and environmental sciences, including the System for Earth and Extraterrestrial Sample Registration (SESAR), which include diversifying our funding streams and refactoring our codebase and vocabularies. I’ll also discuss broader resilience efforts in the US-based Earth science community, including nascent community-building initiatives from the American Geophysical Union. I’ll conclude by reflecting on existing digital preservation insights from scholars in the library and information sciences, and how these present us with important guidance as we seek to persevere through times of uncertainty and resource scarcity.

summary: Andrea Thomer described how Earth science data infrastructures in the US moved from the passive threat of invisibility to active threats in 2025, when NOAA and other agency resources were taken offline and many staff lost their jobs. She presented three resilience efforts at different timescales: SESAR rescuing NOAA's Index to Marine and Lacustrine Geological Samples (IMLGS), the ESIP Repository Crisis Scorecards for self-assessment against four crisis scenarios, and an AGU-led, Hewlett-funded international initiative building roadmaps, business models and mutual aid networks. She concluded that resilience is about prioritisation, doing the best with what we have, and called for advocacy to keep infrastructure appropriately visible.

title: NEON, Community Standards, and the Hyper-Extended Specimen

programme.session: SYM38 Sustaining the Geo- and Biodiversity Data Ecosystem: Standards-Driven Approaches to Long-Term Resilience
programme.abstract:
Each year, the National Ecological Observatory Network (NEON) collects over 400 terabytes of ecological data and more than 100,000 spatially and temporally co-located geochemical samples and biological specimens across the United States. NEON monitors whole ecosystems through repeated field sampling, continuous sensor measurements, remote sensing, and downstream analyses, creating a unique opportunity to support “hyper-extended specimens” while minimizing common data challenges related to standardization.

NEON primarily maintains and publishes its data using internal data models, vocabularies and identifiers. However, many of NEON data conventions align with community standards, such as GBIF vocabularies, Darwin Core, IGSN IDs, Veg-X, MIxS, and USA-NPN phenophase definitions. Selected data are formally translated and republished through standards-based infrastructures such as GBIF, BOLD, AmeriFlux, and Google Earth Engine. In addition, we have explored how ecological monitoring datasets can be represented using emerging standards such as the Humboldt Extension and Darwin Core Data Package. We are also working with broader community efforts to examine and improve the AI readiness of our datasets to increase interoperability and relevance for next-generation analytical tools.

We outline the current state of the Digital Extended Specimen concept within the NEON ecosystem, including ongoing efforts and challenges to connect our physical collections, digital infrastructure, and diverse downstream research communities, while improving provenance tracking and discoverability.

title: Canada’s need for synthesis for Adaptation and Resilience to Climate Change

programme.title: Canada’s need for synthesis for Adaptation and Resilience to Climate Change
programme.session: SYM38 Sustaining the Geo- and Biodiversity Data Ecosystem: Standards-Driven Approaches to Long-Term Resilience
programme.abstract:
The exponential growth of genomic data presents an unprecedented opportunity to mitigate the ecological impacts of climate change. Genomic data is estimated at 30 petabytes available publicly, with likely at least half as much unpublished. The Genomic Research and Development Initiative’s (GRDI) Genomic Adaptation and Resilience to Climate Change (GenARCC) will amass nearly a petabyte of data. Consequently, we may already have the raw genomic data required to address some of the most pressing ecological problems that can be solved using genomics.

To fully realize this potential, a paradigm shift towards systematic reuse of data and synthesis is essential. Synthesis centres have previously demonstrated the value of reanalyzing existing assets to accelerate discovery. This requires realigning incentives to prioritize data reuse over data generation such as by recognizing algorithms, associated pipelines and applications, and the data itself like long term scientific infrastructure. This involves standardization of data, processes, and products, which can only be realized by the community’s will and/or incentivized through funding-related obligations. With improved access and curation of shared scientific resources, researchers can develop novel data management architectures and leverage artificial intelligence, to integrate diverse datasets and reveal cross-system patterns of resilience that isolated studies overlook. To achieve this goal, future efforts should work towards FAIR data, and validation, maintenance, and automation of code and underlying algorithms. Together, these efforts can enhance how scientific data is shared and utilized in conservation and ecology. Prioritizing synthesis will ensure we get the highest return on our collective investment.

title: Architecting the National Biodiversity Information System: Standards-Driven Workflows for South Africa’s Botanical and Zoological Data

programme.title: Architecting the National Biodiversity Information System: Standards-Driven Workflows for South Africa’s Botanical and Zoological Data
programme.session: SYM38 Sustaining the Geo- and Biodiversity Data Ecosystem: Standards-Driven Approaches to Long-Term Resilience
programme.abstract:
To sustain a robust Geo-Biodiversity Data Ecosystem, SANBI has implemented standardised data management strategies for South Africa’s national botanical and zoological collections. The project focuses on transitioning legacy data into FAIR (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, and Reusable) datasets using globally recognised informatics standards. Central to this architecture is the National Biodiversity Information System (NBIS), which integrates data from institutional partners using standardised platforms.

A key challenge in national data integration is metadata harmonisation, particularly taxonomic inconsistencies. To address this, SANBI uses the TaxaMatch algorithm, which matches misspelt or variant species names to an authoritative taxonomic backbone. This ensures high-quality, interoperable data regardless of differing institutional interpretations. For botanical data, SANBI distributes authoritative dictionaries, including taxa with authors and gazetteer data, to improve quality at capture.

Institutions push new or updated data to staging instances where automated quality checks are applied before records move to production. ETL packages synchronise data regularly. For zoological collections, Specify’s taxonomic ranking system accommodates diverse research traditions while maintaining referential integrity.

The system supports spatial searches, enabling users to draw polygons on maps to retrieve species coordinates. SANBI also uses a separate NBIS indexing database with persistent identifiers linked across repositories. By providing shared infrastructure and standards, SANBI enables a scalable web portal that promotes data cleaning, reduces duplication, and supports environmental monitoring and research.

title: FAIR ancient environmental DNA data in practice: developing and implementing interoperable metadata standards in AEGIS

programme.title: FAIR ancient environmental DNA data in practice: developing and implementing interoperable metadata standards in AEGIS
programme.session: CO4 FAIR data in practice - eDNA, modelling and biodiversity concepts
programme.abstract: Ancient Environmental Genomics Initiative for Sustainability (AEGIS) is a seven-year programme investigating how records of adaptive responses stored in ancient environmental DNA (eDNA) coupled with other biomolecular approaches can support understanding of ecosystem resilience and sustainable food production, while preserving biodiversity, under climate change scenarios. The data engine, a core component of AEGIS, includes a strong commitment to FAIR and open data, with enriched metadata to promote findability, access, interoperability and re-use, with eDNA data shared via the European Nucleotide Archive (ENA) and other EMBL-EBI resources. To ensure FAIR, the team engaged with the Genomics Standards Consortium (GSC), which maintain metadata standards for eDNA under MIxS (Minimum Information for any Sequence), the community-led FAIRe (Making eDNA FAIR) project, and with the ancient DNA community working on MInAS (Minimum Information about any Ancient Sequence). The metadata collected under AEGIS was mapped to these existing and developing standards to construct metadata checklists and accurately describe experiment data in AEGIS. To facilitate compliance, AEGIS uses standardised metadata collection templates. This presentation will describe the implementation process, including the development of an ENA ancient DNA metadata checklist, approaches for capturing provenance and contextual metadata, and challenges in harmonising standards across biodiversity, eDNA, and ancient genomics domains. The work demonstrates how machine-readable and interoperable metadata standards can support scalable reuse of ancient eDNA data, improve reproducibility, and strengthen long-term integration of palaeogenomic resources into wider biodiversity and environmental data ecosystems.

title: Rethinking “absence” in biodiversity data collection and modeling

programme.title: Rethinking “absence” in biodiversity data collection and modeling
programme.session: CO4 FAIR data in practice - eDNA, modelling and biodiversity concepts
programme.abstract: The rapid growth of biodiversity data through GBIF and related sites has accelerated the development of species distribution models (SDMs) and occupancy models. Simultaneously, the literature has accumulated many partially overlapping terms related to “absence”, including absence record, confirmed absence, negative detection, zero count, and pseudo-absence. A working group with experience in biodiversity data collection, curation, and modeling met monthly for approximately 18 months to sort out this confusing terminology. Most biodiversity sampling compendia did not explicitly define absence-related terms. When they did, usage varied: some sources used presence-absence language, whereas others used detection-non-detection language. The occupancy-modeling literature provided a stronger conceptual framework for data collection (MacKenzie (2005). Here detection and non-detection characterize observations, whereas presence and absence are inferred ecological states that can be estimated probabilistically with repeated survey data. This perspective motivated a petition, introduced by members of our working group and others, to change the values of occurrenceStatus in the Humboldt Extension from “present/absent” to “detected/nonDetected.” SDMs use another set of absence-related terms, such as pseudo-absence, presence-pseudoabsence data, and true absence. For modeling, ordinary language is insufficient. These terms have technical meanings that depend on model class, data type, sampling assumptions, and historical context. During this innovative phase of model development, it seems difficult to create standardized terminology, MacKenzie, D. I. 2005. What are the issues with presence-absence data for wildlife managers? Journal of Wildlife Management 69: 849-860.

summary: Rob Stevenson presented the outcome of a working group (with Abby Benson, Ruben Perez, Deborah Arlt, Yiming and Wesley Hochachka) on confusing 'absence' terminology. He argued presence and absence are asymmetric (presence is a fact, absence a question) and absence is only meaningful against an expectation frame such as a Humboldt Extension survey target. Surveying methodology and analysis texts, the group found the museum (presence-only) and biological survey (repeated, effort-based) communities use different data and models, with detectability as the unifying concept. The main outcome was the TDWG Executive's approval in May of changing Darwin Core occurrenceStatus values from present/absent to detected/not detected.

title: Challenges and Opportunities for FAIR Marine eDNA Data Publication Workflows

programme.title: Challenges and Opportunities for FAIR Marine eDNA Data Publication Workflows
programme.session: CO4 FAIR data in practice - eDNA, modelling and biodiversity concepts
programme.abstract:
Marine environmental DNA (eDNA) dataset volumes are increasing rapidly as eDNA becomes integrated into routine sampling workflows on research vessels and in monitoring programs. However, challenges related to interoperability, metadata standardisation, and repository integration remain and require further work to support future interoperable biodiversity data infrastructure and FAIR data publication workflows.

In this project, we aim to assess current challenges and community needs associated with marine eDNA data publication and interoperability.

We are designing evaluation instruments to assess the current landscape of marine eDNA data publication workflows. We are reviewing existing workflows, tools, metadata standards, and FAIR requirements associated with biodiversity publication pathways. Through surveys and consultations with key stakeholders, we are mapping workflows from sample collection through to data mobilisation and publication. Stakeholder engagement has included collaboration and discussions with Australian and international biodiversity organisations, data infrastructure initiatives, and sequencing and biodiversity data communities.

Preliminary findings indicate that there is a strong interest within the eDNA community in publishing and reusing biodiversity data. However, results suggest inconsistent adoption of metadata standards, fragmented publication workflows, time-consuming publication processes, and incomplete metadata collection practices that may reduce FAIR compliance and data reusability.

This work will inform approaches to interoperable infrastructure for marine eDNA data publication and support FAIR adoption, thereby increasing reusability of marine biodiversity datasets.

title: Visualising specimens as event chains on the Australian Reference Genome Atlas

programme.title: Visualising specimens as event chains on the Australian Reference Genome Atlas
programme.session: CO4 FAIR data in practice - eDNA, modelling and biodiversity concepts
programme.abstract: The Australian Reference Genome Atlas (ARGA) was built in partnership by the Atlas of Living Australia, Australian BioCommons, and Bioplatforms Australia to index whole genome sequence data from Australian biodiversity species and other eukaryote species relevant to Australia’s needs for the bioinformatics community. As part of the project, we created a new model for tracking the provenance of genomic data, tracing specimens from their wild state through to laboratory processing, and appending data objects to their relevant source samples. Here, we outline the data requirements, the selection of fields, and the backend database structure used to facilitate the provenance chain from specimen to data object. We developed a dynamic and extensible demonstration UI, supported by these fields and architecture, to guide users through a discovery journey within the specimen area of the ARGA interface. Using an example, we will demonstrate how users can navigate from a specimen or tissue to a genomic data packet to reveal collection information, protocols, and agents for a rich provenance history display. Underpinning a card-based interface was the aim of ARGA to facilitate deeper ways of exploring and interacting with data for the genomics user community. The ARGA project has now concluded, and we aim to extract lessons and components that we can reuse within the Atlas of Living Australia (https://www.ala.org.au) and which may be repurposed by other platforms that share DNA-derived biodiversity data. We will explore the applicability of this component within other collections-based online interfaces, such as for museums collections and biobanks.

summary: Kathryn Hall described how the Australian Reference Genome Atlas (ARGA), an index rather than repository, modelled provenance chains from a wild organism through collection, museum registration, tissue subsampling, DNA extraction and lab runs to deposited genomic data products. The result lets users see, for example, 31 derived data products from one specimen with tissue, molecule, file type and custodian preserved.

why_it_matters: Provenance is the 'data seatbelt' that matters when a sequence or phylogeny looks wrong, and ARGA shows a working model for linking specimens to genomic data at fine grain.

Genomic data come from amplicons from extracts from subsamples; one organism can yield hundreds of amplicons and thousands of fragments.

title: Bridging Biodiversity Data Standards and Predictive Ecology: Operationalizing Interoperable Workflows for Species Distribution Modeling in West Africa

programme.title: Bridging Biodiversity Data Standards and Predictive Ecology: Operationalizing Interoperable Workflows for Species Distribution Modeling in West Africa
programme.session: CO4 FAIR data in practice - eDNA, modelling and biodiversity concepts
programme.abstract: Biodiversity data standards have enabled large-scale aggregation of species occurrence records, yet their translation into reproducible analytical workflows remains uneven, particularly in data-limited regions. This study operationalizes standardized biodiversity data for machine learning-based species distribution modeling, using threatened tropical timber species in West Africa as a case study. We develop an interoperable workflow integrating species occurrence records structured with Darwin Core and high-resolution bioclimatic variables. The approach emphasizes data harmonization, metadata completeness, and spatial validation to address challenges such as sampling bias, coordinate uncertainty, and inconsistent taxonomy. By aligning heterogeneous datasets within a standards-compliant framework, the workflow supports reproducible and reusable analyses. Preliminary results suggest that adherence to biodiversity data standards improves model robustness and transparency, particularly in underrepresented regions. Predicted distributions under current and future climate scenarios highlight both suitable habitats and areas where data limitations affect model reliability. This work extends the role of biodiversity data standards from data mobilization to fully integrated analytical pipelines. By linking standards-based data management with predictive ecology, it demonstrates how interoperable workflows can enhance biodiversity data use for conservation decision-making and global assessments, especially in data-sparse regions such as West Africa.

summary: Peter Ugege reported a controlled experiment asking whether standards-informed processing of occurrence records changes species distribution model outcomes for six West African timber species. title: The future is the future - thought about access to data in publications

programme.title: The future is the future - thought about access to data in publications
programme.session: SYM45 Planning the Libroscope: creating research ready biodiversity from scientific publications
programme.abstract:
Scientific publications contain a large share of humanity’s knowledge on biodiversity and are becoming increasingly important as training and reference sources for Artificial Intelligence applications. Yet most biodiversity literature remains difficult for machines to access and interpret. Estimates suggest a corpus of hundreds of millions of printed pages, with 50,000-200,000 biodiversity-related articles and around 2,000 taxonomy-relevant journals published annually. Resources such as the Biodiversity Heritage Library and Plazi demonstrate both the scale of the challenge and the feasibility of extracting structured biodiversity knowledge from publications.

Biodiversity publications not only describe taxa and synthesize research, but also cite specimens, observations and datasets, thereby linking natural science collections, occurrence records and scientific interpretations. However, most publications are still produced primarily for human reading and lack machine-actionable semantic structure. Unlocking this knowledge at scale therefore requires strategic prioritisation.

Within the framework of the Disentis Roadmap, which aims to liberate biodiversity knowledge from the literature by 2034, key questions arise: should limited resources focus on continued digitisation of historical print literature, semantic enhancement of legacy publications, or the promotion of future-ready publishing workflows that produce structured and FAIR-compliant data from the outset, as demonstrated by initiatives such as Pensoft and CETAF?

This contribution argues that a practical compromise is the development of a Biodiversity Libroscope: a framework to systematically digitise, extract and publish semantically standardised biodiversity knowledge from well-defined corpora of literature.

title: Realtime Access to Data in new Taxonomic Publications

programme.title: Realtime Access to Data in new Taxonomic Publications
programme.session: SYM45 Planning the Libroscope: creating research ready biodiversity from scientific publications
programme.abstract:
Taxonomic knowledge is published at an accelerating rate across hundreds of journals, creating major challenges for aggregators and biodiversity databases to keep up. Many articles are available only as PDFs, lack machine-actionable structure, and are often hidden behind paywalls, making automated extraction of taxonomic names, type specimens, and diagnostic data increasingly difficult.

This work presents Plazi's semantics-aware, modular workflow that converts in realtime taxonomic publications published as PDFs or XML into open, FAIR, and machine-actionable biodiversity data and semantically enhanced articles. Structured PDFs are decoded to infer document structure, while XML publications (e.g. JATS-TaxPub) are processed directly through embedded semantic markup. Publication streams are harvested through RSS feeds or direct ingestion as part of editorial workflows.

Extracted taxonomic treatments, figures, tables, materials citations, and bibliographic data are semantically enhanced and linked to external repositories and taxonomic reference systems. Automated quality control is complemented by targeted manual correction where required. Outputs are disseminated in near real time through standards-based formats including DwCA, ColDP, and JATS-TaxPub XML. TreatmentBank currently contributes more than 58,000 datasets to the Global Biodiversity Information Facility, over 80,000 new species records to GBIF and the Catalogue of Life, more than one million treatments to BiodiversityPMC, and 800,000 figures as FAIR digital objects in the Biodiversity Literature Repository.

By transforming legacy and newly published literature into interoperable machine-actionable knowledge, this workflow accelerates biodiversity data access for aggregators, infrastructures, and AI applications.

programme.title: Biodiversity literature as FAIR and AI-ready data by design (and how to get there)
programme.session: SYM45 Planning the Libroscope: creating research ready biodiversity from scientific publications
programme.abstract:
Since the earliest observations of the living world, scientific literature has been the primary medium for documenting and disseminating biodiversity knowledge. Over centuries, this process has generated a vast corpus of taxonomic, ecological, biogeographic, and recently also molecular information. Yet, much of these data remain embedded in PDF-based publications, limiting their findability, accessibility, interoperability, and computational reuse.

Although data extraction and annotation tools have been produced to address this issue and unlock biodiversity data from PDFs, it is crucial to stop extending the legacy backlog. According to the Disentis vision, this presentation proposes to shift toward semantically enhanced publishing workflows designed to readily produce FAIR, interlinked, and AI-ready data, a process that started more than a decade ago as part of the ViBRANT FP7 project and was subsequently carried out successfully through the pro-iBiosphere, EU BON, and BiCIKL projects.

XML-first workflows for prospective literature (MetoTaxa, ARPHA) will be presented from semantic markup to enrichment and publication through interconnected infrastructures. Particular emphasis will be placed on the standards (e.g., JATS-TaxPub), vocabularies (e.g., Darwin Core), and resolvable persistent identifiers.

By supporting large-scale knowledge integration and machine-actionable biodiversity data, such workflows create new opportunities for emerging AI applications and also improve support for many other machine driven forms of reuse.

title: Building digital-native species: Transitioning from PDF liberation to semantic-by-design publishing

programme.title: Building digital-native species: Transitioning from PDF liberation to semantic-by-design publishing
programme.session: SYM45 Planning the Libroscope: creating research ready biodiversity from scientific publications
programme.abstract:
Scientific publications remain the primary vehicle for communicating biodiversity knowledge. The Bouchout Declaration marked an important step toward opening biodiversity literature and mobilising the taxonomic knowledge embedded within publications. Since then, major efforts have focused on liberating biodiversity data from legacy PDFs through text mining, semantic annotation and automated extraction workflows, enabling large-scale mobilisation of taxonomic names, treatments and material citations.

However, PDF-centric approaches remain limited by the publication format itself. Extracting structured knowledge from PDFs is retrospective, heterogeneous and costly, often requiring complex workflows to recover semantics that were never encoded during publication.

In the framework of the Disentis Roadmap and the Biodiversity Libroscope initiative, this contribution argues for a transition from retrospective data liberation to digital-first and XML-first publishing workflows that generate machine-actionable biodiversity knowledge by design. Central to this vision is the concept of “digital-native species”, in which species descriptions and supporting evidence are created, published and maintained in interoperable semantic environments from the outset.

Publications remain the formal scholarly record but are generated from, and linked to, structured specimen-level evidence including images, sequences, measurements, treatments and collection records. Semantic XML publishing enables fine-grained markup, interoperability across infrastructures and direct integration with natural science collections and global biodiversity platforms.

This contribution discusses how semantic-by-design publishing can create interconnected, computable and AI-ready biodiversity knowledge ecosystems.

title: Literature triage to support Island Biodiversity Monitoring

programme.title: Literature triage to support Island Biodiversity Monitoring
programme.session: SYM45 Planning the Libroscope: creating research ready biodiversity from scientific publications
programme.abstract:
Biodiversity research increasingly relies on vast quantities of scientific literature, therefore developing screening tools to better scan the literature is essential. Island biodiversity was selected as a test bed thanks to the support of Biodiversa+. An automatic triage system was developed and applied to Biodiversity Island monitoring.

We started by querying OpenAlex with broad coverage Boolean equations. Further, a binary classifier for island ecosystem publications (BioMoQA project) was developed using pre-trained bidirectional language models. After manual selection, the articles are then indexed into SIBiLS/BiodiversityPMC (https://biodiversitypmc.sibils.org/). Using 5-fold cross-validation on 1,434 abstracts, we compared domain-specific biomedical transformers (e.g., BioBERT, BiomedBERT) for life sciences against general-purpose models (e.g., BERT, RoBERTa), which are combined with ensemble learning. Binary cross-entropy ensembles achieved best performance with ROC-AUC of 0.926. The reported model performance is competitive with curator inter-rater agreement (expert kappa ~0.78). The classifier is now integrated in the SIBiLS\BiodiversityPMC platform, and through weekly screening ensures consistent up to date coverage of island biodiversity literature, thus supporting the harmonization of global island biodiversity monitoring efforts. The service platform is currently being applied to other biodiversity assessment projects and could likely serve a large set of biodiversity communities.
