title: Artificial Intelligence Amplifies Paleontology's Reproducibility Problem

programme.title: Artificial Intelligence Amplifies Paleontology’s Reproducibility Problem
programme.session: SYM46 AI-Readiness Metrics and Metadata for Biodiversity Data
programme.abstract: Paleontology has become a data-intensive science. Along with the specimen, large amounts of associated data are produced. These data are distributed across supplementary files, institutional databases, and discipline-specific repositories, and reproducibility problems are common: missing datasets, character matrices that fail to execute, incomplete documentation, unverifiable specimen vouchers, and missing methodological detail. Many of these problems predate AI, but AI methods are now being applied to paleontological data faster than existing infrastructure was designed to support, particularly LLMs that extract structured data from legacy literature and vision models that classify specimens from images. AI offers reproducibility benefits, including standardization at scale and recovery of data from inaccessible literature. However, it also introduces a specific risk: it can scale and conceal existing data quality problems by converting incomplete, ambiguous, or unverifiable source material into structured outputs that meet FAIR criteria and appear authoritative. A dataset can pass automated validation, receive a persistent identifier, and be reused in computational workflows while lacking the provenance, expert validation, and traceable interpretation required to assess its reliability. AI-readiness in paleontology must therefore be defined by verifiability, including provenance to source evidence, executability of analyses, and traceability of expert judgment. Journals should require disclosure of AI involvement in dataset construction and extend peer review to AI-generated data; repositories should treat AI provenance, validation status, and source linkage as first-class metadata.

actual.identification_notes: Virtual (pre-recorded video) talk played after a search for the uploaded files; speaker introduced as 'Brooke Longfox'. Co-authored with Mark Young, editor-in-chief of Historical Biology. The talk title is phrased as a question ('Is Artificial Intelligence Amplifying...?').

summary: Brooke Long-Fox, a data curation scientist at MorphoBank and data editor for Historical Biology, argued that AI is entering a field that already has reproducibility problems of availability (data not deposited or on personal websites), documentation (no README, undefined characters) and traceability (unclear links from evidence to result). AI can turn ambiguous or incomplete sources into perfectly formatted, schema-valid tables that get DOIs and feed further AI, improving structure without improving scientific validity. Using morphological character matrices, she showed that a binary score can encode expert judgements about homology, preservation and ontogeny, and proposed adding verifiability to AI readiness: tracing assertions to evidence, recording whether they were transcribed, transformed or inferred, and who validated them.
one_line_takeaway: AI can make uncertain paleontological data look clean and authoritative, so AI-ready data must also be verifiable back to evidence and interpretation.
why_it_matters: It distinguishes technical validity from scientific validity, a warning relevant to any biodiversity data being mass-extracted or inferred by AI.
key_points: This is not an argument against AI; she uses AI-assisted curation, but AI can amplify existing reproducibility problems.
Paleontology is data-intensive; the digital extended specimen links a specimen to images, occurrences, stratigraphy, measurements, matrices and outputs, so errors propagate further.
Availability problems: data never deposited, manuscripts claiming no data exist, files on personal websites or cloud links, private or incomplete repository records.
Documentation problems: no README or data dictionary, unexplained abbreviations, 3D models without links to specimens, incomplete character definitions; a PID says where a file is, not what it means.
Traceability problems: data statements not matching deposits, scores not linked to sources, matrices modified across studies without documentation, unclear versions.
AI can produce schema-valid, DOI-bearing structured outputs from ambiguous sources (e.g. OCR column shifts, inconsistent translation), which then feed other AI systems.
Technical validity is not scientific validity: a matrix cell such as character 37 = 0/1 may encode reasoning about homology, absence vs non-preservation, ontogeny, polymorphism or inapplicability.
AI-ready data should be machine-readable, FAIR, documented and validated, and for interpretive data also verifiable.
questions: Can current standards record that an assertion was generated by AI-assisted inference and then confirmed by a domain expert?

notable_claims.claim: AI can transform incomplete or ambiguous information into structured outputs that look ready for reuse, even passing schema validation and receiving a DOI.
Character states in morphological matrices can encode expert judgement rather than simple observations waiting to be extracted.

recommendations: Define the use case (extracting, transforming or inferring).
Preserve source, method, responsible agent, validation status and uncertainty.
Crosswalk existing standards such as Darwin Core and identify gaps.
examples_case_studies: MorphoBank skull image with specimen, photo and character-state information
Historical Biology journal data policy experience

representative_excerpt.text: So the structure has been improved, but the underlying scientific uncertainty has not necessarily improved with it. So that is the distinction I want to make between technical validity and scientific validity.

notable_moments.description: Three categories of existing reproducibility problems.
The failure mode: AI makes uncertainty look structured.
Morphological character matrix example.
Practical path toward verifiable robot-ready data.

title: AI Ready Standards with Croissant for Type Specimens Catalog Datasets

programme.title: AI Ready Standards with Croissant for Type Specimens Catalog Datasets
programme.session: SYM46 AI-Readiness Metrics and Metadata for Biodiversity Data
programme.abstract:
The FAIR principles are fundamental to Open Science. Publishing datasets used in Artificial Intelligence (AI) experiments in accordance with these principles is essential for ensuring reproducibility. Additionally, these FAIR datasets enhance the performance of Machine Learning (ML) applications, e.g., species labeling using named entity recognition models. Recently, ML Commons introduced Croissant, an ML-ready dataset format designed for seamless integration with ML models and with ML-ready dataset-sharing platforms such as Hugging Face.

Biodiversity data mobilization necessitates adherence to FAIR principles that go beyond merely sharing data in structured formats. We present an experimental approach to converting unstructured text from entomological type specimen catalogs into Darwin Core (DwC) metadata using Large Language Models, including GPT and Qwen. Subsequently, we map Croissant metadata fields to DwC terms-such as dwc:genus, dwc:scientificName, and dwc:individualCount-because these terms can be used to make type specimen catalogs machine-readable.

To evaluate whether our datasets align with FAIR principles for ML, we generate and conduct experiments on subsets of them. These metadata are then integrated into the NFDI4DataScience metadata portal, where FAIR metrics are visualized using the Piveau metric service. This portal provides metadata on datasets for AI use and metrics on FAIR principles. Complementing this quantitative assessment, we validate our metadata format using the FAIR Checker service.

Our proposed metadata framework for type specimen catalogs serves as a reference model for broader applications within biodiversity research domains. In addition, we provide a standardized protocol for the open mobilization of entomological type specimen data.

actual.identification_notes: Pre-recorded video played last, although scheduled third (the convener said earlier the third speaker could not make it). She presents the work with Jana Hofmann from Senckenberg.

summary: Sefika Efeoglu presented a workflow for turning historical type specimen catalogues into AI-ready datasets: LLMs (e.g. GPT and Qwen) extract structured information from unstructured catalogue text, which is expressed in Darwin Core and then described with ML Commons Croissant metadata in JSON-LD. She showed how Darwin Core fields map to Croissant fields (scientific name as label, genus as taxonomic feature, individual count as integer, catalogue number as identifier, locality, event date, collector, type status) and how the pipeline evaluates FAIR metrics. The approach aims to bridge biodiversity standards and ML dataset platforms such as Hugging Face, Kaggle and OpenML.
one_line_takeaway: Combining LLM extraction, Darwin Core and Croissant metadata offers a route from historical specimen catalogues to FAIR, ML-ready datasets.
why_it_matters: Croissant is becoming the metadata layer ML platforms understand; mapping Darwin Core into it could make collection data directly discoverable and loadable in ML ecosystems.
key_points: Biodiversity data are used for species identification, named entity recognition, taxonomic knowledge extraction and knowledge graphs, but historical catalogues are largely unstructured text.
FAIRness supports ML reproducibility, clarity, sharing and more reliable model development; the aim is to extend FAIR into ML workflows.

Croissant (ML Commons) is a standardised, machine-readable metadata format for ML-ready datasets supported by platforms such as Hugging Face, Kaggle and OpenML: 'create once, publish anywhere, use everywhere'.
Workflow: type specimen catalogue, unstructured text, LLM-assisted extraction (GPT, Qwen), Darwin Core metadata, Croissant metadata, AI-ready dataset.

Mapping examples: scientificName as label for classification, genus as taxonomic feature, individualCount as integer feature, catalogNumber as unique identifier, locality, eventDate, collector (provenance) and typeStatus.
Records are represented in Croissant JSON-LD with explicit field data types; the pipeline measures FAIR metrics and metadata quality.
methods: schema mapping Darwin Core to Croissant

notable_claims.claim: The workflow transforms type specimen catalogue text via LLM extraction into Darwin Core and then Croissant metadata to produce an AI-ready dataset.
Mapping to Croissant preserves Darwin Core semantics rather than discarding them.

recommendations: Use Croissant as a common metadata layer to connect biodiversity standards with the ML ecosystem.
future_work: Extend the approach to other biodiversity collections.
examples_case_studies: Type specimen catalogues (with Senckenberg)

representative_excerpt.text: The point is not to discard the Darwin Core. Instead, it preserves its biodiverse semantics and expresses those elements with a metadata structure that ML systems can understand.

Darwin Core to Croissant field mapping.

session.title: A consensus taxonomic reference for improved freshwater biodiversity data and knowledge

title: Not just another database: building the future of freshwater taxonomy with FADAtims

programme.title: Not just another database: building the future of freshwater taxonomy with FADAtims
programme.session: SYM37A A consensus taxonomic reference for improved freshwater biodiversity data and knowledge
programme.abstract: Freshwater biodiversity is declining rapidly, yet freshwater taxonomy remains fragmented across databases, standards and expert communities. Maintaining reliable species lists is challenging because names change continuously, new taxa are described, and taxonomic concepts differ between regions and organism groups. These issues limit interoperability between biodiversity infrastructures and constrain large-scale ecological assessments and policy applications. To address this gap, we are developing FADAtims, an online taxonomic information management system for collaborative curation of freshwater biodiversity checklists, which is developed within the Belspo-funded infraFADA project. The platform enables registered experts to curate and continuously update species names, synonyms, classification, distribution and status information through a transparent and traceable workflow. FADAtims is designed as a FAIR, interoperable and machine-actionable infrastructure component for freshwater biodiversity data. Built with open-source technologies and aligned with Biodiversity Information Standards, it supports data exchange with major biodiversity infrastructures including GBIF, Catalogue of Life and the Freshwater Information Platform. Interoperability with systems such as WoRMS and TaxonWorks further supports harmonisation and long-term sustainability. The platform aims to provide an authoritative freshwater taxonomic backbone that can be linked to occurrence, trait and monitoring databases as well as conservation assessments. We present the current status of FADAtims, its role within the emerging freshwater biodiversity data ecosystem and discuss community-driven approaches for sustaining curated freshwater taxonomy infrastructures.

title: Catalogue of Life and Freshwater species data

programme.title: Catalogue of Life and Freshwater species data
programme.session: SYM37A A consensus taxonomic reference for improved freshwater biodiversity data and knowledge
programme.abstract: 30 years ago the activities that led to the Catalogue of Life started. For 25 years the catalogue of described organisms of all life, has been freely available online. GBIF, also celebrating a 25 year anniversary, is now making use of the Catalogue of Life as the taxonomic reference for the 3.7 billion species occurrences it mediates. Although a lot of progress has been made, there are still obvious taxonomic gaps. Some groups are notoriously under-represented and incomplete (like insects). In other cases, taxonomic data from specific ecosystem realms like freshwater is scarce. The Catalogue of Life infrastructure, ChecklistBank, now promotes the open data publishing of taxonomic and nomenclatural resources, and different types of species lists (such as policy-relevant lists). The infrastructure also provides the means to share species interaction data. We will provide an overview of the available information in Catalogue of Life and in its infrastructure. We also discuss how this data could be improved, for example through collaboration with initiatives like the Freshwater Animal Diversity Assessment.

title: A species-level taxonomic catalog of Neotropical freshwater insects: building a consensus reference for occurrence data integration and conservation planning

programme.title: A species-level taxonomic catalog of Neotropical freshwater insects: building a consensus reference for occurrence data integration, and conservation planning.
programme.session: SYM37A A consensus taxonomic reference for improved freshwater biodiversity data and knowledge
programme.abstract: Freshwaters are among the most biodiverse yet data-deficient habitats globally, and the Neotropical region exemplifies this paradox - exceptional aquatic insect diversity combined with critical taxonomic and distributional gaps rooted in historical undersampling. To our knowledge, no equivalent species-level, multi-order catalog of freshwater insects exists for the Neotropical region. Here we present an ongoing effort to compile a DarwinCore-compliant catalog of freshwater aquatic insects for the Neotropical lowlands, covering seven orders: Trichoptera, Coleoptera, Odonata, Ephemeroptera, Plecoptera, Hemiptera, and Megaloptera. All compiled species names are verified against the GBIF Backbone Taxonomy and the Catalogue of Life, documenting nomenclatural discrepancies including synonyms, combinationes novae, and typographic errors. Country-level distribution data are linked to georeferenced occurrence records from GBIF and regional sources. For each verified species, occurrence records are cleaned and linked to stream network segments, with environmental and topographic variables extracted at the sub-catchment scale. This dataset will underpin distribution modelling across the Magdalena-Cauca Basin in Colombia, assessing how river network structure shapes richness, rarity, and endemism, and prioritising conservation areas accounting for cumulative hydropower impacts on freshwater connectivity.

summary: Alejandra Correa-Bedoya presented a Darwin Core-compliant species-level checklist of seven orders of freshwater insects for the Neotropics (southern Mexico to Brazil), compiled over six months for her PhD. She showed that names documented for Colombia (about 1,250 species) often have no occurrence records there, due to taxonomic resolution bias and a data supply gap rather than platform failures, verified names against global infrastructures, and noted her list triples known Odonata species for Colombia compared with a national effort. Grounding it in the free-flowing Samaná Norte river, threatened by planned dams and invasive species, she argued that without species names there are no occurrences, no species distribution models and no evidence for protecting rivers.
one_line_takeaway: Without a reliable species-level checklist, Neotropical freshwater insect occurrences, distribution models and conservation arguments cannot be built.
why_it_matters: It links taxonomic infrastructure directly to conservation decisions under dam development pressure in one of the world's most biodiverse and data-deficient regions.
key_points: Global freshwater populations declined about 83% since 1970 (Living Planet), about 95% in Latin America and the Caribbean; Central and South America are data-deficient hotspots.
Dam expansion is concentrated on the Andean slopes, modifying flows before data exist to assess losses.

It is a taxon-core list (names, synonyms, classification) of officially described species, the naming backbone needed before occurrence data can be resolved.
Colombia has the most documented species of these orders (about 1,250), reflecting its position among heterogeneous biogeographic subregions.
Example stonefly: GBIF shows records across its range but none in Colombia at the range centre, indicating nobody has named and looked for it there.

Verification against GBIF found flags such as recent nomenclatural changes (Coleoptera), typographic/algorithmic errors (Trichoptera) and a genus reassignment (Hemiptera); she frames this as a data supply gap, not a platform problem.
In the Samaná Norte basin, about 600 occurrence records of these orders resolve only to genus, which is not interpretable for conservation decisions.

title: Biodiversity data at your fingertips: open-access freshwater biodiversity information systems for South Africa and Africa

programme.title: Biodiversity data at your fingertips: open-access freshwater biodiversity information systems for South Africa and Africa
programme.session: SYM37A A consensus taxonomic reference for improved freshwater biodiversity data and knowledge
programme.abstract: Freshwater biodiversity data are essential for monitoring ecosystem change, informing conservation, and supporting evidence-based management. However, such data often remain fragmented, inaccessible, or poorly integrated across scales, institutions, and regions. The Freshwater Biodiversity Information System (FBIS) and FBIS-Africa platforms, developed for South Africa and the broader African region respectively, respond directly to this need. FBIS is a powerful, visual, data-rich system designed to host, share, and explore freshwater biodiversity data. Its design and functionality have been shaped by key user groups, including water resource managers, conservation practitioners, planners, researchers, and environmental consultants. Both platforms interoperate with global biodiversity infrastructures, including GBIF and the IUCN Red List of Threatened Species, contributing to a more connected and accessible freshwater biodiversity data ecosystem. By combining regional expertise, open infrastructure, and interoperable data workflows, FBIS and FBIS-Africa demonstrate how community-driven information systems can support FAIR biodiversity data mobilisation and translate knowledge into actionable conservation and management outcomes. The South African platform already supports improved freshwater science, conservation, and decision-making at a national scale, with approximately 14 million occurrence records across eight biodiversity modules. The recently developed FBIS-Africa platform is rapidly expanding in both data coverage and user uptake. Together, these platforms play a critical role in translating freshwater biodiversity data into informed monitoring, management, and conservation action across local, regional, continental, and global scales.

It uses the GBIF taxonomic backbone (with planned FADA integration), links to the IUCN Red List, offers spatial and temporal filters, spatial layers and standardised dashboards, and attaches citation metadata to every record. title: The FIPbio data portal: towards an integrated freshwater biodiversity data ecosystem

programme.abstract:
Freshwater biodiversity research, monitoring and policy increasingly rely on interoperable data infrastructures linking taxonomy, biodiversity observations, abiotic sampling data and remote sensing products. With the renewal of the freshwater biodiversity data portal FIPbio within the Freshwater Information Platform (FIP), we present a framework integrating freshwater occurrence records, eDNA observations, sampling data and satellite-derived environmental time series, including chlorophyll-a dynamics and land-use change, across lakes, wetlands and river catchmentsinto a unified freshwater data ecosystem.

The renewed portal builds on the Biodiversity Information Management System (BIMS), originally developed for the South African Freshwater Biodiversity Information System (FBIS). Central to FIPbio is the global Freshwater Animal Diversity Assessment (FADA) taxonomic backbone, continuously curated through the FADAtims platform. This freshwater-specific backbone enables a comprehensive overview of occurrence data mobilised through infrastructures such as GBIF.

Sampling sites are spatially linked to global freshwater environmental context layers including river networks, basins, lakes, wetlands and land-water interface classes. Occurrence records are automatically annotated with contextual dataset IDs and snapped to river network segments, enabling reproducible freshwater-specific analytical workflows using resources such as Hydrography90m.

FIPbio enhances the discoverability, interoperability and long-term reuse of freshwater biodiversity and monitoring data from local to global scales. The platform supports freshwater data mobilisation efforts, including those within the FWBON network and contributes to an integrated global freshwater biodiversity information landscape.

title: A collaborative perspective on a globally standardised river basin name database

programme.title: A collaborative perspective on a globally standardised river basin name database
programme.session: SYM37B A consensus taxonomic reference for improved freshwater biodiversity data and knowledge
programme.abstract:
When categorising and aggregating data across a given landscape, Earth scientists tend to use grids, broad geographic delineations such as continents, or administrative units such as countries, counties or states. However, when the environmental characteristics and energy flows in a given region come into focus, then the drainage basin becomes an appropriate spatial unit. This is because of the topographic structure of the landscape along rivers, streams, lakes and wetlands that are laterally and longitudinally connected. Especially in light of global change, spatially pinpointing and being able to search a certain drainage basin by name - e.g. to analyse the observed and projected changes - represents a task that is important for the study of biodiversity as well as for neighbouring areas such as transnational water management. To date, though, a comprehensive and globally standardised resource of basin names is missing.

In this contribution, we will outline how such a resource could be developed, maintained and refined collaboratively on the basis of the Wikimedia and OpenStreetMap platforms and their respective communities. The Wikimedia ecosystem comprises of a suite of interconnected open collaborative platforms that already cover multiple facets of both river basins and biodiversity and that are multilingual. Wikidata in particular is a repository of semantic web-compatible general reference information whose entries include river basins, taxa, territorial entities, ecological concepts and scientific publications about any of these. Wikidata and its sister sites are also closely integrated with OpenStreetMap and citizen science efforts, and Wikidata identifiers are widely used in scholarly contexts and frequently mapped to entries in other relevant databases.

actual.identification_notes: Recording resumes mid-introduction (the moderator mentions Vanessa Bremerich and Sami Domisch, apparently as co-authors). summary: Daniel Mietchen argued that river basins are the natural spatial unit for freshwater biology but lack a global, multilingual naming system: geoscience grids and the Pfafstetter coding system ignore biology, naming, karst, flow changes and complex branching. Using Oslo's Akerselva as an example, he showed how Wikidata links the river, its drainage basin (Nordmarksvassdraget) and Norwegian REGINE and ELVIS identifiers, but that Wikidata's drainage basin statements are almost all Norwegian. He listed edge cases (seasonal and split rivers, karst, flow reversal, dams, historic courses and names, oral languages) and asked how TDWG groups, Wikidata and OpenStreetMap could collaborate, proposing an unconference session.
one_line_takeaway: Freshwater biodiversity data need a global, multilingual, collaboratively maintained river basin naming system, and TDWG, Wikidata and OpenStreetMap could build it together.
why_it_matters: Being able to state in a standard way which river basin an occurrence belongs to would support freshwater invasions, connectivity and conservation analyses that grids cannot capture.
key_points: Geosciences put everything on grids set by measurement methods; biology rarely follows grids, so translation mechanisms are needed.
The Pfafstetter coding system is widely used in geodatabases but knows nothing about biology or names, and ignores karst, water level changes and complex branching.
The talk asks questions rather than giving answers: how can TDWG help express, e.g. in Darwin Core, that a fish record belongs to one basin and not another?
Akerselva example: basin delineation from AquaINFRA-style segment data, and Wikidata items linking river, source, mouth and drainage basin (Nordmarksvassdraget).
Norwegian identifiers exist (REGINE for basins, ELVIS for rivers); Wikidata has 431 items with drainage basin/REGINE statements and 1,066 with ELVIS IDs, almost all Norwegian.
Transboundary rivers carry names in several languages (e.g. Norway, Finland, Russia), raising the question of which to use.

Edge cases: seasonally dry or drought-split rivers, hunger stones, karst, seasonal flooding, flow reversal, groundwater, atmospheric rivers, paleohydrology, dams, historic courses and names, oral-only languages.
Candidate collaborators: relevant TDWG interest, task and maintenance groups; Wikidata; OpenStreetMap.

Which TDWG groups are relevant and active for this?
How to record an occurrence in an aquatic environment that changes over time?

Essentially all drainage basins with statements in Wikidata are from Norway.

Build on existing European work (WISE) and look at other regions.

title: From 'Lost in Translation' to Fit-for-Purpose Data: Why Ecologists and Conservation Practice Still Need Groupings and Uncertainties

programme.title: From “Lost in Translation” to Fit-for-Purpose Data: Why Ecologists and Conservation Practice Still Need groupings and cF
programme.session: SYM37B A consensus taxonomic reference for improved freshwater biodiversity data and knowledge
programme.abstract:
This talk highlights mismatches between biodiversity data standards and practical ecological and conservation work in freshwater ecosystems, with a botanical focus. Drawing on NIVA’s experience, we demonstrate why ecologists still need taxonomic groupings such as agg., col., vel., /, sensu lato, and sensu stricto. The talk gives aims to show that honest and effective biodiversity reporting requires standards that allow uncertainty to be expressed-rather than erased.

We will present graphs illustrating how substantial amounts of monitoring data can effectively be cut out from time series, ascf. and grouping annotations are not supported in GBIF. At the same time, we emphasize that management categories should be applied as downstream filters, not embedded in global biodiversity infrastructures.

Further, as hybrids and unresolved taxa are common across many organism groups. Mappers are indirectly pushed towards making uncertain species records that are not flagged for uncertainties, due to requirements linked to red listing, Water Framework Directive monitoring, and invasive species mapping. Combined with a lack of verifiability, this creates serious challenges for biologists-both in carrying out their commissioned work and in submitting truthful, high-quality data to GBIF.

actual.identification_notes: Introduced as 'Bernard Glauskedalen' (ASR). Co-presented with NIVA database colleague Natalie (surname not given), who the moderator noted was missing from the original slide. The title was announced as changed ('...Need Grouping and Uncertainties'). An extended audience discussion of the posed question is included. Speaker label “Natalie (surname not given)” is indexed as “Natalie”; see the correction record for the reason.

summary: Bernhard Askedalen and colleague Natalie performed a sketch in which a botanist tries to record uncertain water plant identifications (cf., agg., col., sensu lato) and a database cannot store them, so records are either overstated or bumped to genus, losing ecological information. They showed herbarium sheets with multiple conflicting determinations and noted that for some groups initial names can be as low as 6% correct on expert revision. Natalie found cf. in only 0.1% of water plant and 1.1% of benthic algae observations in NIVA datasets, because reporting pipelines drop uncertainty. They asked how systems should represent uncertainty and taxonomic groupings consistently; the audience suggested keeping these qualifiers with the data, flexibility across organism groups, an identification-uncertainty term, and a BIMS-style identification certainty column with include/exclude decisions.
one_line_takeaway: Biodiversity data systems must be able to record identification uncertainty and taxonomic groupings, or ecologists face a choice between false certainty and lost ecological information.
why_it_matters: Monitoring data used for ecological status assessments routinely contain cf., aggregates and sensu lato concepts; standards that erase them degrade both data honesty and usability.
key_points: Sketch: 'cf.' for a sterile Sparganium angustifolium cannot be recorded, so it is entered as certain; Utricularia vulgaris without flowers is bumped to genus by a red-list data check; 'agg.', 'col.' and 'sensu lato' are not supported.
Genus-level records lose information useful for within-lake trends and ecological condition assessment based on species assemblages (e.g. eutrophication tolerance).
Paying customers provide little incentive to make records verifiable.

Herbarium sheets can carry three to six different names from different people; for some groups the first name given can be as low as 6% correct, with 94% separated as another species on expert revision.
In selected NIVA datasets from the 1960s to last year, cf. appeared in only 0.1% of water plant and 1.1% of benthic algae observations.
Information exists internally but is lost or transformed when reporting to national systems: uncertain identifications reported as certain, reduced to genus, or aggregates handled via pseudo-taxa.
Question posed: how should biodiversity systems represent uncertainty and taxonomic grouping consistently without losing ecological meaning?
datasets: NIVA water plant and benthic algae monitoring datasets
methods: analysis of qualifier frequency in datasets
questions: How should biodiversity systems represent uncertainty and taxonomic grouping without losing ecological meaning in a consistent way?

notable_claims.claim: For some water plant groups, the first name given on herbarium sheets can be as low as 6% correct, with 94% identified as a separate species on expert revision.
In selected NIVA datasets, cf. appeared in only 0.1% of water plant observations and 1.1% of benthic algae observations.
Uncertainty information recorded internally is lost or transformed when data are standardised and reported to national institutions.

recommendations: Keep uncertainty qualifiers and groupings with the data.
Provide guidelines for consistent representation across domains.
results_findings: Uncertainty qualifiers are rare in reported data because reporting requirements strip them, not because uncertain identifications are rare.
future_work: NIVA is building a new database and seeks guidance on representing uncertainty.
examples_case_studies: Sparganium angustifolium (sterile)
Utricularia vulgaris vs U. australis
Nymphaea alba col. including N. candida

q_and_a.question: The moderator asked the room for opinions on the posed question; a respondent (called on as Olaf) answered.
q_and_a.answer_summary: These qualifiers must remain with the data or GBIF will never be correct, but they cannot be harmonised across organism groups (plants use aggregates, invertebrate people mostly cf.), so infrastructures must be flexible.

q_and_a.question: Dimitri suggested an identification uncertainty value analogous to coordinate uncertainty, as discussed with Peter Desmet.
q_and_a.answer_summary: Such a value, like AI recognition confidence, would not solve everything but could give data users an indication.

q_and_a.question: An audience member described their BIMS-based system with an identification certainty column (expert, high, medium, low, unknown) and include/exclude flags with reasons.
q_and_a.answer_summary: Users can filter uncertain records themselves, and recorded exclusion reasons prevent repeating past decisions, as happened in a decade of invasive alien species analyses.

title: How does human impact change species diversity and composition in 50 types of inland water habitats?

programme.title: How does human impact change species diversity and composition in 50 types of inland water habitats?
programme.session: SYM37B A consensus taxonomic reference for improved freshwater biodiversity data and knowledge
programme.abstract: The revision of inland water habitats for the European Nature Information System (EUNIS) is based on the common types used for the EU Water Framework Directive and related habitat types of the Habitats Directive, as well as on more specific habitats of the Habitats Directive. The presentation describes natural biodiversity for major biological groups in 50 inland water habitat types and how these groups change with human impact. Altogether 23 standing water habitat types and 27 running water habitat types are presented in terms of their natural abiotic conditions and their truly aquatic biological communities, including species richness and characteristic, common and dominant taxa of phytoplankton, aquatic vegetation and fish in standing waters, as well as benthic algae, aquatic vegetation, benthic invertebrates and fish in running waters. The data are based on harmonised taxa lists for each major taxonomic group. While habitats in reference condition have distinct biological communities shaped mainly by geology, altitude, and size, impacted habitats converge towards degraded states with fewer characteristic species due to major pressures, such as nutrient pollution, hydromorphological change and water abstraction. With the EU Biodiversity Strategy 2030 and Nature Restoration Regulation, Europe now has a shared scientific framework to support the monitoring of whether restoration actions effectively improve inland water ecosystems. The work is published as a report from the European Topic Centre for Biodiversity and Ecosystems funded by the European Environment Agency (EEA).

actual.identification_notes: Introduced as 'Anne Luke Solheim'; she introduced herself earlier as 'Anne Lykke Solheim' from NIVA (ASR). ASR renders EUNIS as 'UNIS'.

summary: Anne Lyche Solheim presented work for the European Environment Agency (European Topic Centre on Biodiversity and Ecosystems) revising EUNIS inland water habitat types to align with Water Framework Directive and Habitats Directive types: over 20 standing and over 20 running water types, described mainly by altitude, calcium/alkalinity, humic content and size. Using REBECCA and WISER project data (2004-2011) with expert-harmonised taxonomy, the team compared natural and impacted water bodies by NMDS and clustering and identified characteristic, common and dominant taxa. Natural waters showed distinct, textbook communities, while human impact made habitat types more similar, with fewer characteristic species (e.g. loss of chrysophytes and isoetids, more cyprinids and fewer salmonids).
one_line_takeaway: Human pressures erase the natural distinctness of freshwater habitat types, making their biological communities converge on degraded states with fewer characteristic species.
why_it_matters: The revised EUNIS types and their biological descriptions underpin European habitat reporting and show biotic homogenisation as a measurable outcome of pressure, relevant to stalled Water Framework Directive progress.
key_points: EUNIS is the EEA's European Nature Information System for habitat classification; its freshwater part mixed very broad and very narrow types and needed revision.
Revised types: over 20 standing and over 20 running water habitat types based on WFD broad types, plus rarer Habitats Directive types.
Key type descriptors for biology are much the same for lakes and rivers: altitude, calcium (alkalinity), humic content and size.

Data came from EU projects REBECCA and WISER (2004-2011) covering thousands of lakes and rivers with physicochemical data; taxonomy was harmonised in expert workshops and checked against AlgaeBase and freshwaterecology.info.
Methods: split natural vs impacted water bodies, assess compositional similarity with NMDS and clustering, identify characteristic, common and dominant taxa per habitat.

Natural lakes: richness increases with size and decreases with altitude; e.g. mixotrophic chrysophytes in siliceous, high-altitude and humic lakes; isoetids in siliceous lakes; salmonids in siliceous, high-altitude lakes.

Impacted lakes: types become more similar, fewer characteristic taxa, fewer chrysophytes, fewer isoetids, no characteristic fish species, more cyprinids and fewer salmonids; species richness differences were unclear.
Rivers face multiple pressures; impacts increase similarity between types and reduce characteristic vegetation and invertebrate taxa, with more dominant fish species.
WFD ecological status has stalled at about 60% less than good and 40% good or better since the first river basin management plans in 2009.

entities.name: European Topic Centre on Biodiversity and Ecosystems

datasets: REBECCA and WISER lake and river biological datasets
methods: reference vs impacted comparison using WFD status

notable_claims.claim: Human impact increases the similarity of biological communities between habitat types, which become less specific for all three lake groups.
Impacted lakes of any type had no characteristic fish species, with more cyprinids and fewer salmonids.
Since the first river basin management plans in 2009, WFD ecological status has stood still at about 60% less than good and 40% good or better.

results_findings: Each revised habitat type differs from others for at least one biological community.
Healthy waters have distinct communities shaped by geology, altitude and size.
Impacted habitats converge toward degraded states with fewer characteristic species.
limitations: No clear species richness difference between natural and impacted lakes, possibly due to taxonomic uncertainty in the database.
future_work: EEA will publish a crosswalk table between the old and new classifications and related typologies.
examples_case_studies: Revised EUNIS inland water habitat types (about 50 types)

q_and_a.answer_summary: Using WFD ecological status classes already in the database (high/good vs moderate/poor/bad), with GIS help from a topic centre partner to identify reference rivers and officially reported WFD status where missing.

q_and_a.question: An audience member asked whether the old and new classifications can be translated.
q_and_a.answer_summary: A large Excel crosswalk to the old EUNIS system, Habitats Directive types, WFD broad types, IUCN and MAES classifications will be published by the EEA.

Methods for comparing natural and impacted water bodies.

title: SpecifyaaS: Managing Ephemeral Repositories in Collections-Based Research

programme.title: SpecifyaaS: Managing Ephemeral Repositories in Collections-Based Research
programme.session: SYM20 Meeting Biodiversity Data Standards Using Specify Software
programme.abstract:
Specify 7 has substantially expanded the capacity of institutions to standardize efficient biodiversity data capture, management, and exchange during collections-based research. At the Swedish Museum of Natural History (NRM), data are maintained across multiple Specify instances, which includes databases for research programmes and projects. They support collaborative initiatives characterized by operational constraints that often differ greatly from those of the public repositories where research specimens will ultimately be deposited.

Here I describe the use of Specify 7 instances as “ephemeral repositories” within the biodiversity data network at the NRM. Although they are often broader in scope with respect to the data compiled, and less likely to persist as independent data aggregations, ephemeral repositories are critical staging arenas for data standardization, mobilization, and exchange. As an low-investment outcome from using Specify 7, that reduces reliance on bespoke or isolated data management solutions, Specify-as-a-Service is intended to support efficient transfer of information to downstream systems after phases of active research.

Investment in early standardization improves data quality and reduces duplication of effort during rounds of data capture. Extending IT infrastructure into the broader suite of institutional tools supporting collections-based research promotes the implementation of FAIR practices and consistent workflows. Providing SpecifyaaS to staff and research collaborators will strengthen data integration across research and collections systems, and increase the long-term data usability and applicability across a wider range of use cases.

actual.identification_notes: Introduced by chair Theresa Miller as Kevin Holston; the talk title and content match event-188. The researcher used as the category-one example is rendered by ASR as 'Johannes Beierstein' (probably Johannes Bergsten, NRM); a collaborator is rendered 'Raza'. 'SEC' is ASR for Specify. No Q&A was held.

summary: Kevin Holston explained how the Swedish Museum of Natural History runs its own local Specify 7 instances ('Specify as a Service') as ephemeral or semi-persistent repositories for researchers, rather than pushing them straight into the institutional collection database. He distinguished research-group collections of loaned, persistent vouchers from institutional programmes such as biobanks and the environmental specimen bank, whose semi-persistent vouchers are used up over time. As an example, he showed how a researcher's 16 years of Madagascar aquatic insect inventory became a Specify research database with 808 collecting events, organised event images and field sheets. He argued that these instances bring standards in early and act as laboratories of innovation for Specify.
one_line_takeaway: Giving researchers their own lightweight Specify instances early in the research process standardises data from the start and eases later exchange with the institutional collection.
why_it_matters: Much specimen data is created in project spreadsheets before it ever reaches a collection database. Giving researchers compatible, low-commitment instances is a practical way to get standards and identifiers in early and to track derivatives and loaned material as their own objects.
key_points: NRM runs local Specify installations on its own infrastructure and spins up temporary instances, for example for visiting researchers, that are compatible with the institutional database.
Category 1 (research group/project): material is mostly on loan, vouchers are persistent, and the project repository has little motivation to record where things physically are.

Category 2 (research institution/programme, e.g. biobank, eDNA and environmental specimen bank): vouchers are semi-persistent and subject to depletion, and the repository must reflect the physical collection.
Historically, derivatives have been documented as voucher attributes rather than as independent objects, which limits tracking of objects, attributes and locations over time.

A researcher's Madagascar aquatic insect inventory became a Specify research database with 808 collecting events over 16 years of trips. An unexpected benefit was standardisation and the organisation of event images and field data sheets.
Holston repurposed the Specify storage tree to record provenance, i.e. loans, in his own research database, showing Specify's flexibility.
Instances can be 'furnished' (pre-loaded with collection data, like a furnished house or hotel) to give visitors a head start in digitising.
datasets: Madagascar aquatic insect inventory (808 collecting events)
methods: local Specify instances as staging repositories
storage tree repurposed for loan provenance

notable_claims.claim: Historically, derivatives generated during research have been documented as voucher attributes rather than as independent objects.
One researcher's inventory compiled in Specify represents 16 years of collecting in Madagascar and 808 collecting events.
Instances given to researchers can act as laboratories of innovation that have driven new Specify capabilities.

recommendations: Introduce data standards and compilation early in the research process and strengthen relationships with researchers.
Treat researchers' Specify instances as laboratories of innovation for the platform.
results_findings: Preparing a researcher's data for import into Specify produced additional standardisation and organised collecting-event images and field sheets as a side benefit.
examples_case_studies: Madagascar aquatic insect inventory database at NRM
NRM environmental specimen bank
Holston's own Specify 7 research database using storage for loans

title: Applying Data Standards at the Royal Botanic Garden Edinburgh

programme.title: Applying Data Standards at the Royal Botanic Garden Edinburgh
programme.session: SYM20 Meeting Biodiversity Data Standards Using Specify Software
programme.abstract:
Data standards play a crucial role in enabling the dissemination, interoperability, and reuse of biodiversity knowledge. At the Royal Botanic Garden Edinburgh (RBGE), efforts over more than four decades have focused on aligning herbarium collection data with a wide range of cultural, historical, technological, and biodiversity data standards. This ongoing work reflects both the evolving nature of standards and the need to integrate legacy data with emerging frameworks.

Since the transition to the Specify Collections Management System (CMS) in 2022, RBGE has further refined its use of data standards to enhance data quality, interoperability, and connectivity. These developments support improved sharing and linking of RBGE’s herbarium data with collections and research initiatives worldwide, contributing to a more integrated global biodiversity knowledge infrastructure.

actual.identification_notes: Introduced by name and institution. ASR renders MycoBank as 'MicroBank', CETAF as 'CTAF', DiSSCo as 'Disco', Roger Hyam as 'Roger Higham' and data lake as 'data lock'. No questions were asked.

summary: Robyn Drinkwater described how RBGE, a herbarium of about three million specimens with databasing since the mid-1970s, uses identifiers in Specify to standardise and link its data. She covered merging duplicate agents (up to four or five versions of a person from the legacy system) with Specify's agent merge tool and storing agent identifiers. She also covered IPNI, MycoBank and World Flora Online taxon identifiers, CETAF stable specimen URIs used since 2012, and forthcoming DiSSCo DOIs. The second half showed how identifiers link the herbarium with RBGE's three other collection systems (IrisBG, Koha, AtoM), with examples of watercolours linked to moss specimens and living plants linked to herbarium vouchers.
one_line_takeaway: Identifiers are how RBGE is standardising legacy herbarium data and reconnecting items spread across four separate collection management systems.
why_it_matters: The talk shows why identifiers need to be structured and resolvable, not just stored. It also shows the practical steps (agent disambiguation, field restructuring, cross-system links) that an institution needs to publish linked, citable data.
key_points: RBGE has about three million specimens covering all traditionally 'plant' groups including diatoms, algae and oomycetes; about 1.5 million database records have passed through at least four database systems.
The legacy system had no unified agents table, which left four or five versions of some people. The Specify agent merging tool is helping to disambiguate them.
Specify's dedicated agent identifier field allows several identifiers per agent. Link-outs to ORCID and Wikidata are planned to help staff.

Taxon identifiers: IPNI IDs for vascular plants and MycoBank IDs for fungi, with World Flora Online IDs being tested. Both have been stored in the LSID field, and that mixed content prevents link-outs, so restructuring is needed.
CETAF stable identifiers have been used since 2012. They make specimens citable, and staff can link from the barcode field to images in the herbarium catalogue without importing images into Specify.

RBGE runs four systems: Specify (herbarium), IrisBG (living collection), Koha (library and artworks) and AtoM (archives). Identifiers are used to link, e.g., Greville moss watercolours in Koha to specimens, and living accessions to herbarium vouchers.
Next steps: GenBank/BOLD identifiers for DNA extractions, links to sequencing data, getting identifiers into the Darwin Core export, and a possible Scottish data lake.

RBGE has used CETAF stable identifiers since 2012, making its specimens easily citable in electronic journals.
Using the LSID field for both IPNI and MycoBank identifiers means mixed data that cannot easily support link-outs.
RBGE's Darwin Core export does not yet include all of these identifiers.

title: From Legacy Data to FAIR Workflows: Standardising Biodiversity Collections Using Specify

programme.title: From Legacy Data to FAIR Workflows: Standardising Biodiversity Collections Using Specify
programme.session: SYM20 Meeting Biodiversity Data Standards Using Specify Software
programme.abstract:
The KwaZulu-Natal Museum manages eleven natural history collections supporting biodiversity research, education, and long-term preservation of African heritage. Like many institutions, historical collection data were distributed across spreadsheets, paper records, and inconsistent legacy systems, creating challenges for data quality, interoperability, specimen tracking, and data mobilisation.

To address these challenges, the museum implemented Specify as its primary collections management system. This enabled the development of standardised workflows for specimen cataloguing, accessioning, georeferencing, taxonomic management, loan tracking, image attachment, and data cleaning across eleven collections.

A major focus of implementation has been aligning institutional workflows with biodiversity informatics standards, FAIR data principles, and machine-readable data practices. Centralised data management has improved metadata consistency, reduced duplication, and strengthened quality control. Specify’s querying and export functions have also improved readiness for data sharing and publication to global biodiversity infrastructures such as Global Biodiversity Information Facility.

The museum has observed improved efficiency in data capture, transaction management, researcher support, and standardised staff training. This presentation highlights practical lessons from implementing standardised, interoperability-focused workflows within a South African museum context and demonstrates how legacy collection data can be transformed into FAIR, mobilisation-ready biodiversity datasets.

actual.identification_notes: Introduced by chair as Siyabonga Zamisa from KwaZulu-Natal Museum. ASR renders NSCF as 'an SCF' and Darwin Core as 'down-core'.

summary: Siyabonga Zamisa described how the KwaZulu-Natal Museum moved its 11 natural history collections (over 430,000 records) from Access, Excel, catalogue cards and other systems into Specify by 2019. With support from the Natural Science Collections Facility, it then developed shared workflows. He walked through a Darwin Core-based template spreadsheet used by all collections, quality checks in OpenRefine before WorkBench upload, routine specimen-versus-database QA, and a publishing pipeline through the IPT to GBIF. Before this the museum had no collections in GBIF; seven of eleven are now published.
one_line_takeaway: Standardised workflows, not just a new database, turned 11 differently managed collections into GBIF-ready data.
why_it_matters: This is a concrete African museum example of procedure and standards, not technology alone, driving data mobilisation, with measurable gains in publishing, cataloguing speed and loan processing.
key_points: 11 collections with over 430,000 records, the largest being Mollusca and Insecta. Previous systems included Access, Excel and Rapid, and all collections have been in Specify since 2019.
The problem was inconsistent practice: each collection had its own habits for capturing, tracking and sharing data, which slowed loans and data sharing.
A single template spreadsheet based on Darwin Core terms, with field explanations, is used across all 11 collections to ease WorkBench mapping.
Workflow: capture in template → data technician QC in OpenRefine → Specify WorkBench mapping and validation → upload.
Daily QA: randomly selected specimens are checked against their Specify records and both are corrected.
Publishing: Specify query export → OpenRefine QC → removal of sensitive species → IPT metadata and Darwin Core mapping → GBIF.
Results: from no collections in GBIF to seven of eleven, faster cataloguing and much shorter loan processing.

notable_claims.claim: The museum manages 11 collections in Specify with over 430,000 records.
Digitisation alone was not enough; putting information into a database does not automatically create good data management.
Before Specify and the workflows the museum had no collections in GBIF; now seven of eleven are published.

recommendations: Standardise the workflow around specimens, data, people and standards, not just the database.
results_findings: Seven of 11 collections now published to GBIF (none before).
Faster cataloguing of incoming material.
Significantly reduced loan processing and turnaround time.
examples_case_studies: KwaZulu-Natal Museum's 11 collections

q_and_a.question: Do staff use Specify or only the Excel template, and did you build one common form or separate forms for each collection? How do you balance common templates against collection differences?
q_and_a.answer_summary: Curators were asked how they wanted their forms; roughly 20% is customised per collection and the rest is common across all 11. Staff use Specify at different levels, with the data technician overseeing.

representative_excerpt.text: So we realized that digitization alone was not enough, but putting information into a database doesn't automatically create a good data management.

notable_moments.description: Shared Darwin Core template spreadsheet and import workflow.
Publishing workflow from Specify query to GBIF via OpenRefine and IPT.
From zero to seven of eleven collections in GBIF.

title: Digitize, Standardize, Mobilize: Wildlife Biodiversity Biobanking with Specify

programme.title: Digitize, Standardize, Mobilize: Wildlife Biodiversity Biobanking with Specify
programme.session: SYM20 Meeting Biodiversity Data Standards Using Specify Software
programme.abstract: Biodiversity biobanks are increasingly recognized as critical research infrastructures supporting conservation, genomics, species management, and One Health initiatives through the long-term preservation of samples and associated metadata. While the physical preservation and curation of samples remains central to biobanking, the scientific value of these collections depends on the generation of high-quality, standardized, and interoperable data. As biodiversity research advances toward implementation of FAIR (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, and Reusable) principles and the Extended Specimen concept, these biobanks face challenges in managing multidimensional datasets that extend beyond individual samples to include taxonomic, spatial, genetic, regulatory, and derivative information. Within the SANBI Wildlife Biobank, collections include diverse taxa and sample types such as blood, tissues, DNA extracts, and cell cultures linked to permits, storage records, images, molecular data, and metadata. Historically, these data were distributed across disconnected spreadsheets, paper records, folders, and external drives, creating challenges in data consistency, accessibility, and long-term sustainability. The implementation of Specify has transformed collection workflows from fragmented data management practices into an integrated relational framework capable of linking specimens, tissue collections, storage information, compliance documentation, and taxonomic data within a single system. The use of hierarchical taxonomy structures, controlled vocabularies, unique identifiers, and customizable workflows has improved data consistency, sample traceability, quality control processes, and transformed biodiversity biobanks from static repositories into dynamic digital resources.

title: Integrating Specify in broader Science infrastructure

programme.title: Integrating Specify in broader Science infrastructure
programme.session: SYM20 Meeting Biodiversity Data Standards Using Specify Software
programme.abstract:
At the Royal Botanic Gardens Victoria, Specify is used to deliver high-quality data to the Australasian Virtual Herbarium (AVH), as well as managing the herbarium's holdings and transactions like loan and exchange. Specify is embedded in our broader science infrastructure and we have built various extensions and integrations.

We make use of the flexibility of Specify to handle complex workflows. We use a separate discipline, rather than the Borrows table, to manage loans from other institutions. This way we can link up images and DNA sequences we have taken to specimens data, while keeping the data separate from the National Herbarium of Victoria (MEL) collection. We also use "staging" collections for exchange data, so we can make sure we have the specimens and validate the data before it is incorporated into the main collection. There is also a dedicated collection for the Victorian Conservation Seed Bank, which shares most of its data with the main collection.

We have a "bystander" application that provides functionality that Specify does not have or where the Specify functionality does not quite fit our workflows, e.g., handling ZPL-based label-printing, storage assignment and loan returns.

The Specify taxon tree functions as the taxonomic point of truth for our Digital Asset Management System (DAMS). At the same time, we have applications to sync the Specify taxon tree with national and global taxonomies, including VicFlora, APC, AusMoss, AusFungi, Plants of the World Online (PoWo), Bryonames and Tropicos.

The AVH is our collection's portal in to the world. We use the Global Biodiversity Information Facility (GBIF) Integrated Publishing Toolkit (IPT) to publish collections data to AVH.

title: The Good, the Bad, and the Standardised: A Specify Journey Through 200 Years of the MfN Berlin's Biological Collections

programme.title: The Good, the Bad, and the Standardised: A Specify Journey Through 200 Years of the MfN Berlin’s Biological Collections
programme.session: SYM20 Meeting Biodiversity Data Standards Using Specify Software
programme.abstract: The foundations of the Museum für Naturkunde Berlin (MfN)´s biological collections laid as early as 1810, houses today around 30 million specimens from the fields of palaeontology, zoology, botany and geology, as well as archives and modern media such as a sound library, reflecting 200 years of scientific, technical, colonial and political upheavals. Colonial collections (such as the Tendaguru excavation which returned 225 tons of dinosaur fossils), wars (the 1945 bombings destroyed a considerable number of specimens) and the Cold War isolation have left behind fragmented, multilingual and ethically complex data. Following reunification, resistance to digital transformation and the heterogeneity of legacy systems (paper labels, Excel, local databases), which persist to this day, hinder the standardisation of this complex yet essential biodiversity data. Today, we are in the process of transitioning to Specify as our sole collection management system (CMS): this powerful tool enables us to standardise metadata (Darwin Core), manage the MfN’s 22 collections, fill scientific gaps (missing labels, obsolete taxonomy) and manage permissions for over 100 users, with specific needs, whilst meeting modern requirements (GBIF exports, 3D scanning). We are also exploring ways to fill historical gaps by linking colonial archives to specimens (for example, the roles of workers at Tendaguru via Wikidata in the DTE project), using specific tables to reintegrate overlooked elements. This presentation will share the lessons learnt from 200 years of upheaval: how Specify helps to preserve biodiversity data and reconstruct history, as well as the work that remains to be done to meet all these needs.

summary: Marion Depraetere traced how the Museum für Naturkunde Berlin's history shaped its data: colonial expeditions such as Tendaguru, the 1945 bombing, Soviet confiscation and return, Cold War isolation, pandemic-era reliance on personal Excel files, and an October 2023 cyberattack that ended debate and made Specify the sole CMS. All 30 collections are now in one Specify instance, which enables cross-collection reporting. Specify's flexibility supports decolonisation work through a one-to-many historical-events table and a prototype 'Historical Context' collection linking archive letters to specimens. She highlighted the gap between political geography (ISO 3166) and ecological or marine units, and argued that standardisation should respond to a need rather than be imposed.
one_line_takeaway: Specify's flexibility lets MfN consolidate 30 historically complex collections into one database while starting to reconstruct colonial and wartime history, but geography and historical events remain unsolved.
why_it_matters: Many large museums face the same combination of legacy heterogeneity, colonial provenance and diverse audiences. The talk shows practical data-model workarounds and the open problem of representing administrative and ecological geography together.

title: Meeting Biodiversity Standards with Specify 7

programme.title: Meeting Biodiversity Standards with Specify 7
programme.session: SYM20 Meeting Biodiversity Data Standards Using Specify Software
programme.abstract:
The Specify Collections Consortium (SCC) supports research collections around the world with Specify Software, an intuitive, robust, and highly-customizable software platform for digitizing holdings and managing collections. For over 25 years, Specify has supported biological research collections, biorepositories, and now geological research collections, with its open-source software for managing and publishing collections data.

Data sharing and data publishing is a fundamental requirement for collection management and research. Ensuring your collections data meets Biodiversity Standards means it will be more accessible to the scientific community and research. Over the last year, the SCC has focused our efforts on enabling members to more easily meet biodiversity standards during data entry and making shared data more accessible and interoperable.

In this presentation, SCC staff will discuss the soon to be integrated Darwin Core standards in the data model, making publishing to data aggregators such as the Global Biodiversity Information Facility (GBIF), the Atlas of Living Australia (ALA), the Global Genome Biodiversity Network (GGBN), and Integrated Digitized Biocollections (iDigBio) easier while maintaining the customizability and flexibility upon which Specify was built.

The SCC is a collaborative collections community governed, funded, and sustained by its member institutions. Our software and technical support priorities address member and system infrastructure needs. Specify software enables natural history museums to curate, integrate, and publish data from a single, robustly-engineered platform for biological and geological collections.

summary: Grant Fitzsimmons presented Specify Collections Consortium work that lets collections keep local flexibility while sharing data in standard form. He described exportable schema-configuration packages, an updated, detached web portal (largely contributed by the Florida Museum), and a new Darwin Core mapping tool built on the Specify Query Builder. The tool supports Occurrence, Event and Taxon cores, every GBIF-registered extension, and custom terms by IRI. It shows term definitions in the app, auto-suggests mappings, starts from existing queries or templates, and enforces GBIF's minimum required terms. Release is expected by the first quarter of next year, and the SCC is joining multi-CMS work on the Darwin Core Data Package.

title: From Data Entry to Distribution: Streamlining Biodiversity Workflows with Specify at CSIRO

programme.title: From Data Entry to Distribution: Streamlining Biodiversity Workflows with Specify at CSIRO
programme.session: SYM20 Meeting Biodiversity Data Standards Using Specify Software
programme.abstract:
Since 2022, the Commonwealth Scientific and Industrial Research Organisation (CSIRO) has migrated five of its collections into separate instances of Specify. This undertaking and subsequent support of the curation staff represents a challenge to the Data Management team in terms of ensuring data standards are met consistently for different specimen types across the National Research Collections of Australia (NRCA).

This talk will explain how we configured the Specify schema to facilitate clean data entry, including building standardised queries and 'workbench' bulk data entry templates across all collections. Our promotion and adherence to biodiversity standards such as Darwin Core enabled more efficient internal data discovery and the establishment of clear data ingest principles. This in turn allows for a more streamlined process for sharing data and the use of ETL tools to export the data into external aggregators such as the Atlas of Living Australia (ALA). It also facilitates the use of API-based integration to connect to extended specimen metadata repositories, increasing the reach and interoperability of our data.

We will also cover our strategy of maintaining close relationships with the curation staff and users of Specify to further improve processes, identify data quality issues, and employ the batch edit features to help provide the most accurate specimen data to researchers and the general public alike.

summary: Dan Baker described how CSIRO's National Research Collections Australia migrated five of six collections into separate Specify instances between mid-2021 and end-2025. The collections now hold over two million specimens and more than 150 users. The data management team maintains standards at three levels: field definitions and controlled picklists, collection-specific formatting through a fully used agent table with aggregated views, and holistic minimum-dataset checks in WorkBench templates. They are supported by Excel templates with conditional formatting, a VBA script for collector names, batch edit and Power Query checks. He also covered training, support channels, standard roles, and uptake figures, and ended with a Specify wishlist.

title: A metadata-first FAIR4AI checklist and automated evaluation agent for biodiversity datasets

programme.title: A metadata-first FAIR4AI checklist and automated evaluation agent for biodiversity datasets
programme.session: SYM25A From Mobilizing Data to AI-Ready Knowledge: Infrastructure for Multimodal Biodiversity Data
programme.abstract:
As AI methods become increasingly integral to ecology and biodiversity science, the data that are used must meet standards beyond traditional FAIR principles. In a cross-community workshop with data providers, infrastructure operators, and AI/ML practitioners, we refined definitions for three tiers of data readiness: FAIR data meet established open-science norms; FAIR4AI criteria extend those norms with metadata sufficient for AI systems to discover, assess, and stage datasets to enable their use at scale without manual intervention; and AI-ready data have been fully prepared for specific AI-enabled applications. These distinctions are important because the gap between FAIR and FAIR4AI appears to be primarily a metadata gap, not a lack of technical infrastructure, and closing it is necessary to successfully use emerging AI tools in ecological synthesis.

To make these distinctions actionable, we developed a FAIR4AI checklist adapted from the Earth Science Information Partners (ESIP) AI-Readiness Checklist and the Imageomics Institute's Dataset Card and Metadata Checklists, with additions for biodiversity-specific concerns including taxonomic resolution, spatial and temporal extent, annotation provenance, and instrumentation metadata. Evaluation questions span Provenance, General Information, Data Structure, Data Origin, Data Processing, Data Quality, Guidance and Recommendations, and Data Access. We then built an open-source, LLM-powered evaluation tool to ingest a dataset’s metadata and return evidence-based responses to each evaluation question along with per-category FAIR scores.

Advancing FAIR4AI standards in biodiversity will require community input to ensure they support AI applications in ways that are consistent with community ethics and goals.

summary: Tanya Berger-Wolf presented the NSF-funded FAIR for AI Bio project (FAIROS programme), which has built AI-ready data infrastructure for ecology through a series of community workshops since August 2025. The project distinguishes FAIR, FAIR4AI (machine-findable, accessible, interoperable and reusable, so AI-ready datasets can be prepared with minimal human intervention) and AI-ready (application-specific) data, within a question–data–model round-tripping framework. The team built a checklist that grew from four categories (structural, scientific, provenance, governance) to 96 items, and an LLM agent that scores datasets, gives item-level recommendations and compares FAIR and FAIR4AI scores. Run on NEON datasets, the scores largely track each other but most datasets score very low on CARE.
one_line_takeaway: FAIR4AI is mainly a metadata gap, and a community checklist plus an automated agent can measure and help close it while tracking provenance and governance back to data sources.
why_it_matters: As biodiversity data are fed into AI at scale, provenance, attribution and governance break easily. A measurable intermediate standard gives data providers and aggregators a concrete target.
key_points: Rapidly growing sensor types and modalities are spread across many holders; integration should be decentralised rather than 'one database to rule them all'.
'There is no AI without data'; nature knows no borders but policies and licensing do.

The FAIR for AI Bio project (NSF FAIROS) runs expanding workshops with GBIF, Movebank, Smithsonian, NatureServe, iNaturalist and others. The next workshop is February 2027 in California, with funding to bring participants.
Data sovereignty and value round-tripping emerged as primary use cases at a conservation technology conference in Lima.
Three tiers: FAIR; FAIR4AI (machine-actionable metadata enabling preparation of AI-ready data with minimal human intervention); AI-ready (application-specific).
The checklist (developed starting with ESIIL) has four top-level categories (structural, scientific, provenance, governance) expanded to 96 items, and is open to community comment.
An agent evaluates datasets against the checklist, giving scores, item-level recommendations, strengths and gaps, side by side with traditional FAIR.
Across NEON datasets on GBIF, FAIR and FAIR4AI scores generally track, but most datasets score very low on CARE.

How can value flow back from models to primary data collectors?

The checklist has expanded to 96 items and is still growing.
Most datasets evaluated, including NEON and other US datasets, score very low on CARE.
