title: Phenobase: a harmonized, AI-ready knowledge base of global plant phenology

programme.title: Phenobase: a harmonized, AI-ready knowledge base of global plant phenology
programme.session: SYM25A From Mobilizing Data to AI-Ready Knowledge: Infrastructure for Multimodal Biodiversity Data
programme.abstract: Plant phenology shapes ecosystem dynamics, species interactions and serves as a sensitive indicator of environmental change. Sources of global phenology data have exponentially increased but remain siloed and fragmented. In situ monitoring networks produce rigorous repeated observations, but are typically regional and disconnected. Digitized herbarium specimens and community-science platforms such as iNaturalist offer vast spatial, temporal, and taxonomic breadth but phenology information is latent in images and unstructured metadata. Phenobase addresses these gaps by assembling these sources into a harmonized knowledge base. We first applied computer-vision models (PhenoVision and PhenoVision-Leaf) to score presence of open flowers, fruits, breaking leaf buds, green leaves, and colored leaves across tens of millions of iNaturalist records. We used an different, ensemble-based ML model approach trained via expert annotations for labeled flowers on herbarium sheets to score millions of available imaged herbarium sheets. Finally, we assembled in-situ monitopring data from USA-NPN, NEON, PhenObs, Budburst, and SeasonWatch. Phenobase harmonizes these sources using the Plant Phenology Ontology which maps source-specific phenophase terms to shared trait concepts while preserving contextual metadata. Model certainty thresholds, validation accuracies, ML model version, and family-level performance metrics travel with each record, so downstream users can filter on quality. Phenobase data are openly available and show how machine-learning extraction, ontology-based integration, and standardized provenance metadata turn heterogeneous biodiversity collections into AI-ready data products. We close by discussing next-step challenges with maintaining and growing such resources.

actual.identification_notes: Introduced as 'Saurabh Goralnik' by ASR (Robert Guralnick). ASR renders Phenobase as 'PhenoBase', PhenObs as 'Phenops' and quality as 'whole.data'; team member names (e.g. 'John Dack', 'Russell Dittmann', 'Dai-Jung Li') are unreliable. Questioner self-identified as Martin Freiberg from PhenObs.

summary: Robert Guralnick presented Phenobase, an open, integrated database of global in situ plant phenology. It rests on the Plant Phenology Ontology, which harmonises monitoring-programme terms and supports inference, with extensions for observations of only part of a plant. To fill large geographic and taxonomic gaps, the team trained models on 1.5–2 million iNaturalist phenology annotations (masked-autoencoder pre-training) and a separate ensemble for herbarium sheets. They reached about 98% accuracy for flowers and 95% for fruits, and machine-labelled records now make up about 97% of records and fill many empty grid cells. He said making Phenobase AI-ready was the hard part: per-record model URIs and quality scores, provenance links back to sources, data dictionaries, update strategies and citation policies.
one_line_takeaway: Combining ontologies with machine learning lets Phenobase close global phenology data gaps, but making the result AI-ready requires per-record model provenance, quality and citation.
why_it_matters: Phenology is a key climate-change indicator. Phenobase shows a working pattern for turning images from citizen science and herbaria into trustworthy, reusable trait data with provenance attached to each record.
key_points: Phenology monitoring programmes use incompatible, bespoke terminology; the Plant Phenology Ontology provides URIs and logical axioms for integration and inference (e.g. count of leaf buds implies presence).
Images show only part of a plant, so absence inferences differ from whole-plant monitoring; the ontology was adapted accordingly.
Integrated sources include USA-NPN, herbarium specimens, NEON and the Pan-European Phenology dataset.
iNaturalist has about 110 million angiosperm observations (150,000 in one recent weekend) and 1.5–2 million human phenology annotations.

Model uses masked autoencoder pre-training with threshold tuning and humans in the loop: about 98% for flowers and 95% for fruits (present), close to human performance; a separate ensemble model scores GBIF-imaged herbarium sheets.
About 97% of Phenobase records are machine-annotated; new data fill many previously empty grid cells.

AI-readiness requires per-record model URI (Hugging Face), per-record quality scores from family-level accuracy, traceable links to source records, data dictionaries, a portal plus Zenodo deposit, and clear data use and citation policies.
Sustainability is an open question: about 75,000 new records per day and growing, plus model updates.
questions: How can Phenobase keep up with ~75,000 new records per day and update models sustainably?
How should observer bias (e.g. toward peak flowering) be corrected downstream?

notable_claims.claim: Flower annotation accuracy reached about 98% and fruit presence about 95%, close to human annotation rates.
About 97% of Phenobase phenology records come from machine annotation rather than human annotation.
Every record carries the model URI linking to the model on Hugging Face and a record-level quality score.
The term 'round-tripping' was coined by Deb Paul.

recommendations: Ship model provenance, quality scores, data dictionaries and citation policies with AI-generated records.
results_findings: Machine labelling of iNaturalist and herbarium images substantially reduces global gaps in flower and fruit phenology data.
limitations: Phenobase does not itself correct observer and reporting biases (cities, charismatic plants, event spikes such as the City Nature Challenge); insight generation sits downstream.
future_work: Sustainable updating of data and models as volumes grow.
examples_case_studies: Cornus canadensis record from iNaturalist traced through Phenobase
iNaturalist annotation of flower buds, flowers and breaking leaf buds

q_and_a.question: How do you deal with photographers' bias toward pictures of mass flowering rather than first flowers or senescing leaves?
q_and_a.answer_summary: Bias is recognised (cities, charismatic plants, City Nature Challenge spikes). Phenology methods can account for it, but Phenobase aims to produce the best possible data, and bias correction and inference happen downstream with best practices and human–machine collaboration.

notable_moments.description: The Plant Phenology Ontology as lingua franca for integration.
Model accuracy ~98% flowers, ~95% fruits.
Machine-annotated data fill many new global grid cells.
Why making Phenobase AI-ready was the hard part.

title: From 1.5 Billion Raw Queries to AI-Ready Biodiversity Data: Human-AI Collaborative Curation Pipelines in Pl@ntNet

programme.title: From 1.5 Billion Raw Queries to AI-Ready Biodiversity Data: Human-AI Collaborative Curation Pipelines in Pl@ntNet
programme.session: SYM25A From Mobilizing Data to AI-Ready Knowledge: Infrastructure for Multimodal Biodiversity Data
programme.abstract:
Large biodiversity platforms collect massive volumes of opportunistic observations that are valuable for ecological research and AI model training. However, transforming these heterogeneous user contributions into trustworthy and reusable biodiversity data remains a major challenge. Pl@ntNet currently processes more than 1.5 billion user queries consisting of plant images and associated metadata submitted by a large international community. Only a small fraction of these data ultimately become AI-ready training data (~25M images) or research-grade occurrences shared with GBIF (~2.5M images).

We present the human-AI collaborative curation pipeline used in Pl@ntNet to progressively transform raw multimodal observations into fitness-for-use biodiversity datasets. The pipeline combines automated filtering, community moderation, collaborative taxonomic revision, image-quality assessment, and governance constraints. Automated filters remove non-plant content, malformed observations, duplicate or low-quality images, and sensitive media. Taxonomic quality is refined through a collaborative validation process combining AI predictions, community interactions, and expert feedback across species galleries and observation streams. Community moderation signals help identify problematic observations, including off-topic or unreliable content. Dataset construction also incorporates licensing and provenance constraints, excluding observations that cannot be redistributed or reused.

We further show how downstream objectives require different curation levels. While AI training datasets prioritize taxonomic consistency, visual relevance, and diversity, GBIF publication requires stricter filters on geolocation, cultivation status, metadata completeness, and interoperability standards.

actual.identification_notes: Introduced as 'Alexis Jolie'. ASR renders Pl@ntNet as 'PlantNet/PlopNet/PlotNet'. The new Aarhus-led project name is garbled ('BIGEL') and is not reproduced. Questioners are unnamed; one speaks from a GBIF perspective (mentions talks with FAO).

summary: Alexis Joly described the curation pipeline that turns Pl@ntNet's 1.6 billion raw, highly opportunistic image queries (from about 20 million users a year, including house plants, tattoos, people and sensitive content) into AI training data and GBIF occurrences. Every image passes a main model trained on about 25 million human-validated images, which includes 'reject' classes. He called that reject classifier the hardest part and an editorial choice. Opt-in public observations enter human curation with weighted majority voting, where each user's weight reflects expertise estimated by an EM algorithm. Other observations contribute only automatically filtered occurrences above a strict confidence threshold (<0.01% error) and a wildness classifier to GBIF. He warned about feedback loops in which users follow AI errors.
one_line_takeaway: Pl@ntNet's human–AI pipeline filters a vast, noisy stream into two GBIF datasets and training data, with separate branches for opted-in human-validated and automatic occurrence-only data.
why_it_matters: Opportunistic AI apps are among the largest sources of biodiversity observations. How they filter, validate, licence and publish data determines the quality of downstream models and species distribution analyses.
key_points: Pl@ntNet is 15 years old, has about 20 million users a year, 1.6 billion raw observations and about 20,000 plants per hour.
The raw stream includes cultivated and potted plants, plants on clothing and tattoos, humans (e.g. classroom sessions), non-living objects, nudity and drug-related images.

The main model, trained on ~25 million human-validated images, outputs species, genus, family, diseases and reject classes. The reject classifier is the hardest and involves editorial choices about user intent.

Branch 1: observations users opt in to share publicly (CC BY-SA, named) are curated by weighted majority voting, with user expertise estimated by an EM algorithm based on the number of species a user can recognise.
Validated data retrain the model regularly, and old queries are reprocessed.
Branch 2: non-shared observations contribute only occurrences (no images) above a per-model threshold with <0.01% error; about 150 million remain after this filter.

A wildness classifier (trained on anthropised context and the app's cultivated tag) and WCVP level-2 country flora filtering remove cultivated plants before GBIF publication; two GBIF datasets result.
Feedback loops: when users follow AI errors, contamination can cause some species' identifications to drift over a decade.
questions: Should cultivated observations be published to GBIF flagged as cultivated?
Should Pl@ntNet move to a more liberal default licence than share-alike?

notable_claims.claim: Since its start, Pl@ntNet has collected about 1.6 billion raw observations from about 20 million users per year.
Automatically published occurrences are limited to predictions above a threshold guaranteeing less than 0.01% error.
Not publishing cultivated/potted plants was a GBIF requirement.
Users following AI predictions can contaminate the model, causing some species to drift ten years after the start of Pl@ntNet.

results_findings: About 150 million observations remain after the automatic confidence filter.
Two datasets are published to GBIF: human-validated and automatic.
limitations: The reject and wildness classifiers are imperfect and hard to tune; some cultivated plants still get through.
future_work: A new Aarhus University-led project on AI-driven workflows, new sensors with participatory science, data curation and feedback-loop dynamics.
examples_case_studies: Pl@ntNet real-time query viewer
Books photographed to game identifications

q_and_a.question: How do you prevent users from levelling up their expertise by copying AI predictions or others' identifications?
q_and_a.answer_summary: Known tricks (e.g. photographing books) are detected; identifications that just follow the AI are down-weighted; errors by such users show up; and manual curators identify and 'ghost' them.

q_and_a.question: Cultivated plants also affect the environment; why not publish them to GBIF flagged as cultivated using Darwin Core terms?
q_and_a.answer_summary: GBIF asked them not to publish potted plants, which are probably more numerous than wild ones, and many would bias SDMs. Publishing with a cultivated flag remains an open community discussion.

q_and_a.question: (GBIF perspective) Agrobiodiversity communities and FAO want cultivated data in GBIF; and would a more liberal default licence than share-alike increase reuse, as at iNaturalist?
q_and_a.answer_summary: Joly agreed attribution matters but the share-alike element could be changed or made a user choice; it is open for discussion.

notable_moments.description: Real-time viewer showing the diversity of what users photograph.
The reject classifier is the hardest part and an editorial choice.
Expertise-weighted voting via EM estimation of recognisable species.
Negative feedback loops when users follow AI errors.

title: From Sensor to Species: AI-Assisted Segmentation, Deep Learning Workflows, and Persistent Biodiversity Records from Earth Observation Systems

programme.title: From Sensor to Species: AI-Assisted Segmentation, Deep Learning Workflows, and Persistent Biodiversity Records from Earth Observation Systems
programme.session: SYM25A From Mobilizing Data to AI-Ready Knowledge: Infrastructure for Multimodal Biodiversity Data
programme.abstract:
Advances in airborne and spaceborne Earth observation systems are enabling increasingly detailed ecological analyses across global spatial and temporal scales. RGB, multispectral, and hyperspectral imaging platforms (ie: Landsat, Sentinel-2, NASA AVIRIS-NG, EMIT, and the National Ecological Observatory Network (NEON) Imaging Spectrometer) provide opportunities to identify vegetation structure, phenology, and potentially species-level ecological patterns from remotely sensed imagery . However, airborne and spaceborne remotely sensed biodiversity observations remain comparatively underrepresented within biodiversity informatics infrastructures such as the Global Biodiversity Information Facility (GBIF).

This presentation explores a biodiversity informatics workflow for transforming sensor-derived ecological observations into persistent, interoperable biodiversity records. The workflow integrates foundation-model segmentation approaches, including the Segment Anything Model (SAM), object-based image analysis [8], and DeepForest tree crown delineation workflows. These approaches are combined with AI-assisted species classification and Darwin Core standards to generate candidate biodiversity occurrence records from remotely sensed vegetation objects.

A central focus of the project is the introduction of persistent identifiers for segmented vegetation objects, enabling longitudinal monitoring of ecological entities across repeated temporal observations. The presentation will discuss interoperability challenges, provenance and uncertainty representation, and opportunities for integrating AI-generated ecological observations into biodiversity informatics infrastructures and biodiversity monitoring workflows.

speakers.name: Kit Lewers
speakers.affiliation: University of Colorado Boulder; NASA Goddard Space Flight Center (FINESST fellow)

actual.identification_notes: Speaker used a changed title, 'From Spectra to Species: Persistent Biodiversity Records from Multimodal Remote Sensing'. ASR renders TDWG as 'TadWig' and FINESST as 'FINES'. The questioner described the 2024 unique animal ID / Digital Life History Museum paper and Movebank; the chair (Hilmar Lapp) closed by pointing to an Imageomics Institute innovation.

summary: Kit Lewers argued that remote sensing has a longitudinal biodiversity problem: repeat airborne and satellite acquisitions are processed as separate images, so the same tree can appear in many datasets without a connected history. GBIF would not link such records a year apart. In a proof of concept at NEON's SJER oak savanna, they used off-the-shelf DeepForest crown delineation on RGB imagery, IoU matching across 2023 and 2024, and species candidates constrained by NEON vegetation records from GBIF. The pipeline output Darwin Core occurrences with organismID, identifiedBy 'AI' and basisOfRecord MachineObservation. The weak results (rocks and shadows detected as crowns, a generic cloud model giving one species) were a 'useful failure' showing that model provenance and uncertainty at every step must travel with records. Next steps use NASA G-LiHT's 15-year multi-sensor archive.
one_line_takeaway: Persistent organism identifiers for remotely sensed individual trees could turn repeat Earth-observation imagery into longitudinal biodiversity records, but only if uncertainty and model provenance travel with every record.
why_it_matters: Remote sensing could add millions of tree-level records to biodiversity infrastructures, and linking detections of the same individual over time is needed to capture growth, disturbance and loss.
key_points: Most remote-sensing workflows treat each acquisition separately, so one organism can appear in 10 datasets without an accumulated history.
GBIF fuzzy matching would probably not link observations of the same organism made a year apart (per conversation with Tim Robertson).
Test site NEON SJER (San Joaquin Experimental Range), an oak savanna deliberately outside DeepForest's typical use case.
Pipeline: high-resolution RGB → DeepForest crown delineation → candidate species constrained with NEON field records pulled via pygbif → provenance-rich occurrence export.
Detected crowns went from 222 in 2023 to 232 in 2024. IoU matching found overlaps but also persistent false detections of rocks and shadows.
A generic off-the-shelf cloud model identified all trees as one type; biodiversity constraints helped but also hurt a general model.
Output Darwin Core occurrences used occurrenceID, organismID, scientificName, identificationRemarks, identifiedBy = AI and basisOfRecord = MachineObservation.

Next: NASA G-LiHT (LiDAR, hyperspectral, thermal; nine sensors; 15-year archive), site-specific models for Puerto Rico tropical, temperate mixed hardwood (Smithsonian) and Arctic boreal forests, and linking Landsat/EMIT pixels to individuals.
datasets: NEON vegetation structure records via GBIF
methods: uncertainty tracking at each pipeline stage
questions: Who should hold a registry of persistent identifiers for individual plants and trees?
What should identifiedBy contain for AI-generated identifications?

notable_claims.claim: The same organism can appear in 10 remote-sensing datasets without accumulating one connected history.
Crown detection found 222 crowns in 2023 and 232 in 2024 for the same area.
Model provenance is biodiversity data provenance because uncertainty can enter before identification, during preprocessing, segmentation or temporal matching.

recommendations: Carry model version, training ecology, operating domain and segmentation confidence with each record sent to aggregators.
results_findings: An off-the-shelf pipeline validated the workflow shape but produced results not good enough to publish (rocks and shadows as crowns, single-species identifications).
limitations: Proof of concept only, constrained to species in NEON survey records (cannot detect e.g. invasive species).
Off-the-shelf models performed poorly outside their domain.
Not colour-blind-friendly figures (acknowledged).
future_work: Apply to G-LiHT's 15-year archive and multiple forest biomes with site-specific models.
Include detection of species not in survey records.
examples_case_studies: NEON SJER oak savanna
Panama mangrove forest with airborne, Landsat and EMIT data

q_and_a.question: Given the precedent of unique animal IDs and a Digital Life History Museum registry (Movebank), who would hold the registry for individual plants/trees?
q_and_a.answer_summary: Lewers suggested a collaboration among remote-sensing agencies or a GBIF-like model where institutions running campaigns hold and push data, admitting the question was not fully answered; the chair suggested continuing the discussion and pointed to an Imageomics Institute innovation.

notable_moments.description: Remote sensing has a longitudinal biodiversity problem.
222 vs 232 crowns detected in consecutive years.
The 'useful failure' and why model provenance must travel with records.
Darwin Core output with identifiedBy 'AI' and MachineObservation.

title: On-Device AI for Data Cleaning, Standardisation, and Exploration in Collections Management

programme.title: On-Device AI for Data Cleaning, Standardisation, and Exploration in Collections Management
programme.session: SYM25A From Mobilizing Data to AI-Ready Knowledge: Infrastructure for Multimodal Biodiversity Data
programme.abstract: Museums operate across a diverse landscape of legacy data systems and formats, reflecting the long history of collections management and digitisation efforts. These include heterogeneous database structures, varied metadata standards, and unstructured or semi-structured records derived from historical catalogues and specimen labels. A key component of ongoing work is the standardisation and transformation of these legacy data into consistent, interoperable formats aligned with modern biodiversity data standards. This presentation focuses on the use of local/on-device AI systems to support the cleaning, standardisation and exploration of collections dataspread across legacy systems, including collections management records, storage location data, specimen locality information, geographic coordinates and bibliographic references. We demonstrate how AI can be applied to transform unstructured and semi-structured records into consistent, interoperable data aligned with modern biodiversity standards. Using dedicated hardware such as Dell GB10 systems and high-performance development devices, the platform provides AI-assisted suggestions for improving data quality, identifying inconsistencies and highlighting missing or ambiguous information across both collections management systems and exported datasets. It also enables interactive exploration, allowing users to query, interrogate and summarise collections data in real time.This allows the platform to generate summarised insights, identify patterns and relationships, and highlight areas requiring further curation or standardisation. A live demo will show how local AI systems can support large-scale data transformation and contribute to the development of standardised, high-quality and AI-ready collections data.

actual.identification_notes: Programme lists only Jack Hollister; the talk was a 'double act' with an unnamed IT project manager who is building NHM's new CMS and gave the introduction and conclusions. ASR renders GB10 as 'GP10', Nemotron as 'Nematron', DiSSCo as 'DISCO' and 'verbatim string' as 'vibitamin string'; 'medium accuracy' means median error. The main commenter works at the Florida Museum. Speaker label “Unnamed co-presenter (IT project manager building the NHM collections management system)” is indexed as “Unidentified co-presenter”; see the correction record for the reason.

summary: Jack Hollister and an NHM colleague tested whether local LLMs on borrowed Dell GB10 hardware (two clustered units, models up to ~400B parameters) could clean legacy collections data. They held out about 10% of records as test data. Using NVIDIA Nemotron Super with a custom prompt and harness, 24-hour runs recovered missing countries for over 4,000 site records (about 80% correct). Title recovery for bibliography records was hampered by websites blocking LLM scraping. Georeferencing about 6,500 localities gave a median error of about 5.3 km. Scaling to the 6.4 million DiSSCo UK records lacking coordinates would take over 1,000 days on GB10s. A GB300 workstation (~£100,000) ran 100 concurrent models to process a deduplicated 4.2 million records in 9.1 days (median ~12 km). They stressed that validation, side-by-side storage of enrichments and local 'token economics' are the key open issues.
one_line_takeaway: Local LLM hardware can clean and enrich millions of legacy collection records at predictable cost, but validation of the outputs is the unsolved problem.
why_it_matters: Museums hold large amounts of incomplete legacy data that are sensitive or costly to send to cloud APIs. On-premises AI with a safe institutional sandbox offers a different cost and governance model.
key_points: The idea is to bring AI onto local hardware rather than the cloud, giving researchers a safe environment to prototype. NHM IT initially refused agents, which led the museum to build a safer isolated infrastructure.

Three 24-hour experiments on full data loads: sites (~700,000 records, 58 columns, recover missing country), bibliography (missing titles, 113 fields, ~60,000 records), GPS (6.2 million records, 4.4 million without usable coordinates).
About 10% of records with known answers were held out as test data.

They tested Qwen and open GPT models and chose NVIDIA Nemotron Super. The prompt defines the task and allowed evidence; the harness prepares data, calls the model and checks output. 'The LLM is only a small part of the system.'
Country recovery: over 4,000 records in 24 h, ~80% exactly correct on test data, ambiguous cases rejected; the full set would take 46 days.
Bibliography: 2,300 records examined, 66 duplicates found, but only 125 titles recovered because websites block LLM scraping.
Georeferencing: ~6,500 records in 24 h with ~5.3 km median error. DiSSCo UK has ~6.4 million records with verbatim localities but no coordinates, which would need over 1,000 days on GB10s.

GB300 (~£100,000) ran 100 concurrent Nemotron instances at ~22,000 records/hour, processing a deduplicated 4.2 million records (incl. 2.7 million test records with coordinates) in 9.1 days, with ~12 km median error.
datasets: NHM sites, bibliography and GPS data
DiSSCo UK records with verbatim localities lacking coordinates
questions: How can millions of AI-generated coordinates be validated before being fed back into a CMS?

Benchmark AI against human performance (from Q&A).

Optimised laptop-scale workflows (a separate talk the next day).

DiSSCo UK georeferencing at scale

q_and_a.answer_summary: They considered adding tools but wanted to test local models alone; other tools could do or validate the job, and their next talk uses an optimised laptop setup focused on what the model is good at.

title: FAIR, CLEAR, and Causal: A semantic framework for ecological knowledge synthesis

programme.title: FAIR, CLEAR, and Causal: A semantic framework for ecological knowledge synthesis
programme.session: SYM25A From Mobilizing Data to AI-Ready Knowledge: Infrastructure for Multimodal Biodiversity Data
programme.abstract:
Ecological synthesis produces knowledge that is human-interpretable but rarely machine-actionable. Attempts to address this through RDF/OWL-based semantic representations introduce a new problem: structures become opaque even to domain experts. We present the Semantic Units Framework, a modular approach to structuring ecological data and knowledge as logic-aware, independently addressable units aligned with the FAIR (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, Reusable) and CLEAR (Cognitively interoperable, semantically Linked, contextually Explorable, easily Accessible, human-Readable and -interpretable) Principles.

The central contribution is embedding causal knowledge within this architecture. Universal causal statement units encode causal hypotheses as addressable graph entities forming a navigable semantic grid, like a spatial map, to which evidence, publications, and contextual qualifiers can be anchored. Individual observations can be linked to causal hypotheses they support or contradict, enabling queries such as “Which data support this causal claim?” This supports semi-automated causal reasoning, confounder detection, and AI-ready evidence-gap maps.

The framework decomposes knowledge graphs into (a) statement units as single propositions with a persistent identifier, provenance, and method links and (b) compound units grouping related statement units into reusable knowledge objects, both serializable as nanopublication FAIR Digital Objects. Machine-interpretable structures are decoupled from human-facing representations via dynamic labels and graphs, keeping OWL/RDF accessible without specialist knowledge. Currently conceptual with partial prototypes, we invite discussion toward its community-driven realisation.

He introduced universal causal statement units with their own identifiers, provenance and asserted/not-asserted status, so contradictory claims can coexist without logical inconsistency. Paths, networks and causal perspectives get addresses in a 'semantic grid', like map addresses. title: Mobilising and integrating extracted information from the literature into a biodiversity data ecosystem - the BIOfid approach

programme.title: Mobilising and integrating extracted information from the literature into a biodiversity data ecosystem - the BIOfid approach
programme.session: SYM25B From Mobilizing Data to AI-Ready Knowledge: Infrastructure for Multimodal Biodiversity Data
programme.abstract:
Insufficient data availability is a critical bottleneck for biodiversity research. The fact that countless species are going extinct before they can even be collected and described is a particularly alarming aspect of our lack of knowledge and data. Another aspect is that vast quantities of data already exist but remain largely inaccessible-namely, data locked in unstructured, unindexed literature. These biodiversity data must be urgently mobilized to support research. The term 'mobilization' can take on different meanings. The most basic approach is to digitize printed publications and make them freely available online, allowing them to 'circulate globally' and allowing their content be discovered through keyword searches. However, since the vocabulary, organism names, and geographic terms used in publications vary considerably over time, normalization is essential to enable both efficient searches and integration with other data sources.

This normalization is achieved through annotation based on generic and domain-specific standards, with TDWG playing a central role in defining the latter. Two examples illustrate this: Only when species names are linked to a taxonomic backbone like GBIF’s, and when terms for morphological traits are connected to TraitBank, can researchers efficiently explore the wealth of data on a species’ characteristics hidden in literature-despite its heterogeneity in language, publication year, or writing style. Against this background, this presentation demonstrates how the Discipline-Specific Information Service Biodiversity Rersearch (BIOfid) addresses these challenges and how biodiversity data from the BIOfid corpus can be transformed into a graph-compatible format and made robot-ready for AI applications.

title: Camtrap DP: extending data standard designed for camera trapping research to support AI workflows and new data sources

programme.title: Camtrap DP: extending data standard designed for camera trapping research to support AI workflows and new data sources
programme.session: SYM25B From Mobilizing Data to AI-Ready Knowledge: Infrastructure for Multimodal Biodiversity Data
programme.abstract:
Passive sensor monitoring is generating multimodal biodiversity data at unprecedented scale. As AI becomes central to processing these datasets, standards must evolve to capture not only what was observed, but how, preserving the full provenance of human and machine annotations.

Camtrap DP is an open data exchange standard for camera trap data, developed under TDWG. Built on the Frictionless Data framework, it natively integrates AI-relevant data (bounding boxes, classification probabilities, method attribution and model name). With multiple datasets published via GBIF, it has demonstrated clear value for interoperable, research-ready wildlife monitoring data.

Expanding adoption has now exposed important gaps. The Safe and Sound bioacoustics project and the Insect AI community - both evaluating Camtrap DP as a candidate standard for their data - highlight shared needs alongside feedback from traditional camera trap users: including more expressive hardware description, flexible recording schedule specification, and richer support for AI-generated data.

While the framework's flexibility permits ad-hoc extensions, community-wide standardization is essential to ensure data remains FAIR and comparable across projects. We are therefore developing a new version of Camtrap DP that formalizes these needs through new standardized tables covering AI model provenance and the complete record of detections and annotations, rather than only final consensus results.

We present the community consultation process driving these developments and the proposed changes to the data model and controlled vocabularies, situating this work within the broader challenge of evolving domain-specific standards to meet a rapidly changing, AI-driven data landscape.

programme.title: FAIR² Drones: An AI-Ready Standard for Cross-Domain Wildlife Drone Dataset
programme.session: SYM25B From Mobilizing Data to AI-Ready Knowledge: Infrastructure for Multimodal Biodiversity Data
programme.abstract: Animal ecology data collection using drones requires a substantial investment of time, expertise, and financial resources. Yet most existing datasets serve only a single research community, limiting interdisciplinary reuse. We propose a unified drone dataset standard, FAIR² Drones, that bridges ecology, robotics, and computer vision by building on existing FAIR and AI-ready data frameworks while adding essential platform metadata and annotation specifications. Our standard enables datasets to simultaneously support ecological analysis, robotics algorithm development, and computer vision model training and benchmarking. We provide open-source validation tools, reference implementations, and multimodal extensions linking drone imagery with complementary sensors, such as camera traps, GPS, and acoustics. By standardizing metadata across disciplines, this framework maximizes the scientific return on investment for costly field deployments and accelerates cross-domain collaboration in environmental monitoring.

title: Causal Mosaic Schema: Encoding Causal Claims in Ecological Literature as Machine-Actionable Knowledge Graphs

programme.title: Causal Mosaic Schema: Encoding Causal Claims in Ecological Literature as Machine-Actionable Knowledge Graphs
programme.session: SYM25B From Mobilizing Data to AI-Ready Knowledge: Infrastructure for Multimodal Biodiversity Data
programme.abstract:
Ecological evidence synthesis increasingly relies on large language models to extract knowledge. Yet most extraction pipelines discard the very information that makes causal claims scientifically defensible: what type of evidence supports the claim, how strong is it, and what kind of causal relationship is established. Without a schema that encodes these properties, extracted claims are superficially machine-readable but epistemically opaque.

Causal Mosaic is a LinkML schema that addresses this gap. It merges the Ecolink Model (ELM) entity structure with an annotation framework based on Illari and Russo’s "causal mosaic" approach. We represent causation as a relation between state changes. Each causal node decomposes into an entity, a measurable attribute, and a direction of change. Each edge carries four annotation layers: claim strength, philosophical account of causation (mechanistic, interventionist, probabilistic, and others), fifteen features that further characterize the causal relationship, and an evidential basis grounded in the view that mechanistic and probabilistic evidence is jointly required to establish causation.

The schema produces a single canonical labeled property graph renderable as natural language (cf. Rosetta Statements), Fuzzy Cognitive Maps, Evidence Gap Maps, and RAG retrieval indices. Edges are grounded in source text spans and carry full provenance, supporting round-tripping from graph back to literature.

We present the schema design, an LLM-assisted extraction pipeline validated against author-reviewed annotations, and a construct validity study for a DFG-funded expert elicitation workshop. Causal Mosaic enables biodiversity knowledge graphs that represent not just what causes what, but how we know it and how confident we should be.

actual.identification_notes: Speaker name rendered 'Tim Almen' by ASR; the chair earlier referred to a 'causal Bayesian schemas' talk. Co-author names are garbled (e.g. 'Lars Voet' = Lars Vogt). The questioner is unnamed.

summary: Tim Alamenciak opened with the Bandon Marsh restoration in Oregon, where re-flooding produced a salt marsh mosquito outbreak because restoration and mosquito ecology knowledge were siloed. He then presented the Causal Mosaic Schema, a LinkML labelled property graph schema based on Illari and Russo's mosaic view of causality. Nodes describe changes in ontology-grounded entities and attributes. Edges carry four annotation layers (claim strength and linguistic expression, philosophical account, 16 causal features, evidential basis) plus provenance, and annotation needs LLM assistance to scale. The resulting graph can feed evidence gap maps, fuzzy cognitive maps, Bayesian belief network structures and priors, and RAG for practitioners. He also set out its limits: no effect sizes, a Western-science and peer-reviewed-literature focus, and reliance on LLM annotation.
one_line_takeaway: Encoding how and how strongly the literature claims causation, not just what causes what, can link siloed ecological knowledge into decision-support tools for practitioners.
why_it_matters: Restoration and conservation decisions depend on causal knowledge scattered across disciplines. A schema that preserves evidential strength and provenance makes LLM-assisted synthesis more defensible.

title: LifeGate: Extending a Global Visual PhyloMap into a Structured Biodiversity Knowledge System

programme.title: LifeGate: Extending a Global Visual PhyloMap into a Structured Biodiversity Knowledge System
programme.session: SYM25B From Mobilizing Data to AI-Ready Knowledge: Infrastructure for Multimodal Biodiversity Data
programme.abstract:
LifeGate (https://lifegate.idiv.de/) is a biodiversity information platform centered on the “PhyloMap”, a visual representation of biodiversity that enables exploration of taxa across multiple hierarchical levels of the Tree of Life. Unlike conventional biodiversity portals based mainly on text search, the PhyloMap provides a navigable overview of phylogenetic relationships from kingdoms to species. The platform integrates taxonomy, images, phylogenetic information, and links to biodiversity literature.

A new project aims to transform LifeGate into a structured and interoperable biodiversity knowledge system by converting descriptive taxonomic knowledge into machine-interpretable biodiversity data. We combine ontology-based modeling, biodiversity knowledge graphs, and AI-assisted information extraction workflows. Domain-specific templates and OWL ontologies are being developed to represent morphological, ecological, and taxonomic characteristics and to support semantic integration with infrastructures such as GBIF.

The workflow integrates expert curation with semi-automated extraction from taxonomic literature using natural language processing and large language models. Extracted entities and relationships are validated through ontology constraints before integration into the LifeGate knowledge graph. A major long-term objective is the development of structured, visually supported identification and faceted search workflows derived from taxonomic descriptions and trait information.

This contribution presents the existing PhyloMap and its extension toward structured biodiversity knowledge integrating visualization, semantic interoperability, and AI-assisted curation.

summary: The SYM25 speakers took questions on AI-ready biodiversity data, moderated by Hilmar Lapp. Panellists agreed that AI-readiness depends on purpose, like fitness for use. That is why FAIR4AI is distinguished from task-specific AI-readiness, though aggregation mixes purposes and shared benchmark snapshots remain valuable. On benefits to data providers, Tanya Berger-Wolf described dataset-side 'recipes' for agents, identifiers propagating from the smallest data unit through aggregations, and a CyVerse/NEON pilot where models register their use against operationalised permissions. Asked what is hardest now, panellists named reluctance to open data to tech-giant harvesting, pushback in Latin America and Africa over data sovereignty and digital sequence information, and data heterogeneity as the root of AI bias. A GBIF voice countered with strong demand for open data in the BID programme and Indigenous data work. A final question on ontologies drew views on ontology governance, explainability and knowledge graphs as the part of LLM systems that users can control.

title: How Literature Services can Support & Benefit from Biodiversity Publication and Data Standards?

programme.title: How Literature Services can Support & Benefit from Biodiversity Publication and Data Standards ?
programme.session: CO5 Digital Tools for Data Discovery, Resolution and Exchange
programme.abstract:
Rapid growth of biodiversity literature makes it difficult to retrieve precise, relevant, and interoperable knowledge. Traditional bibliographic catalogues mainly rely on metadata and abstracts, limiting fine-grained discovery and large-scale reuse.

This presentation explores how literature services can support biodiversity publication and data standards. Using BiodiversityPMC, developed within the SIB Literature Services (SIBiLS), we demonstrate how structured, machine-readable publications enable advanced indexing, semantic enrichment and concept-based retrieval across heterogeneous sources.

The SIBiLS platform integrates taxonomic treatments from Plazi, biodiversity-related documents from Zenodo and full-text articles from biodiversity journals (e.g., EJT, Pensoft). By leveraging structured formats, persistent identifiers and domain ontologies, it transforms publications into AI-ready contents that can be cross-linked and queried at scale. We will also demonstrate how pre-computed literature selection through Triage supports Biodiversa+ communities.

Through simple examples, attendees will perform advanced searches via the web interface, explore semantic annotations and test selected API calls for programmatic access, including MCP calls from AI bots.

speakers.name: Patrick Ruch
speakers.affiliation: SIB Swiss Institute of Bioinformatics (SIB Literature Services)

summary: Patrick Ruch presented BiodiversityPMC, a SIB Literature Services front end that indexes MEDLINE, an extended PubMed Central including Pensoft and other non-PubMed journals, a supplementary-data index with about 24 million OCR'd images, Plazi treatments and Zenodo. It is a life-science-focused superset of PubMed. All content is pre-annotated with about 50 terminologies (close to nine million concepts), so vernacular names, synonyms and taxa normalise to identifiers. He showed concept-normalised question answering: an extractive mode that returns facts from papers (F1 above 70% for the top answer on a SQuAD-style benchmark) and a generative RAG mode that answers from a few retrieved documents, contrasted with verbose general chatbots. The generative mode was due to become public in October.

title: From NetCDF to Web Maps: Building an Open-Source Web GIS for Biodiversity Data Cubes

programme.title: From NetCDF to Web Maps: Building an Open-Source Web GIS for Biodiversity Data Cubes
programme.session: CO5 Digital Tools for Data Discovery, Resolution and Exchange
programme.abstract:
Essential Biodiversity Variables (EBVs) provide a standardized framework for monitoring global biodiversity change and supporting international biodiversity assessments. However, there is still a lack of accessible web-based infrastructures that allow multidimensional biodiversity datasets to be explored consistently across spatial and temporal scales. This limits the usability of biodiversity information for research, policy support, and decision-making.

In this presentation, we introduce the EBV Visualizer, a lightweight open-source Web GIS for the interactive exploration of biodiversity data cubes. The application complements the EBV Data Portal by enabling users to visualize and analyze multidimensional raster datasets directly in the browser. The visualizer is built entirely with open-source technologies using vanilla JavaScript, Leaflet.js for interactive web mapping, and Chart.js for temporal analytics and visualization. The backend infrastructure relies on THREDDS Data Server and ncWMS to serve NetCDF datasets efficiently through dynamic tile rendering and caching of multidimensional raster data.

The platform enables users to explore biodiversity variables across space, time, and thematic dimensions, while supporting interactive analyses such as temporal trends for countries, protected areas, or other regions of interest. By combining OGC data standards (netCDF, WMS) with lightweight web technologies, the EBV Visualizer lowers technical barriers to biodiversity data access and contributes to open, interoperable, and FAIR biodiversity infrastructures.

speakers.name: Christian Langer
speakers.affiliation: iDiv (German Centre for Integrative Biodiversity Research)

actual.identification_notes: The speaker said he had changed the title slightly but covered the same topic (the EBV Data Portal visualiser). ASR renders GEO BON as 'GeoBon', ncWMS as 'NCWMS/NC WMS', THREDDS as 'SWATS' once, and COG as 'Currant' (uncertain). Questioner self-identified as Guillaume Body, French Biodiversity Agency.

summary: Christian Langer presented the EBV Data Portal (portal.geobon.org) and its visualiser for Essential Biodiversity Variable data cubes. EBVs are modelled datasets that sit between raw observations and indicators, and the EBV Cube format stores them as NetCDF with metadata and four dimensions (x, y, time, entity). The portal offers a metadata catalogue, API, DOIs and versioning. The lightweight vanilla-JavaScript web GIS talks to a THREDDS server through ncWMS for map tiles (e.g. gorilla habitat suitability in 1990) and time series for trends in any user-defined region, with DAP4 chunked access. The cons are server limits for very high-resolution global layers (downscaled ×10 for display), THREDDS not being cloud-native (Zarr would be needed) and ncWMS not being a strict OGC WMS.
one_line_takeaway: A simple open-source stack of NetCDF, THREDDS/ncWMS and vanilla JavaScript makes multidimensional biodiversity data cubes browsable and analysable in the browser.
why_it_matters: EBVs are meant to link raw biodiversity data to policy indicators. Making their data cubes easy to explore spatially and over time lowers barriers for researchers and decision-makers.

The EBV Data Portal provides a searchable metadata catalogue, API, automatic DOIs and version control.

The visualiser uses THREDDS and ncWMS requests (GetMap for tiles, GetTimeSeries in JSON/CSV) from a vanilla JavaScript front end; parameters in the URL select metric, entity, time, CRS and bounding box.
Users can browse by entity, scenario, metric and time and calculate trends for any area of interest, e.g. a national park.

Pros: lightweight, open source, fast, DAP4 chunk access without downloading whole files. Cons: high-resolution global layers must be downscaled ×10 for display; THREDDS/NetCDF are not suited to S3/cloud storage; ncWMS is only OGC-compliant, not strict OGC WMS.

title: Local scientific name resolution using custom data sources

programme.title: Local scientific name resolution using custom data sources
programme.session: CO5 Digital Tools for Data Discovery, Resolution and Exchange
programme.abstract:
Scientific name verification is crucial for biodiversity informatics workflows, enabling researchers to reconcile name-strings against authoritative taxonomic databases, detect misspellings, resolve synonyms, and retrieve accepted names and vernacular names. GNverifier is a tool that provides this capability with high quality and a throughput exceeding 2,000 name-strings per second. For several years, it has operated exclusively as a centralized web service.

Here, we present GNverifier as an easily installed local application that supports custom datasets, including private ones, not available in the centralized service. Data can be seamlessly converted from Darwin Core Archives, CSV, TSV, pipe-delimited files, Catalogue of Life Data Packages, and plain scientific name-string text files.

This functionality is driven by two new applications: sf and gndb. The sf tool converts the aforementioned data formats into an intermediate Species File Group Archive (SFGA) format, which gndb then imports into the GNverifier database. While standard GNverifier datasets are downloaded automatically by gndb, custom and private datasets are imported directly from the local file system. Once the database is built, the local GNverifier instance exposes the same REST API and web interface as the centralized service, but provides the specific datasets required for a given research project. This enables workflows that demand strict data sovereignty or reproducibility.

GNdb is open-source under the MIT license at https://github.com/gnames/gndb. Pre-built binaries for Linux, macOS, and Windows are available on the releases page, and the tool can also be installed via 'go install' or compiled from source.

actual.identification_notes: Pre-recorded video played after the moderator could not find the scheduled 4:30 talk's recording. Speaker name rendered 'Dima Mazarin' and GNverifier as 'Gen vérifier' by ASR; SFGA/sfwork rendered 'SF WORK'. No Q&A.

summary: Dmitry Mozzherin presented GNverifier, a scientific name reconciliation tool with fuzzy, partial and authorship matching, over 80 million pre-indexed records from more than 100 datasets, and throughput above 2,000 names per second. It can now run locally as well as at verifier.globalnames.org. Local use suits proprietary, institutional or specialised datasets, offline fieldwork, frequent updates and faster, slimmer databases. The new GNdb tool, part of the Species File Group's SFWork approach, ingests Species File Group Archive (SFGA) files. SFGA can be used directly without database conversion, and the sf and harvester programs produce it from Darwin Core archives, ColDP, CSV/TSV or plain name lists. This replaces error-prone ad-hoc parsing and ingests Catalogue of Life in minutes rather than hours.
one_line_takeaway: GNverifier can now be run locally over any custom or private name datasets, using the standardised SFGA format and GNdb, with the same API as the central service.
why_it_matters: Local, reproducible name verification against private or project-specific checklists supports data sovereignty and field use, a need that centralised services cannot meet.

title: Standardizing Multimodal Insect Monitoring Data for AI-Ready Pipelines: Lessons from an InsectAI Community Datathon

programme.title: Standardizing Multimodal Insect Monitoring Data for AI-Ready Pipelines: Lessons from an InsectAI Community Datathon
programme.session: CO6 AI Driven Monitoring and Species Identification
programme.abstract:
The growing availability of automated insect monitoring systems is capturing huge volumes of media containing insects. Translating these heterogeneous datasets into interoperable, AI-ready resources remains a major bottleneck for biodiversity research. Within InsectAI, an international network advancing AI for insect monitoring, we organized a community "datathon" - a hackathon for implementing data exchange standards. Teams mapped eleven datasets from platforms including Mothbox, Diopsis, Lepmon, and AMI traps to the Camtrap DP standard, producing (1) curated before/after examples, (2) concrete proposals to refine Camtrap DP, and (3) conversion scripts, templates, and documentation.

We summarize key data management challenges exacerbated by entomological sensors as "the five Cs": Certainty (confidently separating taxa from morphology or sound alone); Consensus (reconciling determinations from multiple experts and/or AI models); Counting (hundreds of insects entering and leaving the frame); Cropping (storing regions of parent media while retaining provenance); and Coverage (spatial, temporal, and taxonomic scope, crucial for quantifying sampling effort and true negatives).

We proposed targeted adaptations to Camtrap DP addressing each challenge, and reflect on how this community-driven process offered insights unlikely to emerge from a top-down approach. All datasets, scripts, templates, and documentation are openly available at https://github.com/InsectAI-COST-Action/example-datasets.

speakers.name: Jamie Alison
speakers.affiliation: Aarhus University; InsectAI COST Action Working Group 3

actual.identification_notes: Chair invites 'Jamie' as first speaker; speaker introduces himself as Jamie from Aarhus University representing InsectAI Working Group 3; content matches the abstract. Slide text failed to render during the talk, so the speaker presented largely from memory.

summary: Jamie Alison described an InsectAI community 'datathon' in which participants brought their own insect-camera datasets and tried to map them to the Camtrap DP standard, using a GitHub repository of mini-datasets with automated traffic-light progress reporting and the BioWatch tool as a reward for conformant data. He then set out the data challenges posed by insect sensing systems as a set of 'Cs' (consensus, cropping, counting, coverage and customisation), giving for each a recommendation for what can be done within Camtrap DP today and what might be added beyond it. His overall message was that Camtrap DP works well and should ideally not be changed much, but that the community needs ratified guidance on how to use it for insect data, with longer-term additions such as parent media IDs, track IDs, target taxonomic scope and an assertions table.
one_line_takeaway: Camtrap DP can largely accommodate automated insect monitoring data today, but the community needs agreed guidance and a few targeted extensions (track IDs, parent media and crop offsets, target taxonomic scope, identification provenance) to handle insect-specific challenges.
why_it_matters: Automated insect cameras produce huge, high-temporal-resolution datasets that could offer standardised, relatively unbiased biodiversity measurements, but only if the data can be shared in a common format; the datathon gives concrete, community-derived proposals for how an existing camera-trap standard can be stretched to cover them.
key_points: A datathon is like a hackathon but focused on converting real data rather than writing code; participants brought stratified 'mini datasets' and conversion code to a shared GitHub repository.

An automated GitHub traffic-light report on how many standardisation criteria each dataset met motivated participants; BioWatch, which reads Camtrap DP datasets, showed immediate payoff from standardising.

Consensus: many human and machine agents now identify the same media; within Camtrap DP use the classifiedBy field, and beyond it proposed detections and pipelines (models) tables capture agent provenance; for now avoid multiple determinations per individual within a dataset.

Cropping: retain media with no observations in the media table (they define temporal scope) and record the parent media ID of crops, e.g. in media comments now, with a future parent media ID and bounding-box offsets in the media table.

Counting: insects coming and going make Camtrap DP's summable event-based observations hard to apply; recommendation is to use eventID for tracks for now and avoid individualID, with a longer-term 'track ID' concept sitting between event and media-based observation.

Coverage: Camtrap DP's taxonomic descriptor describes what a dataset contains, not what was searched for; recording target taxonomic scope and invalid samples enables true negatives, possibly by absorbing Humboldt Extension terminology.

Customisation: diverse monitoring systems should be captured as distinct sampling protocols, and extra data can be added as frictionless resources keyed to existing tables, but best-practice guidance is lacking; an assertions table from the Safe and Sound acoustics project is a candidate.
Many of these issues are long-standing in other sensing modalities, so the community should prioritise which are worth pushing forward.

programme.session: CO6 AI Driven Monitoring and Species Identification
programme.abstract: Automated biodiversity monitoring can deliver repeatable, high-throughput observations across sites and years, but only if standardization extends beyond field methods into the data infrastructure itself. In practice, images, locality information, detections, taxonomic predictions, human annotations, expert validations, and quality-control decisions are often fragmented across files, spreadsheets, and project-specific workflows. This fragmentation increases harmonization costs, weakens comparability, and limits the creation of trustworthy AI-ready biodiversity data. The LAUP software stack, developed for the German LEPMON project, addresses this by linking deployments, localities, media records, detections, AI-assisted classifications, human annotations, expert review, and publication outputs in one traceable workflow. Rather than treating standards as a final export step, LAUP makes structured curation, provenance tracking, and quality control part of routine operations. This preserves context, supports corrections, and documents how records change over time. A key extension is the integration of Camtrap DP as a core standard for data exchange and reuse. The aim is not merely to generate a Camtrap DP export at the end of the workflow, but to reflect its key concepts in the data infrastructure itself: by aligning deployments, media, and organism records with Camtrap DP concepts LAUP produces machine-actionable outputs that are easy to integrate into downstream analytical pipelines. We present LAUP as a practical bridge between standardized field monitoring, non-standardized data realities, and AI-ready biodiversity knowledge infrastructure, showing how domain-specific systems can turn raw image streams into curated, comparable, and reusable biodiversity evidence.

He described the LAUP (LepMon Annotation and Upload) portal, which couples AI localisation and classification, citizen-science annotation and expert validation, and demonstrated a new map-based filter and download that exports data as a Camtrap DP package, with crops referenced as IIIF URLs rather than stored derivatives.

programme.abstract:
This study evaluates a spatially explicit, ecosystem-based framework across 35 Biodiversity Protection Areas (BPAs) in Saudi Arabia. The network spans diverse ecosystems, from the hyper-arid Rub' al Khali, supporting reintroduced populations of Arabian Oryx, Sand Gazelles, and Red-necked Ostrich, to the high-altitude Abha BPA, a global biodiversity hotspot currently undergoing Nubian Ibex reintroduction. Coastal and marine sites further protect Red Sea mangrove forests, sea turtle breeding grounds, and Arabian Gulf marine megafauna.

Ecological assessments have recorded 906 species, including 44 native and 189 avian species, with 26 taxa listed on the IUCN Red List. Key fauna include the Arabian Striped Hyena, Asir Magpie, Arabian Wolf, and various shark and fish species. Integrated monitoring utilizes a technological stack comprising satellite transmitters, camera traps, Remote Sensing (RS), GIS, and Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs) to facilitate high-resolution population assessments. Strategically located within the African-Eurasian flyways, these BPAs also serve as vital stopovers for billions of migratory birds, including the threatened Socotra Cormorant and Steppe Eagle. This model demonstrates how advanced technology and spatial prioritization can effectively safeguard global biodiversity across complex, high-value ecosystems.

title: Evaluating Four Machine Learning Using Google Earth Engine for Analyzing LULC Dynamics of Sandwip Island, Bangladesh

programme.title: Evaluating Four Machine Learning Using Google Earth Engine for Analyzing LULC Dynamics of Sandwip Island, Bangladesh
programme.session: CO6 AI Driven Monitoring and Species Identification
programme.abstract: Sandwip Island is a highly dynamic coastal environment experiencing continuous geomorphological changes driven by erosion, accretion, and sediment deposition. This study analyses shoreline changes from 1995 to 2026 using the Digital Shoreline Analysis System (DSAS) in ArcGIS and evaluates Land Use Land Cover (LULC) changes from 2000 to 2024 using Google Earth Engine and machine learning algorithms, including Classification and Regression Tree, Gradient Boosting Trees, Random Forest, and Support Vector Machines. A total of 140 ground-truth points representing seven LULC classes were used to assess model accuracy. Among the models, RF demonstrated the highest overall accuracy (93.57%), producing clearer boundaries and better separation of major land-cover classes. GBT achieved an accuracy of 92.14%, showing reliable classification across most LULC types. SVM reached a moderate accuracy of 90%, although some overgeneralization was observed in spectrally similar classes. CART showed the lowest accuracy (87.14%), with increased mixed-pixel occurrence in dense and heterogeneous regions. The findings reveal a gradual increase in the total area of Sandwip Island due to sediment deposition, contributing to the expansion of sandy areas (61.628 km²), mangroves (27.412 km²), vegetation (58.618 km²), cropland (31.587 km²), and built-up areas (60.031 km²). These results highlight the significant influence of natural coastal processes on land-cover dynamics and demonstrate the effectiveness of remote sensing and machine learning techniques for monitoring dynamic coastal environments. The study further suggests that integrating sediment transport modeling and tidal-current analysis with machine learning approaches could improve the accuracy of future coastal change assessments.

title: The Planetary Knowledge Base: an infinite solutions engine converting data into action for nature

programme.title: The Planetary Knowledge Base: an infinite solutions engine converting data into action for nature
programme.session: SYM47A Large Language Models for Biodiversity Data Discovery, Integration, and Curation. Part A: AI- enabled knowledge creation and extraction
programme.abstract:
The accelerating nature crisis demands more than fragmented evidence and retrospective reporting. It requires trusted systems that can turn biodiversity knowledge into action. The Planetary Knowledge Base (PKB), led by the Natural History Museum, is being developed as an AI-enabled global infrastructure to meet that need. Its success will depend on wider community participation, bringing together collections institutions, researchers, source communities, data infrastructures and users to ensure biodiversity evidence is connected, governed and applied in reciprocal ways. The PKB combines a biodiversity foundation model, trained across literature, specimen records, observations, images and genetic and environmental data, with a provenance-aware knowledge graph linking species, specimens, traits, interactions and change.

This emerging neuro-symbolic architecture is designed to extract information at planetary scale while grounding every inference in traceable evidence. Through retrieval-augmented generation, APIs and natural-language interfaces, the PKB aims to make biodiversity knowledge accessible to researchers, policymakers, communities and businesses, while reducing hallucination and opaque AI decision-making.

The PKB is conceived as an infinite solutions engine. This living infrastructure that can absorb data, test hypotheses, identify relationships and support scenario exploration for nature-positive decisions. Coupled with ecological modelling, it is intended to move from evidence synthesis to intervention design, evaluating restoration, migration and resilience planning. By linking centuries of natural history evidence with AI, digitisation and global data networks, the PKB seeks to transform collections into actionable intelligence for planetary stewardship.

programme.abstract: There are over 120 million objects housed in natural history collections in the UK. With DiSSCo UK, 90+ institutions will be coming together, in order to make over 50% of UK natural history collections digitally available and accessible. As well as specimen imaging, a crucial goal is the building of datasets extracted from the millions of textual records. These records can include labels and index cards associated with specimens, collection registers and more. Our aim is to provide a service to aid the automatic extraction of structured data from collection records. SCRIBE (Structured Collection Record Interpretation and Bio-entity Extraction) is a new platform, being developed by a team at the NHM UK for automatic data extraction. The proposed software has the potential to revolutionise data extraction, for curation, as well as ecological analysis, by utilising Artificial Intelligence (AI), and providing an easy-to-use interface, to help unlock a plethora of data. While traditionally this task would involve manual transcription, or traditional OCR methods, taking up days and weeks, the proposed tool will for some collections, reduce this to minutes. The tool follows a computer vision and LLM based workflow that utilises customised prompts depending on visual differences within images uploaded by users, enabling users to upload datasets from varied collections concurrently. SCRIBE is a DCMS (UK Department for Culture, Media, Sport) funded and externally-funded program that will sit within the DiSSCo UK workflows. The software will be shared with institutions and evaluations will be jointly collected to further improve the online tool. Finally, the SCRIBE online tool will be supported in-house, helping to scale AI-assisted digitisation across museum and heritage sectors.

title: From Historical Oology Cards to Structured Biodiversity Data: Multimodal LLM Transcription, Uncertainty Metrics, and Human Review

programme.title: From Historical Oology Cards to Structured Biodiversity Data: Multimodal LLM Transcription, Uncertainty Metrics, and Human Review
programme.session: SYM47A Large Language Models for Biodiversity Data Discovery, Integration, and Curation. Part A: AI- enabled knowledge creation and extraction
programme.abstract:
Historical biodiversity collections contain vast quantities of ecological information embedded in handwritten and typed archival records that remain difficult to access at scale. This project explored the use of multimodal large language models (LLMs) to transcribe and structure oological information found in historical specimen cards from the Cornell University Museum of Vertebrates. These cards record collectors' data associated with bird egg sets, breeding phenology, nest materials, and habitat descriptions collected between the late 19th and mid-20th centuries.

Using GPT-4o and Clause Sonnet 4.6-based workflows, I evaluated methods for extracting both literal transcriptions and semantically structured biodiversity data from heterogeneous card layouts containing handwriting, typewriting, annotations, and mixed narrative content. Beyond transcription accuracy, my project investigates methods for estimating review effort and transcription reliability using token-level uncertainty signals and a human-in-the-loop validation workflow. I developed a "hesitation" score based on token-level probabilities and found that this score correlates with human correction effort and may support scalable triage of records requiring expert review.

This project demonstrates how historical narrative records can become machine-actionable biodiversity data while preserving provenance, interpretability, and curatorial oversight. I discuss implications for biodiversity data mobilization and the integration of semantically enriched collection records into standards-based biodiversity infrastructures.

summary: Grete Pasch transcribed historical oology (egg-set) cards with GPT-4o and used token log-probabilities to build a 'hesitation' score. The score does not flag every error, but it predicts how much human review a card needs. Cards were sorted into light, standard and expert review lanes; the expert lane held about a fifth of the cards but took half to two-thirds of the correction time, on both the Cornell set and 2,303 Western Foundation cards. Newer models (Gemini 3.1 Pro, Opus 5) are more accurate but do not expose log-probs; where two of them agree they are right about 997 times in 1,000, but that still does not certify a transcription.
one_line_takeaway: Token-level hesitation from log-probabilities does not tell you which transcriptions are wrong, but it reliably predicts where human review effort will go.
why_it_matters: Most LLM transcription work stops at accuracy. This talk offers a practical way to triage expert review and estimate curation effort for millions of archival cards, and warns that the best models no longer expose the signals needed for it.
key_points: Nest descriptions on historical egg cards record changes in nest materials (e.g. plastic in modern Baltimore oriole nests), but they are rarely transcribed.
GPT-4o transcribed 193 of 262 cards exactly (about three in four). Typed cards were nearly perfect; handwritten cards were about two in three exact.
With logprobs enabled, the model reports its confidence in each token and its top alternatives. On a gull card it wrote '7,000' at 58% where the correct '2,000' was the runner-up at 27%.
A token counts as 'hesitant' when the top choice is less than 2.7 times as likely as the runner-up; the card hesitation score is the number of hesitant tokens.
Some cards with no hesitation still had errors (confident errors), so hesitation marks uncertainty, not correctness.
Three lanes (0-1, 2-4, 5+ hesitant tokens): median correction time was under a second in the light and standard lanes and 11 seconds in the expert lane.
The pattern held on 2,303 harder handwritten cards from the Western Foundation of Vertebrate Zoology.
Gemini 3.1 Pro and Opus 5 read about nine in ten cards correctly and agree on 98.5% of words, but even agreement is not proof.
datasets: Western Foundation of Vertebrate Zoology handwritten cards (2,303)
questions: If frontier models no longer expose log-probs, what uncertainty signal can guide review?

Use GPT-4o or open-weight models run locally if log-probability signals are needed.

title: Using Large Language Models to enhance biodiversity knowledge extraction: From taxonomic treatments to graph-based knowledge systems

programme.title: Using Large Language Models to enhance biodiversity knowledge extraction: From taxonomic treatments to graph-based knowledge systems
programme.session: SYM47A Large Language Models for Biodiversity Data Discovery, Integration, and Curation. Part A: AI- enabled knowledge creation and extraction
programme.abstract:
Taxonomic treatments contained in checklists, floras, monographs and ecological literature compile centuries of detailed documentation on the world’s biodiversity. They typically appear as structured, peer-reviewed sections within scientific publications describing the taxonomy, morphology, distribution and ecology of a taxon, representing valuable and authoritative resources on past and present biodiversity.

Although a large collection of treatments is now freely available as Findable, Accessible, Interoperable and Reusable (FAIR) digital objects, ecological information contained within these data, such as habitat notes, remains largely underutilised, leaving untapped a vital source of knowledge for ecological modelling and conservation assessment.

Here, we present a practical framework for structuring, extracting and mapping habitat information stored in taxonomic treatments using an Artificial Intelligence (AI)-assisted, ontology-aware knowledge graph system (a formal, machine-readable representation of domain entities and their relationships). This work forms part of a broader initiative aimed at improving the mapping of data-poor species, with a focus on vascular plants.

We propose to (a) create a knowledge graph to store evidence related to plant species habitats, (b) link this graph with semantic environmental and geospatial layers, and (c) connect this system to a large language model (LLM) to automate, query and reason over this complex knowledge base.

By reducing hallucinations and linking extracted habitat information to spatial layers, we demonstrate a viable pathway towards more reliable and transparent geospatial AI applications, supporting a more responsible use of generative AI for species distribution and habitat mapping.

actual.identification_notes: Introduced as 'Yann Ondoh' and thanked as 'Ian'; he gives his affiliation as UNEP-WCMC. Content matches the abstract. Talk was compressed and later slides skipped.

summary: Ian Ondo presented a framework that turns habitat information in taxonomic treatments into a structured, evidence-traceable knowledge base. Plazi TreatmentBank RDF becomes a source graph; an instruction-tuned LLM (Qwen 2.5) extracts explicit habitat statements into an evidence graph; the evidence is linked to environmental ontologies, WWF/One Earth terrestrial ecoregions and IUCN habitat classes. A trained habitat-environment compatibility model (HECC) put the correct ecoregion in its top three 75% of the time (top five 87%), and 65% zero-shot. A data-deficient Dalbergia species showed that the model's most compatible ecoregions matched its few known GBIF occurrences.
one_line_takeaway: Taxonomic treatments hold underused habitat knowledge that LLMs and a provenance-preserving knowledge graph can structure and link to ecoregions, helping map data-poor species.
why_it_matters: There is no comprehensive resource for species habitat preferences. Mining treatments with traceable evidence could support conservation assessments of data-deficient species.
key_points: Plazi's TreatmentBank has made over 1.2 million treatments from about 94,000 articles machine accessible, but their ecological content is not immediately reusable.
There are structured resources for taxonomy and occurrences, but nowhere comprehensive to ask what habitat a species prefers.
Framework: TreatmentBank RDF -> source graph (publication and treatment structure) -> AI habitat extraction -> evidence graph -> integration with environmental and spatial knowledge.
Existing standards and ontologies are reused wherever possible rather than new vocabularies.
Qwen 2.5 is prompted to extract only explicit habitat statements, not to infer from altitude, place names or coordinates, and to return nothing when there is none.
Around 40,000 treatment sections were processed. HECC, an embedding model, learns semantic compatibility between habitat text and ecoregion descriptions.
Ecoregion retrieval: correct in top 3 75%, top 5 87%; zero-shot ecoregions 65%.
questions: How should free-text habitat descriptions be normalised against ontologies such as ENVO?

notable_claims.claim: Over 1.2 million taxonomic treatments from about 94,000 articles are now machine accessible through TreatmentBank.
There is no comprehensive resource to answer what habitats species prefer.
The compatibility model placed the correct ecoregion in the top three 75% of the time and top five 87%, dropping to 65% for unseen ecoregions.

results_findings: Top-3 ecoregion retrieval 75%, top-5 87%, zero-shot 65%.
For a data-deficient Dalbergia with four GBIF records, the most compatible ecoregions matched observed occurrences.
limitations: Performance drops for ecoregions not seen in training.
examples_case_studies: Data-deficient Dalbergia species (ASR 'Dalbergia menoides') from Thailand and the Malay Peninsula, habitat mangrove swamps along rivers

q_and_a.question: How is natural-language habitat text mapped to ecoregion categories? Is it normalised to ENVO first?
q_and_a.answer_summary: No intermediate normalisation. He trained an embedding model on ecoregion descriptions (from One Earth) and habitat text from treatments with known ecoregions, so it learns the semantics of how each ecoregion is described rather than name matching.
